editorialDecl.p: New English translation produced by the Falsafa project (Thothica) using an in-house agentic AI translation system, rendered from the Perseus source edition and reviewed by the project. Contributed to provide a translation for a work that previously had no English translation in the corpus.

div.p: As many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God, says the divine Apostle. And to be counted worthy of the Holy Spirit and to become sons of God is the last and highest of all things to be desired; once it is attained there is the repose from every contemplation, as it is written. This wonderful blessedness, then, the highest of all that can be longed for, the saints from the beginning of the ages were counted worthy to obtain through the practice of the virtues: some by struggling as martyrs and standing fast against sin even to the shedding of their blood, others by contending in the discipline of the ascetic life, walking the narrow road, and becoming martyrs in their resolve. Their feats of valour and their achievements

— both of those who were perfected through blood and of those who imitated the angelic life through ascetic discipline — to commit to writing, and to pass on a pattern of virtue to the generations that come after, the Church of Christ has received from the inspired Apostles and the blessed Fathers, who laid this down as a law for the salvation of our race. For the road that leads to virtue is rough and steep, especially for those who have not yet given themselves wholly to the Lord, but are still warred upon by the tyranny of the passions. For this reason we have need of many things that call us toward it: exhortations on the one hand, and on the other the histories of the lives of those who have travelled it before us, which more painlessly draws a man to it and prepares him not to despair at the difficulty of the journey. For when a man is about to set out on a road that is hard to pass and rough, one who advises and urges him on would persuade him less; but one who points out many who have already crossed it, and who in the end have rested well, would the more persuade him to lay hold of the journey himself. Following this rule, then, and besides this looking with apprehension at the danger that hangs over the servant who, having received the talent from his master, buried it in the ground and hid what was given for trading without putting it to use,

I shall by no means pass over in silence an edifying narrative that has come down to me; one that devout men of the inner country of the Ethiopians — those whom our account knows to call Indians — recounted to me, having translated it without falsehood from trustworthy records. It runs as follows.

The country called India lies far from Egypt, being large and densely peopled. On the side toward Egypt it is washed by seas and by waters that ships can sail; from the mainland it draws near to the borders of Persia. In ancient times it was darkened by the gloom of idol-madness, barbarous in the extreme and given over to lawless practices. But when the only-begotten Son of God, who is in the bosom of the Father, could not bear to see his own handiwork enslaved to sin, and was moved by his own inward compassion concerning it, he appeared among us in our likeness, yet without sin; and, without leaving the throne of the Father, he dwelt for our sake in a Virgin, that we might come to dwell in the heavens, and be called back from the ancient fall, and be delivered from sin, receiving back the adoption we had at first.

And when he had accomplished the whole dispensation in the flesh on our behalf — taking upon himself the cross and death, and, beyond all wonder, making one the things of earth with the things of heaven — and had risen from the dead and been taken up in glory into the heavens, and had sat down at the right hand of the majesty of the Father, he sent forth the Spirit, the Comforter, upon those who had been eyewitnesses of him and initiates of his mysteries, according to the promise, in the form of fiery tongues; and he sent them out into all the nations to give light to those sitting in the darkness of ignorance, and to baptize them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. So it was that some of them, having received the regions of the east as their portion and others those of the west, went about, and ran through the northern and southern climes, fulfilling the command laid upon them. At that time the most holy Thomas also, who was one of the company of twelve disciples of Christ, was sent out to the land of the Indians, proclaiming to them the saving message.

And as the Lord worked together with him and confirmed his word through the signs that followed, the darkness of their superstition was driven away; and, freed from the libations and abominations of the idols, they were joined to the unerring faith. Thus reshaped by the apostolic hands, they were made the household of Christ through baptism, and, growing by additions made little by little, they advanced in the faultless faith and built churches throughout all the regions. And when in Egypt too the monasteries began to be established and the multitudes of monks to be gathered together, and the fame of their virtue and their angelic manner of life spread to the ends of the inhabited world and came also to the Indians, it stirred these as well to the like zeal, so that many of them, leaving all things behind, took to the deserts and, in a mortal body, took up the way of life of the bodiless ones.

While matters stood thus well, and many, as the saying goes, were flying up to heaven on golden wings, there arose a certain king in that same country, Abenner by name. He had become great in wealth and in power and in victory over his adversaries; he was noble in war, and prided himself on the stature of his body together with the comeliness of his face, and gloried in all those advantages of the world that swiftly wither. But in his soul he was pressed by the utmost poverty and choked by many evils, for he belonged to the Greek party and was greatly excited about the superstitious error of the idols. Living in great luxury and in the enjoyment of the pleasant and delightful things of life, and deprived of nothing of his wishes and desires, he had one thing that cut short his gladness and struck his soul with anxieties: the evil of childlessness. For being without children, he was greatly concerned how, freed from such a bond, he might be called the father of children — a thing most to be prayed for by most men. Such was the king, and such was the state of his mind. But the most glorious race of the Christians and the multitudes of monks counted the king's worship as nothing, and, not fearing his threat at all, advanced by the grace of Christ, increasing to a number beyond words. They made little account of the king, but held fast above all to the things that lead to the service of God; and for this reason many of those who had taken up the monastic order spat alike upon all the delights of this place, and yearned with love for this one thing alone, godliness, and thirsted for death on behalf of Christ, and reached out for the blessedness that comes from thence.

They proclaimed, therefore, not with any fear or shrinking back, but with the fullest boldness of speech, the saving name of God; and nothing was on their lips but Christ. They plainly showed to all the fleeting and quickly-withering nature of present things, and the firm and incorruptible nature of the life to come, and they furnished, as it were, beginnings and seeds toward becoming the household of God and being counted worthy of the life that is hidden in Christ. From this many, enjoying that most sweet teaching, withdrew from the bitter darkness of deceit and were added to the sweet light of the truth; so that even some of the men of renown and of the senate laid aside all the burdens of life and became monks thereafter. But the king, when he heard these things, was filled with the greatest wrath and, boiling over with rage, at once set forth a decree to compel every Christian to forswear godliness. Hence he devised and practised new kinds of tortures against them, and threatened new manners of death. And letters were sent throughout all the country subject to him, to rulers and governors, pronouncing punishments and unjust slaughters against the godly. But raging most of all against the chosen ones of the monastic habit, he raised against them a truceless and herald-less war.

By this means many of the faithful were shaken in their mind, and others, unable to bear the tortures, yielded to his unlawful command. But the leaders and chiefs of the monastic order — some, reproving his lawlessness, endured the end that comes through martyrdom and attained the blessedness that never ceases; others hid themselves in deserts and mountains, not from fear of the tortures that were threatened, but by some more divine dispensation.

Such a moonless darkness, then, having fallen upon the land of the Indians, and the faithful being driven on every side while the shield-bearers of impiety grew strong — the very air itself being defiled by the blood and the reek of the sacrifices — one of the king's men, by rank a chief satrap, surpassed all the others in steadfastness of soul, in stature and beauty, and in everything else by which the bloom of the body and the noble courage of the soul are wont to be marked. When this man heard that impious decree, he bade farewell to that vain glory and luxury that drag a man downward, and mingled himself among the chosen ones of the monks, going beyond the borders into desert places. By fasting and by vigils and by the diligent study of the divine oracles he purified his senses most excellently, and his soul, freed from every passionate attachment, he made bright with the light of dispassion.

But the king, who loved this man greatly and held him in honour, when he heard these things, grieved in his soul at the loss of his friend, yet was kindled the more with anger against the monks. And so, sending everywhere in search of him, and leaving no stone unturned, as the saying goes, to find him out, after a considerable time those who had been sent in quest of him learned that he had his dwelling in the deserts, and, having searched him out and seized him, set him before the king's tribunal. When the king saw him in so poor and rough a garment — him who had once been clothed in splendid robes — and saw that one who had lived in great luxury was now withered by the hard regimen of the ascetic life, and plainly clad about with the marks of the desert life, he was filled at once with grief and with anger; and, mingling his speech from the two, he said to him: "O senseless and crazed man, for what reason have you exchanged honour for shame, and your splendid glory for this unseemly appearance? You, the chief of my kingdom and the commander-in-chief of my dominion, have made yourself a plaything of boys, not only consigning to far oblivion our friendship and freedom of speech, but rising up against nature itself, taking no pity even on your own children, and reckoning as nothing your wealth and all the renown of life,

preferring such great disgrace to your enviable glory. To what end is this for you? And what will you gain by it, that you have honoured the one called Jesus above all gods and men, and this hard, ill-clad way of life above the pleasant and enjoyable things of the sweetest life?" When that man of God heard these things, he answered gracefully and evenly: "If you wish to join speech with me, O king, put your enemies out of the court, and then I will answer you concerning whatever you may seek to learn; for while they are present with you, I have no word for you. But apart from speech, punish me, kill me, do what you will; for to me the world has been crucified, and I to the world, as my divine teacher says." And when the king said, "And who are these enemies whom you order me to put away?" the godly man said: "Anger and desire. For these were at first brought forth by the Creator as helpers of nature, and so they remain still for those who order their life not according to the flesh but according to the spirit; but in you, who are wholly flesh, having nothing of the spirit, they have become adversaries, and do the work of foes and enemies. For desire in you, when it is at work,

rouses pleasure, and when it is thwarted, anger. Let these, then, be far from you today; and let prudence and justice sit in their place, to hear and to judge what is said. For if you put anger and desire out of the way and bring in instead prudence and justice, I will tell you everything in the love of truth." To this the king said: "See, yielding to your request, I will cast desire and anger out of the council, and will make prudence and justice hold the middle place. Tell me now, without fear, whence came upon you so great an error, and this preferring of things resting on empty hopes to the things seen at hand." And the hermit answered and said: "If you seek the beginning, O king, of how it came to me to despise temporal things and to give my whole self to eternal hopes, listen. In days of old, while I was still quite young, I heard a certain good and saving word, and its power seized me utterly; and, like some divine seed, the memory of it was planted in my heart and kept inseparable forever, so that it took root and sprouted and bore in me the fruit you see. The power of that word was of this kind. 'It seemed good,' it says, 'to the senseless to despise the things that are as though they were not, and to cling to and hold fast the things that are not as though they were. He, then, who has not tasted the sweetness of the things that are will not be able to learn the nature of the things that are not; and not having learned it, how shall he despise them?' Now by 'the things that are' the saying meant the eternal and unshaken things, and by 'the things that are not' this present life and luxury and lying prosperity — to which, O king, alas, your heart is, for ill, nailed fast.

I too once clung to these things; but the power of that word, piercing my soul without ceasing, roused my ruling mind to the choice of the better. Yet the law of sin, warring against the law of my mind and binding me as with iron fetters, held me captive in attachment to present things. But when the kindness and goodness of God our Saviour was pleased to take me out of that grievous captivity, he strengthened my mind to overcome the law of sin, and opened my eyes to discern the worse from the better. Then indeed, then, I understood and saw, and behold, all present things are vanity and a striving after wind, as Solomon the most wise also says somewhere in his writings. Then was the veil of sin taken away from my heart, and the dimness laid upon my soul from the body's coarseness was scattered, and I knew for what I was made and that I must ascend to the Creator through the working of his commandments.

Therefore, leaving all things, I followed him; and I give thanks to God through Jesus Christ our Lord, that he rescued me from the clay and the brick-making, and from the harsh and ruinous ruler of the darkness of this age, and showed me a short and easy road, by which I shall be able, in this earthen body, to embrace the angelic way of life. Seeking to attain it, I chose to walk the narrow and afflicted road, utterly condemning the vanity of present things and their unstable course and whirl, and refusing to call anything else good before the good that truly is — from which you, O king, have pitiably been torn and have stood apart. Hence we too have stood apart from you and have been separated, because you are falling into clear and confessed ruin and are forcing us to be brought down into equal danger.

For so long as we were tried only in the warfare of the world, we fell short in none of our duties — you yourself will bear me witness that we were never charged with any slackness or negligence. But since you have striven to take away from us the very chief of good things, godliness, and to wrong us in God by this last and greatest loss, and on this account remind us of honours and ambition — how should I not justly say that you are ignorant of the good, since you set these things side by side at all, godliness toward God, I mean, against human friendship and a glory that flows away like water? And how shall we share with you in this, and not rather renounce friendship and honour and the love of children and whatever else is greater — seeing you, O king, ungrateful toward God, who himself grants you your very being and your breath, who is Christ Jesus, the Lord of all? He, being without beginning together with the Father and coeternal with him, and having set the heavens and the earth in place by his word, fashioned man with his own hands and honoured him with immortality and made him king of the things on earth, setting apart for him, as a kind of royal palace, the fairest of all things, paradise.

But man, beguiled by envy and lured — alas — by pleasure, wretchedly fell from all these things; and he who was before enviable was now seen to be pitiable and worthy of tears for his calamity. Therefore he who formed us and fashioned us, looking again with eyes of love upon the work of his own hands — without changing from being God, which he was from the beginning — became for our sake, without sin, what we are; and, willingly enduring the cross and death, he cast down the enemy who from the beginning had envied our race, and, rescuing us from that bitter captivity, in his love of good he restored our former freedom; and from where through disobedience we had fallen, there again through his love for mankind he led us back, counting us worthy of a greater honour than before. Him, then, who suffered such things for our sake and counted us worthy again of such things, you yourself set at nought and mock at his cross? And, wholly nailed to the luxury of the body and to ruinous passions, you proclaim as gods the idols of dishonour and shame? Not only have you made yourself a stranger to communion with the heavenly goods, but you have already torn away from it all who obey your commands,

and have handed them over to peril of soul. Know, then, that I will not obey you, nor will I share with you in such ingratitude toward God, nor will I deny my benefactor and Saviour, even if you give me to wild beasts, even if you hand me over to sword and fire, which are within your power. For I neither fear death nor desire present things, having utterly condemned their weakness and vanity. For what among them is useful, or lasting, or sufficient? And not this alone, but in their very existence there is bound up much misery, much grief, much and unbroken anxiety. For with their gladness and enjoyment is yoked every dejection and pain; their wealth is poverty, and their height the utmost lowliness. And who shall number their evils? — which my own theologian showed me in a few words. For he says: 'The whole world lies in the power of the evil one'; and, 'Do not love the world, nor the things in the world, for all that is in the world is the desire of the flesh and the desire of the eyes and the boasting of life'; and, 'The world is passing away, and the desire of it; but he who does the will of God abides forever.' Seeking this good will of God, I left all things and joined myself to those who possess the same longing and seek the same

God; among whom there is no strife or envy, no griefs or anxieties, but all run the same course, that they may attain the eternal dwellings which the Father of lights has prepared for those who love him. These I have gained as my parents, these as brothers, these as friends and acquaintances; but from those who were once my friends and brothers, I went far away in flight, and I lodged in the desert, waiting for God, who saves me from faint-heartedness and from the storm." When these things had been so fittingly and pleasantly set forth by the man of God, the king was moved by anger and wished to torment the saint bitterly; yet again he hesitated and put it off, out of regard for the man's dignity and renown. But he answered and said to him: "From every side, wretched man, you have studied your own destruction, driven to it, it seems, by fortune; you have whetted your mind and your tongue together, and so you have run through some obscure and idle babbling. And had I not at the beginning of our talk promised you to put anger out of the council, I would now have given your flesh to the fire. But since you took your precaution beforehand and secured yourself with such words, I bear with your insolence, for the sake of my former friendship toward you. Rise, then; flee henceforth from my eyes, that I may see you no more and destroy you cruelly."

And the man of God went out and withdrew into the desert, grieved that he had not been martyred, yet bearing witness day by day in his conscience and wrestling against the principalities and powers, against the world-rulers of the darkness of this age, against the spiritual forces of wickedness, as the blessed Paul says. Now when he had departed, the king, more angered, plotted a fiercer persecution against the monastic order, and counted the worshippers and temple-keepers of the idols worthy of still greater honour. While the king was in such dreadful error and deceit, a child was born to him, very beautiful, and from the very loveliness that bloomed upon him foreshadowing what was to come. For it was said that nowhere in that land had so charming and surpassingly beautiful a child ever appeared. Filled with the greatest joy at the birth of the child, the king named him Josaphat; and he himself went off senselessly to the idol-temples to sacrifice to those gods more senseless than himself and to render hymns of thanksgiving, not knowing who is truly the cause of all good things, to whom he ought to have offered the spiritual sacrifice. He, then, attributing the cause of the child's birth to things lifeless and deaf, sent everywhere to gather the multitudes for the child's birthday celebrations; and one could see them all flocking together in fear of the king, bringing the things prepared for the sacrifice, as each man's hand could afford and as his goodwill toward the king inclined. But most of all the king himself stirred them to rivalry,

bringing as many great bulls as possible to be slaughtered; and so, having held a festival for the whole people, he showered gifts upon all — upon those who were of the council and those in office, upon those of the army, and upon those who were common and obscure.

At the very festival of the child's birthday there came together to the king, chosen out, about fifty-five men who had devoted themselves to the star-gazing wisdom of the Chaldeans. Setting these very near him, the king asked each one to declare what the child born to him would become. They, after much deliberation, said that he would be great in wealth and in power, and would surpass all who had reigned before him. But one of the astrologers, the most distinguished of all who were with him, said: "From what the courses of the stars teach me, O king, the advancement of the child now born to you will not be in your kingdom, but in another, a better one and beyond all comparison surpassing it. And I think too that he will take hold of the religion of the Christians, which you persecute; nor do I suppose that he will be cheated of his aim and his hope." This the astrologer said, like Balaam of old — not because astrology spoke the truth, but because God set forth the things of the truth through its opposites, so that every pretext might be taken away from the impious.

When the king heard these things, he received the message heavily, and grief cut short his gladness. Nevertheless, in a city set apart he built a very beautiful palace and skillfully wrought splendid dwellings, and there he set the boy to live, after the completion of his early childhood; and he commanded that he should not go out, appointing for him tutors and attendants young in age and most comely to look upon, charging them to make none of the sorrowful things of life known to him — not death, not old age, not sickness, not poverty, nor anything else grievous and able to cut short his gladness — but to set before him all things delightful and enjoyable, so that his mind, taking pleasure and luxuriating in these, might be quite unable to reason about things to come, nor hear so much as a bare word concerning Christ and his teachings. For this above all things he was minded to hide from him, fearing the astrologer's prediction. And if any of those serving him happened to fall sick, he ordered that man to be cast out from there at once, and gave another in his place, vigorous and in good health, so that the boy's eyes might behold nothing whatever amiss. So the king devised and did these things; for, seeing, he did not see, and, hearing, he did not understand.

And learning that some of the monks still survived, of whom not even a trace had seemed to be left, he was filled to overflowing with rage and was moved most sharply against them; and he ordered heralds to run throughout the whole city and the country, crying aloud that after three days no one at all of the order of the monks should anywhere be found. And if any were found after the appointed days, let them be handed over to destruction by fire and sword; "for these," he said, "persuade the people to give heed to the crucified one as to God." Meanwhile something of this kind also happened, at which the king was the more harshly angered and enraged against the monks.

For there was a certain man in the palace, foremost among those in office, decent in his manner of life and godly in his faith; and, trading, so far as he could, for his own salvation, he kept it hidden for fear of the king. Hence some men, envying his freedom of speech with the king, set about slandering him, and made this their constant care. And once, when the king went out to the hunt with his usual bodyguard, this good man was among those hunting with him. As he walked alone — this happening, I think, by a divine dispensation — he found a man cast upon the ground in a thicket, his foot grievously crushed by a wild beast, who, seeing him pass by, entreated him not to hurry past, but to take pity on his misfortune and bring him to his own house, adding this also: "May I not be found," he said, "useless to you and altogether without effect."

That illustrious man said to him: "For the sake of goodness itself I will take you up and grant you such care as I am able; but what is the benefit which you said would come to me from you?" And that poor and feeble man said: "I am a man who heals words. For if ever in words or conversations some wound or hurt should be found, I will heal these with fitting remedies, that the evil may not go further." Now that godly man counted what was said as nothing, but for the commandment's sake ordered him to be brought home and did not deny him fitting care. But those envious and spiteful men mentioned before, bringing into the light the malice they had long been in labour with, slandered the man to the king, saying that, not only had he forgotten the king's friendship and slighted the worship of the gods and inclined toward Christianity, but he was also plotting dreadful things against his kingdom, perverting the crowd and making all men his own. "But if you wish," they said, "to be assured that we are saying nothing made up, call him privately and say, to test him, that you wish to leave the ancestral religion and the glory of the kingdom, to become a Christian, and to put on the monastic habit which you once persecuted, as though it had not rightly come into being."

For those who were thus cunningly scheming against the man knew the easily-moved bent of his mind, that if he heard such things from the king he would, supposing the king to have resolved on the better course, advise him not to delay over what was well resolved — and from this they would be found to be speaking the truth. But the king, not unaware how great the man's goodwill toward him was, held what was said to be improbable and false; and resolving that he must not accept these things without testing, he determined to prove the matter and the slander. And, calling the man privately, he said, to test him: "You know, my friend, all that I have shown against the so-called monks and against all the Christians. But now, having repented of this and condemned present things, I wish to gain those hopes of which I have heard them speak — of some immortal kingdom that is to be in another life; for the present one is altogether cut short by death. And I do not think this can be brought about for me and that I shall not fail of my aim, unless I become a Christian, and, bidding farewell to the glory of my kingdom and to the rest of the pleasant and delightful things of life, seek out those ascetics and monks wherever they may be, whom I unjustly drove away, and mingle myself among them. To this, what do you yourself say, and what counsel do you give? Speak, by the truth itself; for I know you to be truthful and well-meaning above all men." When that good man heard these things, not at all recognizing the deceit hidden within them,

he was pricked in his soul, and, overcome with tears, answered in his simplicity: "O king, live forever; for you have resolved a good and saving resolution. Though the kingdom of heaven be hard to find, yet one must seek it with all one's power; for 'he who seeks,' it says, 'will find it.' But the enjoyment of present things, even if to appearance it delights and gives pleasure, is good to thrust away; for in its very being it has no being, and those whom it gladdens it afterward grieves sevenfold. For both its goods and its sorrows are weaker than a shadow, and, like the tracks of a ship sailing the sea or of a bird passing through the air, they vanish more swiftly. But the hope of things to come, which the Christians proclaim, is sure and most secure; though it has affliction in the world. For our present pleasures are short-lived, while there they bring nothing at all but only punishment and a chastisement unending forever; for the pleasure of these things is temporary, but the pain perpetual; whereas with the Christians the toil is temporary, but the pleasant and profitable thing is immortal. May the good resolution of the king, then, be set straight; for it is good, exceedingly good, to exchange the eternal for the corruptible."

The king heard these things and was greatly displeased, yet he held back his anger and for the time said nothing to the man. But the man, being shrewd and quick of mind, perceived that the king had received his words heavily and that he had been testing him by deceit. Returning home, he was distressed and troubled, at a loss by what means he should appease the king and escape the danger that hung over him. And as he lay sleepless the whole night, there came to his memory the man whose foot had been crushed; and, bringing him to himself, he said: "I remember that you said you were a healer of hurt words." And he said, "Yes; and, if you have need, I will show forth the things of my art." Then the senator related to him his goodwill toward the king from the beginning, and the freedom of speech he had enjoyed, and the deceitful conversation lately set before him, and how he himself had answered well, but the king, receiving the words ill, had shown by the change of his face the anger lurking within him. That poor and feeble man considered and said: "Be it known to you, most honoured one, that the king has an evil suspicion of you, that you seek to seize his kingdom, and that, testing you, he said what he said. Rise, then, and cut your hair, and cast off these splendid garments,

and, putting on a garment of hair, go at dawn to the king. And when he asks, 'What does this attire mean for you?' answer: 'Concerning the things you spoke to me yesterday, O king, behold, I am present, ready to follow you on the road you have desired to travel; for though luxury is desirable and most sweet, yet may it not be mine to take it up after you; but the road of virtue which you are about to walk, though hard and rough, yet to one who is with you it is easy and pleasant and desirable. For as you have had me a sharer in the goods here, so you shall have me a sharer in the sorrows, that I may share with you in things to come as well.'" That illustrious man, accepting the words of the feeble one, did just as he had been told; and when the king saw and heard him, he was glad at it, marvelling greatly at the man's goodwill toward him, and, knowing that what had been said against him was false, he made him enjoy still greater honour and freedom of speech with him. But again he was filled to overflowing with anger against the monks, saying that these were their teachings — that men should abstain from the pleasant things of life and dream after uncertain hopes. And going out once more to the hunt, he saw two monks passing through the desert, and, ordering them to be seized and brought to his chariot,

he looked angrily upon them and, breathing fire, as the saying goes, he said: "Did you not hear, you deceivers and impostors, the heralds crying out plainly that no one of your wretchedness should after three days be found in a city or country of my dominion, or surely be burned with fire?" The monks said: "Behold, just as you commanded, we are going out from your cities and countries; but a long road lies before us to go to our brethren, and being in want of food, we provided ourselves with this, that we might have supplies and not become a victim of famine." The king said: "He who fears the threat of death does not busy himself with the providing of food." The monks said: "You have spoken well, O king. Those who fear death make it their care how they may escape it. But who are these, except those who are wasted away with attachment to fleeting things and excited about them, who, hoping to find no good thing from thence, hold to present things and can hardly be torn from them, and for this reason fear death? But we who long ago hated the world and the things in the world, and walk the narrow and afflicted road for Christ's sake, neither fear death nor desire present things, but reach out for things to come alone. Since, then, the death you bring upon us becomes a passage to

the everlasting and better life, it is to us a thing to be desired rather than feared." At which the king, wishing, with feigned shrewdness, to catch the monks, said: "What then? Did you not just now say that you were withdrawing, just as I commanded? And if you do not fear death, why did you take to flight? See, in this too you have lied, boasting in vain." The monks answered: "It is not from fear of the death you threaten that we flee, but, pitying you, that we might not become to you the cause of a heavier condemnation, we were eager to withdraw; since, so far as concerns us, we never in the least dread your threats." At this the king, angered, ordered them to be burned with fire; and the servants of Christ were perfected through fire, obtaining the crowns of martyrdom. And he set forth a decree that, if anywhere a monk should be found, he should be put to death without inquiry. And no one of that order was left in that country, save those who hid themselves in mountains and caves and the holes of the earth. Such, then, were these things.
Now the king's son, of whom from the beginning the account set out to speak, being shut up without going out in the palace built for him,

came to the age of youth, having gone through all the learning of the Ethiopians and the Persians. He was gifted and comely in soul no less than in body, sensible and prudent and shining with all good excellences; and he put forward questions of nature to his teachers, so that they too marvelled at the boy's quickness and understanding, and the king was astounded both at the charm of his face and at the composure of his soul. He gave commands to those about him to make none of the sorrowful things of life known to him in any way, nor that death at all succeeds present delights. But he was leaning upon empty hopes, and — as the saying goes — attempting to shoot at the heaven. For how could death escape the notice of human nature? Yet it did not escape the boy either. For having a mind thick-crowned with all understanding, he considered within himself for what reason his father had condemned him to be kept without going out and did not allow entrance to him to anyone who wished it. For he knew within himself that this was not without his father's command. Yet he was ashamed to ask him, saying on the one hand that it was improbable his father did not intend what was profitable for him, and considering on the other that, if the matter were according to his father's mind, even if he asked, his father would not make the truth known to him.

Hence he resolved to learn these things from others, and not from his father. And having one of his tutors dearer and more intimate to him than the rest, he made him still more his own, and, winning him over with generous gifts, inquired from him what the king meant by his confinement within that enclosure, saying: "If you teach me this plainly, you shall be preferred above all by me, and I will make with you a covenant of unbroken friendship." The tutor, being himself prudent and knowing the boy's intelligent and full discernment, and that he would not become to him an occasion of danger, related everything to him part by part: the persecution decreed by the king against the Christians and especially against the ascetics, how they were driven out and cast forth from that region, and what the astrologers had foretold at his birth. "So that you may not," he said, "hearing their teaching, prefer it to our religion, the king contrived that few, and those easily counted, should associate with you, giving us commands to make none of the sorrowful things of life known to you." When the young man heard these things, he added nothing further to say; but a saving word touched his heart, and the grace of the Comforter set about opening his spiritual eyes, leading him by the hand to the God who does not lie, as the account will show as it goes on. And when his father the king came often to see the boy — for he loved him with a surpassing love — on one occasion the son said to him: "There is something I have longed to learn from you, my lord and king, over which a continual grief and an unceasing anxiety devour my soul."

The father, pained in his inmost being at the very words, said: "Tell me, my most beloved child, what is the grief that holds you, and I will hasten to change it speedily into joy." And the boy said: "What is the reason of my confinement here, that you have shut me up within walls and gates, making me altogether unable to go out and unseen by all?" And the father said: "I do not wish, my child, that you should see any of the things that grieve your heart and cut short your gladness. For I intend that you should live the whole of your life in continual luxury and all joy and delight." "But know well, my lord," said the son to his father, "that in this way I do not live in joy and delight, but rather in affliction and great distress, so that even my very food and drink appear to me unpleasant and bitter. For I long to see all the things outside these gates. If, then, you wish me not to live in pain, command that I may go out as I wish, and delight my soul with the sight of things hitherto unseen by me."

The king was grieved when he heard these things, and considered that, if he forbade the request, he would become the occasion to him of greater distress and anxiety. And saying, "My child, I will do what is in your heart," he at once ordered choice horses and a bodyguard befitting a king to be made ready, and appointed that the boy should go out whenever he wished, charging those about him to bring nothing unpleasant to meet him, but to show the boy everything that was good and produced delight, and to set up in the streets choirs harmoniously singing songs and forming various shows, so that his mind might be occupied and delighted with these. And indeed, going out thus often in his processions, the king's son saw one day, through the negligence of his attendants, two men, one of whom was maimed and the other blind. Seeing them, and grieved in his soul, he said to those with him: "Who are these, and what is the unpleasant sight of them?" They, unable to hide what had come into his sight, said: "These are human afflictions, which are wont to befall mortals from corrupted matter and a body of ill humours." And the boy said: "Do these things usually befall all men?" They said: "Not all, but those in whom health is turned aside by the corruption of the humours." Again, then, the boy inquired: "If this does not usually befall all men, but some, are those known beforehand whom these dreadful things are to seize? Or do they come without distinction and unforeseen?" They said: "And who among men can foresee things to come and know them exactly? For this is beyond human nature, and allotted to the immortal gods alone."

And the king's son ceased asking, but was pained in his heart at what he had seen, and the form of his face was changed by the strangeness of the thing. And after not many days, passing by again, he met an old man worn out with many days, wrinkled in face, slack in his legs, bent over, and altogether grey, deprived of his teeth, and speaking with broken words. Astonishment seized him; and, bringing the man near, he inquired to learn the strangeness of the sight. Those present said: "This man is now of very many years, and as his strength has little by little diminished and his limbs grown weak, he has come to the misery you see." "And what," he said, "is the end of this?" They said to him: "Nothing else but death will succeed him." "But is this set before all men," he said, "or does it befall only some of them?" They answered: "Unless death takes someone away from these things first, it is impossible, as the years go on, not to come to the trial of this condition." And the boy said: "In how many years, then, does this come upon a man? And if death is altogether set before us, and there is no means to escape it and not to come to this misery?" They said to him: "In eighty, or even a hundred, years men come to this old age, and then they die, there being no other way. For death is a debt of nature, laid upon men from the beginning, and its coming cannot be turned aside."

When that intelligent and prudent young man saw and heard all these things, he groaned from the depth of his heart and said: "Bitter is this life, and full of all pain and unpleasantness, if these things are so. And how shall anyone be free from care in the expectation of uncertain death, whose coming is not only inescapable but also uncertain, as you have said?" And he went away turning these things over within himself, and reasoning unceasingly, and making frequent reflections on death, living thereby with toils and despondencies and having an unceasing grief. For he said within himself: "Will death then one day seize me? And who will keep my memory after death, since time gives all things over to oblivion? And shall I, when I die, be dissolved into non-being? Or is there some other life and another world?" Thinking unceasingly on these and like things, he grew pale and wasted away; but in his father's sight, when it happened that the king came, he feigned cheerfulness and freedom from grief, not wishing the things he was pondering to come to his father's knowledge. And he longed with an uncontrollable longing, and yearned, to meet someone able to satisfy his heart and to sound a good word in his ears. He inquired again of the aforementioned tutor whether he knew anyone able to help him toward what he desired and to make firm his mind, which was dreadfully reeling among its reasonings and unable to throw off its concern about these things.

And the tutor, recalling again what had been said before, replied: "I told you before too how your father, against those wise men and ascetics who were ever philosophizing about such things, killed some and persecuted others in anger; and I do not now know any such man in this region." At this the youth was filled with much heaviness, and grievously wounded in soul, and was like a man who had lost a great treasure and occupied his whole mind in its search. Thenceforth he lived with continual struggle and anxiety, and all the pleasant and delightful things of the world were in his eyes as a pollution and an abomination. While the young man was in such a state, and crying out in his soul to find the good, the eye that sees all things saw him, and he who wills that all should be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth did not overlook him; but, showing in this too his accustomed love for mankind, he made known the road which he was to travel, in the following manner.
For there was at that time a certain monk,

wise in divine things, adorned in life and in speech, and one who had gone through to the height every monastic way of life. From where he came and from what family I cannot say, but he made his dwelling in a certain utter wilderness of the land of Senaar, and had been perfected in the grace of the priesthood. Barlaam was the name of this old man. He, then, learning by a certain revelation that came to him from God the things concerning the king's son, went out from the desert and came down to the inhabited world. And, changing his habit and putting on worldly garments, and going aboard a ship, he came to the kingdom of the Indians; and, slipping on the mask of a merchant, he reached the city where the king's son had his palace. And, spending many days there, he inquired carefully into the things concerning him and who those were who came near him. Learning, then, that the tutor mentioned above was the most intimate to him of all, he came to him privately and said: "I wish you to know, my lord, that I am a merchant come from a far country, and I have a precious stone, the like of which has never been found. And to no one until now have I shown it; but to you I now make it known, seeing you to be an intelligent and sensible man,

that you may bring me in to the king's son, and I will give it to him. For it surpasses all good things beyond comparison; it can give to those blind in heart the light of wisdom, open the ears of the deaf, give voice to the speechless, and grant strength to the sick; it makes the foolish wise, drives out demons, and bestows ungrudgingly upon its possessor everything good and lovely." The tutor said to him: "I see you to be a man of steady and settled mind; but your words show that you boast beyond measure. For how could I tell you how many costly and precious stones and pearls I have seen? But ones having such powers as you have said, I have neither seen nor heard of. Still, show it to me, and, if it is according to your word, I will quickly bring it in to the king's son, and you will receive the greatest honours and gifts from him. But before I am assured by the truthful sight of my eyes, it is impossible for me to report such extravagant things about an unseen matter to my lord and king." Then Barlaam said: "You have spoken well in saying that you have never seen or heard of such powers and workings; for my word to you is not about a common thing, but about something wonderful and great. But since you have sought to behold it, hear my words. This precious stone, besides the workings and powers already mentioned, possesses also this strength: it cannot be readily beheld by one who does not have his sight strong and sound,

and his body pure and altogether undefiled. For if anyone not having these two good things should rashly look upon this precious stone, he would lose even the very power of sight that he has, and his wits besides. Now I, being not uninstructed in the science of medicine, see that your eyes are not sound, and I fear lest I be the occasion of depriving you even of the sight you have. But of the king's son I have heard that he has a chaste life and eyes that are beautiful and see soundly; for this reason I have taken courage to show this treasure to him. Do not, then, be careless about this, nor deprive your lord of such a thing." And he said to him: "If these things are so, do not show me the stone; for my life is befouled with many sins, and I do not, as you have said, have sound sight. But I, persuaded by your words, will not hesitate to make these things known to my lord and king." He said this, and going in, he reported everything part by part to the king's son. And he, when he heard the words of the tutor, felt a certain spiritual joy and gladness breathed into his heart; and, becoming as it were inspired in his soul, he ordered the man to be brought in quickly. When, then, Barlaam came in and had given him the fitting greeting of peace, he allowed him to be seated; and, the tutor having withdrawn, Josaphat said to the old man:

"Show me the precious stone, of which my tutor told me you spoke certain great and wonderful things." And Barlaam began his discourse with him thus: "It is not just, O king, that I should say anything falsely or rashly to the eminence of your glory; for all that has been declared to you by me is true and not to be gainsaid. But, unless I first take proof of your understanding, it is not lawful to reveal the mystery to you. For my Master says: 'The sower went out to sow his seed; and as he sowed, some fell beside the road, and the birds came and devoured it; and other fell upon rocky ground, where it had not much earth, and at once it sprang up, because it had no depth of earth; but when the sun rose it was scorched, and, because it had no root, it withered; and other fell among the thorns, and the thorns came up and choked it; and other fell upon the good earth, and yielded fruit a hundredfold.' If, then, I find in your heart an earth fruitful and good, I will not hesitate to plant in you the divine seed and to reveal the great mystery; but if it is rocky and thorny, and a road trodden by everyone who wishes, it is better not to cast this saving seed at all and set it for plunder to the birds and beasts, before whom I am altogether commanded not to throw the pearls. But I am persuaded

concerning you of the better things and those that belong to salvation, that you will both see the priceless stone, and by the radiance of its light be counted worthy yourself to become light, and bear fruit a hundredfold. For it was for your sake that I undertook the labour and accomplished a long road, to show you what you have never seen and to teach you what you have not heard." And Josaphat said to him: "For my part, honoured elder, with a certain longing and uncontrollable desire I seek to hear some new and good word, and a fire has been kindled within in my heart, grievously burning me and urging me to learn certain necessary inquiries; but until now I have not met a man able to satisfy me concerning these things. But if I should meet some wise and knowing man, and hear a word of salvation, I will not, I think, give it over to birds, nor to beasts, nor will I appear rocky, as you said, nor thorny, but will both receive it gratefully and keep it knowingly. So, if you know anything of this kind, do not hide it from me, but declare it to me. For when I heard that you had come from a far land, my soul was glad, and I became of good hope to attain through you what I long for. For this reason I quickly brought you in to me and received you kindly, as one of my familiars and of my own age, if indeed I shall not be cheated of my hope." And Barlaam said: "You have done well in this, and worthily of your royal magnificence,

that you gave no heed to the lowliness that appears, but laid hold of the hidden hope. For there was a certain great and glorious king, and it happened, as he was passing by on a gold-inlaid chariot with the bodyguard befitting a king, that two men met him, clothed in torn and filthy garments, their faces wasted and very pale; and the king knew them to have worn away their flesh by the mortification of the body and the sweats of ascetic discipline. So when he saw them, leaping down at once from the chariot and falling to the ground, he did them reverence; and rising, he embraced them and kissed them most affectionately. But his nobles and rulers were displeased at this, thinking that he had done a thing unworthy of the royal glory; and, not daring to reprove him to his face, they urged his own brother to speak to the king, that he should not thus dishonour the height of the diadem. And when the brother had said these things and blamed his untimely lack of dignity, the king gave him an answer which his brother did not understand. For it was the custom of that king, whenever he gave sentence of death against anyone, to send a herald to that man's door with a trumpet appointed for this purpose; and by the sound of that trumpet all understood that man to be liable to death.

So when evening came, the king sent the trumpet of death to sound at the door of his brother's house. When his brother heard the trumpet of death, he despaired of his own safety and set his affairs in order the whole night; and at dawn, clothing himself in black and mourning garments, with wife and children he went to the door of the palace, weeping and lamenting. The king brought him in, and, seeing him thus mourning, said: "O senseless and foolish man, if you so dreaded the herald of your brother and equal — against whom you know yourself to have done no wrong at all — how have you brought blame upon me for greeting in lowliness the heralds of my God, who announce to me, more sweetly than a trumpet, death and the fearful meeting with the Master, against whom I know myself to have sinned much and greatly? Behold, then, reproving your folly, I have used this very device, just as I shall soon reprove those who prompted your blame against me for their folly." And so, having healed his brother and done him good, he sent him home. And he ordered four caskets to be made of wood. Two of them he covered all over with gold, and, putting into them the foul-smelling bones of dead men, he secured them with golden clasps; the others he smeared with pitch and bitumen, and filled them with precious stones and costly pearls and every fragrance of perfumery.

And, binding these fast with cords of hair, he called the nobles who had blamed him over the meeting with those men, and set before them the four caskets, that they might appraise of how much these, and of how much those, were worth. And they declared the two gilded ones to be of the greatest value. "For it is possible," they said, "that royal diadems and girdles are laid up in them; but those smeared with pitch and bitumen are of some cheap and pitiful value." The king said to them: "I knew that you would say such things; for with the senses' eyes you regard the sensible appearance; but it ought not so to be done. Rather, with the inner eyes one must see the honour or dishonour that is laid up within." And he ordered the gilded caskets to be opened. When they were opened, a dreadful stench breathed out and a most loathsome sight was seen. So the king said: "This is the figure of those clothed in splendid and glorious garments, who pride themselves on great glory and power, but within reek of dead men and wicked works." Then, ordering the ones pitched and bituminized to be uncovered, he gladdened all present with the brightness and fragrance of the things laid up in them. And he said to them: "Do you know what these are like? They are like those lowly men clad in cheap garments, whose outward appearance you saw,

and counted my reverence to them, face to face on the ground, an outrage; but I, regarding with the eyes of the mind the precious and surpassing beauty of their souls, was glorified by touching them, and held them more precious than any crown and any royal purple." Thus, then, he shamed them, and taught them not to be deceived by things that appear, but to give heed to things perceived by the mind. According to that godly and wise king, then, you too have done, in receiving me with good hope, of which you will not be cheated, as I think." And Josaphat said to him: "All these things you have said well and fittingly; but this I wish to learn: who is your Master, of whom at the beginning of your discourse, concerning that sower, you said you spoke?"

So Barlaam, taking up his discourse again, said: "If you wish to learn who my Master is, it is the Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of those who reign and Lord of those who rule, who alone has immortality, dwelling in unapproachable light, who is glorified with the Father and the Holy Spirit. For I am not of those who proclaim these many and disorderly gods, and worship these lifeless and deaf idols;

but I know and confess one God, glorified in three persons — the Father, I mean, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit — yet in one nature and essence, in one glory and kingdom undivided. This, then, is the one God in three persons: without beginning and without end, eternal and everlasting, uncreated, unchanging and bodiless, invisible, uncircumscribed, incomprehensible, alone good and just. He, having brought all things into being out of nothing, both the visible and the invisible, first creates the heavenly and invisible powers — certain innumerable multitudes, immaterial and bodiless, ministering spirits of the majesty of God; then this visible world, heaven and earth and the sea, which he made bright with light and adorned — heaven with the sun and moon and the stars, earth with all manner of growing things and various living creatures, and the sea in turn with the teeming kind of swimming things. These all, he spoke and they were brought forth; he commanded and they were created. Then he creates man with his own hands, taking dust from the earth for the fashioning of the body, and giving him a soul rational and intelligent through his own in-breathing — which soul is written to have been created according to the image and likeness of God: according to the image, by reason of its intelligence and free will; according to the likeness, by reason of its likeness to virtue, so far as is possible.

This man, having honoured him with free will and immortality, he made king of the things on earth; and out of him he made the female, a helper for him answering to himself. And, having planted a paradise in Eden toward the east, full of all gladness and delight, he set in it the man whom he had fashioned, commanding him to partake without hindrance of all the divine plants there, but laying down a commandment to taste of one alone not at all — which is called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil — speaking thus: 'On whatever day you eat of it, you shall surely die.' Now one of the aforesaid angelic powers, a leader of one host, having in himself no trace whatever of natural evil from the Creator, but having come into being for good, by his own free choice turned from the good to the evil, and was lifted up in madness, wishing to rise against the Master and God. Therefore he was cast out of his rank and his dignity, and, instead of that blessed glory and angelic name, was called the devil and was given the name Satan. For God cast him out as unworthy of the glory above; and there was dragged down with him and cast out also a great multitude of the order of angels under him,

who, having become evil in their choice, and, instead of the good, following the apostasy of their ruler, were named demons, as deceivers and impostors. The devil, then, having altogether renounced the good and taken on an evil nature, conceived envy against man, seeing himself cast out from so great a glory while man was being raised to such honour; and he contrived to cast him out from that blessed manner of life. Taking, then, the serpent as the workshop of his own deceit, through it he spoke with the woman, and, persuading her to eat of that forbidden tree in the hope of becoming a god, through her he deceived Adam also — for so the first-formed man was called. And the first man, having eaten of the plant of disobedience, is made an exile from the paradise of delight by the Creator, and, instead of that blessed life and undying manner of existence, falls — alas — into this wretched and miserable life, and at the last is condemned to death. Hence the devil, taking strength and glorying in his victory, when the race of men had multiplied,

set before them every road of evil. So that, wishing thence to cut off the great course of sin, God brought a flood upon the earth, destroying every living soul; but finding one alone righteous in that generation, he preserved him with wife and children in a certain ark and set him, sole survivor, upon the earth. But when the race of men began again to advance into a multitude, they forgot God and went forward into worse impiety, enslaved to various sins and corrupted by dreadful enormities, and divided into manifold error. For some thought that the universe was borne along of itself, and decreed that there was no providence, as though no Master presided over it; others introduced fate, committing the whole to the moment of birth; others worshipped many evil and passion-ridden gods, that they might have them as advocates of their own passions and dreadful deeds — of whom they fashioned forms and set up deaf images and senseless idols, and, shutting them up in temples, did them reverence, serving the creation rather than the Creator: some the sun and the moon and the stars, which God set to give light to this earthly world, though they are lifeless and senseless, enlightened and held together by the providence of the Creator and able of themselves to do nothing;

others fire and water and the remaining elements of the earth, lifeless and senseless as they are; and they, being living and rational, were not ashamed to worship such things. Others rendered worship to wild beasts and reptiles and four-footed cattle, showing themselves more brutish than the things they worshipped. Others fashioned the forms of certain shameful and base men, and called these gods, and named some of them male and some female — men whom they themselves set forth to be adulterers and murderers, irascible and jealous and full of wrath, slayers of fathers and of brothers, thieves and robbers, lame and crippled, sorcerers and madmen, some of them dead, some struck by thunderbolts, and beaten and bewailed, and enslaved to men, and become fugitives, and transformed into animals for wicked and shameful unions; whence men, taking occasion from their very gods, defiled themselves without fear with every uncleanness. And a dreadful darkening held our race in those times, and there was none who understood, none who sought after God. But a certain Abraham was found in that generation alone, having the senses of his soul in vigour, who through the contemplation of created things came to know the Creator. For, regarding heaven and earth and sea, sun and moon and the rest, he marvelled at this harmonious ordering; and, seeing the world and all things in it, he did not think them to have come into being and to be preserved of themselves,

nor did he ascribe the cause of such an ordering to the elements of the earth or to the lifeless idols; but through these he came to know the true God, and understood him to be the Creator and Sustainer of all. And God, receiving this man for his good sense and right judgement, made himself manifest to him — not as he is in his nature, for it is impossible for created nature to see God, but by certain providential manifestations, as he himself knows — and, putting a more perfect knowledge of himself into his soul, glorified him and made him his own servant; and Abraham, handing down godliness by succession to those who came of him, taught them to know the true God. For this reason the Master was pleased that his seed should come to a boundless multitude, and named them a people for his own possession; and when they had been enslaved to the Egyptian nation and to a certain tyrant Pharaoh, he led them out from thence with signs and dreadful and extraordinary wonders through Moses and Aaron, holy men glorified with the grace of prophecy — through whom he both chastised the Egyptians worthily of their wickedness, and led the Israelites (for so that people, the descendants of Abraham, was called) through the Red Sea on dry ground, the waters being divided and a wall made on the right and a wall on the left; and when Pharaoh and the Egyptians had entered in upon their track, the waters, returning, utterly destroyed them.

Then, leading the people through the desert for forty years with the greatest wonders and divine manifestations, and feeding them with bread from heaven, he gave a law written by God on tablets of stone, which he put into the hands of Moses upon the mountain — a figure and outline of things to come — leading them away from the idols and from all wicked deeds, and teaching them to worship the God who truly is, alone, and to hold fast to good works. By such marvels, then, he brought them into a good land, which long before he had promised to give to the seed of that patriarch Abraham. And it would be long to relate how many great and wonderful things, glorious and extraordinary, beyond number, he showed toward them — through all of which this was his aim: to draw the race of men away from every lawless worship and deed, and to lead it back to its ancient estate. But still our nature was enslaved to the self-rule of error, and death reigned over men, sending all, by the tyranny of the devil and the condemnation of Hades, on their way. When we, then, had come into such calamity and misery, he who fashioned us and brought us from non-being into being did not overlook us, nor abandon to the end the work of his own hands,

but, by the good pleasure of God the Father and the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, the only-begotten Son and Word of God, who is in the bosom of the Father, who is of one essence with the Father and the Holy Spirit, the pre-eternal, the without beginning, who is in the beginning, and is with God the Father, and is God, condescends to his own servants by a condescension unspeakable and incomprehensible; and, being perfect God, he becomes perfect man of the Holy Spirit and of Mary the holy Virgin and Mother of God — not from the seed of man, or will, or union — conceived in the undefiled womb of the Virgin, but of the Holy Spirit, just as also, before the conception, one of the archangels was sent to announce to the Virgin that strange conception and that unspeakable birth. For without seed was the Son of God conceived of the Holy Spirit; and, framing for himself in the womb of the Virgin flesh ensouled with a rational and intelligent soul, he came forth in one person, but in two natures, perfect God and perfect man, keeping the virginity of her who bore him undefiled even after the birth, and, becoming in all things subject to like sufferings with us, yet without sin, he took up our weaknesses and bore our diseases. For since through sin death entered into the world,

it was necessary that he who was to redeem should be sinless and not liable to death through sin. And having lived among men for thirty years, he was baptized in the river Jordan by John, a holy man and one set above all the prophets. And when he was baptized, a voice came from heaven from God the Father, saying: 'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.' And the Holy Spirit came down upon him in the form of a dove. And from then he began to do great and wonderful signs, raising the dead, giving light to the blind, driving out demons, healing the deaf and the crippled, cleansing lepers, and on every side renewing our nature that had grown old, instructing and teaching by deed and word the road of virtue, leading away from corruption and guiding to the eternal life. Hence he chose twelve disciples, whom he also called apostles; and he charged them to proclaim the heavenly way of life which he came upon the earth to show forth, and by his dispensation to make us, the lowly and earthly, heavenly. But out of envy of his wonderful and godlike manner of life and of his boundless miracles, the chief priests and leaders of the Jews, among whom indeed he made his dwelling, raging madly, and forgetting all those wonderful signs and marvels which he had done for them, condemned him to death,

seizing one of his disciples for the betrayal; and, having taken him, they gave over the life of all things into the hands of the heathen — he accepting these things by his own free will. For he came to suffer all things for us, that he might free us from our passions. And, having shown much insolence toward him, at the last they condemned him to the cross. And he endured all things in the nature of the flesh which he had taken up from us, while his divine nature remained without suffering. For being of two natures, the divine and that which he had taken up from us, the human nature suffered, but the godhead remained without suffering and immortal. So our Lord Jesus Christ was crucified in the flesh, being sinless. For he did no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth, and he was not subject to death; for through sin, as I have said before, death entered into the world; but for our sake he died in the flesh, that he might redeem us from the tyranny of death. He went down into Hades, and, having crushed it, freed the souls shut up there from the beginning of the ages. Laid in a tomb, on the third day he rose again, conquering death and granting to us the victory over it,

and, having made the flesh incorruptible — he the giver of incorruption — he appeared to the disciples, granting them peace and through them to the whole race of men. And after forty days he ascended into the heavens, and so sits at the right hand of the Father; and he is also to come again to judge the living and the dead, and to render to each according to his works. And after his glorious ascension into the heavens, he sent the all-holy Spirit upon his holy disciples in the form of fire, and they began to speak in strange tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance. From this, then, by his grace they were scattered into all the nations, and proclaimed the orthodox faith, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to keep all the commandments of the Saviour. So they gave light to the nations that had gone astray, and abolished the superstitious error of the idols. And though the enemy, not bearing his defeat, even now raises wars against us the faithful,

persuading the foolish and senseless still to hold fast to idolatry, yet his power has become weak, and his swords have failed utterly before the power of Christ. Behold, I have made known to you my Master and God and Saviour in a few words; but you will know him more perfectly, if you receive his grace in your soul and are counted worthy to become his servant."

When the king's son heard these words, a light flashed about his soul; and, rising from his throne in his great joy, and embracing Barlaam, he said: "Perhaps this, as I conjecture, most honoured of men, is that priceless stone which you fittingly keep in secret, not showing it to everyone who wishes, but to those whose senses of the soul are in vigour.

For behold, as I received these words with my ears, a most sweet light entered into my heart, and that heavy veil of grief, which has now for a long time lain about my heart, was swiftly taken away. If, then, I conjecture rightly, tell me; and if you know anything better than what has been said, do not delay to reveal it to me at once." Again, then, Barlaam answered: "Yes indeed, my lord and king, this is the great mystery, hidden from the ages and from the generations, but in the last times made manifest to the race of men, whose manifestation many prophets and righteous men of old foretold by the grace of the divine Spirit, being initiated in many parts and in many ways; and, proclaiming it with a loud voice, and all foreseeing the salvation that was to come, they longed to behold it, and did not behold it; but this last generation was counted worthy to receive the salvation. He, then, who believes and is baptized shall be saved, but he who does not believe shall be condemned." And Josaphat said: "I believe without doubt all that you have said, and I glorify the God whom you proclaim.

Only make these things clear to me without error, and teach me exactly what I must do; and what baptism is, which you said believers receive, make known to me, with all that follows from it in due order." And he answered him: "The root, and as it were the secure foundation, of this holy and faultless faith of the Christians is the grace of divine baptism, which has the cleansing of all sins from birth, and the complete washing away of the defilements that have come upon us from evil. For so the Saviour commanded that we be born again through water and the Spirit, and led back to the ancient dignity — through prayer, that is, and the saving invocation, when the Holy Spirit comes upon the water. We are baptized, then, according to the word of the Lord, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit; and so the grace of the Holy Spirit dwells in the soul of the baptized, making it bright and rendering it godlike, and renewing in it that which is according to the image and likeness. And thereafter, casting off all the old works of evil, we make a covenant with God of a second life and a beginning of a purer way of living, that we may become also fellow-heirs with those who have been born again to incorruption and have laid hold of eternal salvation. But without baptism it is not possible to attain that good hope,

even if one should become more godly than all the godly. For thus the Word of God, made man for the salvation of our race, said: 'Truly I say to you, unless you are born again through water and the Spirit, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.' Therefore, before all things, I beg you to receive the faith in your soul, and to come at once to baptism with the most fervent longing, and by no means to put it off; for delay is full of peril, since the appointed time of death is uncertain." And Josaphat said to him: "And what is that good hope, which you said cannot be attained without baptism? And what is it that you call the kingdom of heaven? And whence have you heard the words of the God made man? And what is the uncertain appointed time of death, the great anxiety about which, settling upon my heart, consumes my flesh in griefs and pains and lays hold even of my very bones? And shall we men, when we die, be dissolved into non-being, or is there some other life after the departure from here? These things and what follows on them I have longed to learn."

And Barlaam gave to these such answers: "The good hope of which I spoke is the kingdom of heaven; and this is altogether inexpressible by a mortal tongue. For the Scripture says: 'Things which eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and which have not entered into the heart of man, the things which God has prepared for those who love him.' And when we are counted worthy, having laid aside this coarse flesh, to attain that blessedness, then he himself, who has counted us worthy not to fail of the hope, will teach and make known the glory of those good things, which surpasses all understanding, the unspeakable light, the life that is not cut short, the manner of life with the angels. For if we are counted worthy to be with God, so far as is attainable by human nature, we shall know from him all things which now we do not know. For this I, instructed by the teaching of the God-inspired Scriptures, set above all things as the kingdom of heaven: to come near to the contemplation of the holy and life-giving Trinity, and to be illumined by its unapproachable light,

and more clearly and purely, with unveiled face, to behold as in a mirror its unspeakable glory. And if it is not possible to set forth in words that glory and that light and those secret good things, it is no marvel; for they would not be great and surpassing, if they were grasped by reason and set forth in words to us, who are earthly and corruptible and clothed about with this heavy and passible flesh. Knowing these things, then, by faith alone, receive them without doubt, holding that they have nothing feigned, and hasten through good works to lay hold of that immortal kingdom, which, when you attain it, you will learn in its perfection. And as to what you asked, how we have heard the words of the God made flesh, know that through the sacred Gospels we have learned all the things of the divine-human dispensation. For so that holy book is called, inasmuch as it brings the good news of immortality and incorruption and eternal life and the forgiveness of sins and the kingdom of heaven to us who are mortal and corruptible and earthly — which the eyewitnesses

and ministers of the Word wrote, those whom I said above that Christ our Saviour chose as disciples and apostles. And they handed it down to us in writing, after the glorious ascension of the Master into the heavens, delivering in writing, so far as could be, the teachings and miracles of his life upon earth. For thus, toward the end of his account, the most distinguished of those divine evangelists said: 'There are,' he says, 'also many other things which Jesus did, which, if they were written one by one, I do not think that the world itself could contain the books that would be written.' In this most divine Gospel, then, is set forth the history of his incarnation, his manifestation, his miracles, and his deeds, written by the Spirit of God; then also of the undefiled passion which the Lord endured for our sake, and of his holy resurrection on the third day, and of his ascension into the heavens, and besides of his glorious and fearful second coming. For the Son of God is to come again upon the earth, with unspeakable glory and a multitude of the heavenly host, to judge our race and to render to each according to his works. For when God in the beginning had fashioned man out of earth, as I told you before too, he breathed into him a breath,

which is called a rational and intelligent soul; and since we have been condemned to death, we all die, and there is none of men who can pass by this cup. Now death is the separation of the soul from the body. That body, then, fashioned out of earth, separated from the soul, returns to the earth from which it was taken, and, decaying, is dissolved; but the soul, being immortal, goes where the Creator commands, or rather as it has itself prepared a dwelling for itself while still joined to the flesh. For as a man lives here, so is he to receive there. Then, after very many years, Christ our God will come to judge the world in fearful and indescribable glory, at the fear of whom the powers of the heavens will be shaken, and all the hosts of the angels stand with trembling before him.
