Then, at the voice of an archangel and at the trumpet of God, the dead will rise and stand before his fearful throne. Now the resurrection is the joining together again of soul and body. The very body, then, which decays and is dissolved, that same body will rise incorruptible. And let no thought of unbelief about this come upon you; for it is not impossible for him who in the beginning fashioned it out of earth,

and then, when it had returned to the earth from which it was taken, according to the sentence of the Creator, to raise it again. For if you consider how many things God has made out of nothing, this will be sufficient proof for you. For indeed, taking earth, he made man, earth that was not before; how, then, did the earth become man? And how was it brought forth, not existing before? What foundation has it? And how were the countless kinds of the irrational creatures, of the seeds, of the plants, brought forth from it? But consider now even our own birth: is not a small seed cast into the womb that receives it? Whence, then, the so great fashioning of the living creature? For him, then, who fashioned all these things out of nothing, and still fashions them, it is not impossible to raise from the earth the bodies that are dead and corrupted, that each may receive according to his works. For the present time, he says, is a time of work, and the time to come of recompense. For where is the justice of God, if there were no resurrection? For many, being righteous, have been much ill-treated in this present life and put to death violently after torment; while some, being impious and lawless, have spent the present life in luxury and prosperity. But God, since he is good and just, has appointed a day of resurrection and of trial, that each soul, receiving back its own body, the evil man,

having received good things here, may there be punished for the things in which he sinned, and the good man, having been punished here for the things in which he sinned, may there become heir of good things. For 'those in the tombs,' says the Lord, 'will hear the voice of the Son of God, and they who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life, but they who have practised evil to the resurrection of judgement,' when also thrones will be set, and the Ancient of Days and Creator of all will sit in the chief place, and books will be opened, having written in them all our deeds, words, and thoughts, and a river of fire is drawn forth, and all hidden things are uncovered. There no advocate, nor persuasiveness of words, nor false defence, nor power of wealth, nor weight of dignities, nor lavish giving of gifts, will be able to steal away the right judgement; but that incorruptible and true Judge will distinguish all things in the balances of justice — both deed and word and thought. And those who have done good will go to eternal life, into the light unspeakable, rejoicing with the angels, enjoying the secret good things, and purely standing before the

holy Trinity; but those who have practised evil, and all the impious and sinners, to eternal punishment, which is called Gehenna, and outer darkness, and the worm that does not sleep, and the gnashing of teeth, and ten thousand other torments — or rather, the hardest of all, to be estranged from God and cast away from his most sweet face, and to be deprived of that indescribable glory, and to be made a public example before all creation, and to be put to a shame that has no end. For after that fearful sentence is given, all things will remain unchangeable and unalterable, neither the bright manner of life of the righteous having an end, nor the misery and punishment of sinners receiving any limit; for there is no judge higher than him, nor any defence by second deeds, no appointed time of amendment, no other means for those who are punished, the chastisement enduring with them forever. These things being so, what manner of men ought we to be in holy conduct and godly ways of life, that we may be counted worthy to escape the threat to come and to stand at the right hand of the Son of God? For this is the standing of the righteous; but for sinners the most wretched portion at the left hand is allotted.

From there the Master, calling the righteous 'blessed,' brings them into the kingdom that has no end; but the sinners, casting them out with wrath and a curse from his gentle and serene face — which is of all things the bitterest and also the hardest — he sends forth into eternal punishment.

And Josaphat said to him: "You tell me certain great and wonderful things, my friend, worthy of much fear and trembling, if indeed they are so, and if there is again, after dying and being dissolved into ashes and dust, a resurrection and a new birth, and recompenses and a reckoning of the things one has lived. But what is the proof of these things? And how have you, having learned what has hitherto not been seen, believed so firmly and beyond all doubt? For the things already done and made manifest in deeds, even if you yourselves did not see them, yet you heard them from those who recorded them; but how, proclaiming such great and extraordinary things about things to come as well, have you gained a sure conviction concerning them?" And Barlaam said: "From the things already done I have gained conviction concerning things to come; for those who proclaimed these things, having failed in nothing of the truth, but having established what they said with signs and wonders and various powers, themselves also taught about things to come.

As, then, here they taught nothing perverse and feigned, but everything they said and did shone brighter than the sun, so there too they decreed true things — which our Lord and Master Jesus Christ himself confirmed by word and deed. For 'Truly,' he says, 'I say to you that an hour is coming, in which all those in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live'; and again: 'An hour is coming, when the dead will hear his voice, and will come forth, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, but those who have practised evil to the resurrection of judgement'; and again, concerning the resurrection of the dead, he says: 'Have you not read what was said to you by God, saying: I am the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob? God is not the God of the dead, but of the living.' For 'As the tares are gathered and burned with fire, so it will be at the consummation of this age; the Son of God will send forth his angels, and they will gather all the stumbling-blocks and those who do iniquity, and will cast them into the furnace of fire; there will be the weeping and the gnashing of teeth; then the righteous will shine forth as the sun in the kingdom of their Father.' Saying these things, he added: 'He who has ears to hear, let him hear.' With such words and many others the Lord

made manifest the resurrection of our bodies; and he confirmed the words by deed, raising many dead, and, near the end of his life upon earth, calling from the tomb a certain Lazarus, his friend, already decayed and stinking after four days, and presenting alive the man who had no breath. And besides these things the Lord himself became the first-fruits of the perfect resurrection that no longer falls under death, having tasted of death in the flesh, but having risen on the third day and become the first-born of the dead. For others too were raised from the dead, but they died again and did not come to present an image of the true resurrection to come; but he alone became the author of that resurrection, the first to be raised to the immortal resurrection. These things also they who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word proclaimed. For the blessed Paul says, whose calling was not from men but from heaven: 'I make known to you, brethren, the Gospel which I preached to you; for I delivered to you among the first things what I also received, that Christ died for our sins, according to the Scriptures.' And: 'If Christ is proclaimed, that he has been raised from the dead,

how do some say that there is no resurrection? For if the dead are not raised, neither has Christ been raised; and if Christ has not been raised, our faith is vain, you are still in your iniquities; if in this life only we have hoped in Christ, we are of all men the most pitiable. But now Christ has been raised from the dead, having become the first-fruits of those who have fallen asleep; for since through a man came death, also through a man comes the resurrection of the dead; for as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive.' And a little later: 'For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality; and when this corruptible has put on incorruption and this mortal has put on immortality, then will be fulfilled the word that is written: Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your sting? Where, O Hades, is your victory?' For then the power of death is wholly abolished and made to vanish, no longer working at all, but immortality henceforth and incorruption is given to men, eternal. There will be, then, there will be beyond doubt the resurrection of the dead, and this we believe without hesitation; but we know also of recompenses and a reckoning of the things one has lived, on the fearful day of the coming of Christ, through which the heavens, set on fire, will be dissolved, and the elements, burning, will melt, as one of the inspired writers says,

but we look for new heavens and a new earth, according to his promise. For that there are recompenses and a reckoning of works there, and that nothing at all of good or evil things will be overlooked, but that the requitals of deeds and words and thoughts are laid up, is plain. For the Lord says: 'Whoever gives one of these little ones only a cup of cold water in the name of a disciple, will by no means lose his reward.' And again he says: 'When the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the holy angels with him, then all the nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them one from another, as the shepherd separates the sheep from the goats, and he will set the sheep at his right hand, but the goats at the left. Then the King will say to those at his right hand: Come, you blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world; for I was hungry and you gave me to eat, I was thirsty and you gave me to drink, I was a stranger and you took me in, naked and you clothed me, I was sick and you visited me, I was in prison and you came to me.' Why does he say this? Because he makes the kindnesses done by us toward the needy his own. And in another place he says: 'Everyone who confesses me before men, I also will confess him before my Father who is in heaven.' Behold, through all these things and many others he showed that the recompenses

of good works are sure and secure; but he also foretold that a reckoning of the opposite things is laid up, through wonderful and extraordinary parables, which the fountain of wisdom related most wisely: at one time bringing in a certain rich man clothed in purple and fine linen, and faring sumptuously every day, but ungiving and unmerciful toward the needy, so that he overlooked a certain poor man named Lazarus cast at his gate, and did not give him even of the very crumbs of his table. When, then, both had died, that poor and ulcered man was carried, he says, into the bosom of Abraham, thus signifying the company of the righteous; but the rich man was given over to the flame of bitter torment in Hades; to whom Abraham said: 'You received your good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise the evil; but now this man is comforted, and you are in anguish.' And elsewhere, likening the kingdom of heaven, he says: 'The kingdom of heaven is like a man, a king, who made a wedding for his son,' thus signifying the gladness and splendour to come. For making his discourse to lowly men who minded earthly things, he gave his parables from things familiar and known to them. Yet he did not mean that there are weddings and tables in that age; but, condescending to their dullness, he used such names, wishing to make known to them things to come.

"The king, then," he says, "called all by a lofty proclamation to come together to the wedding and to be filled with those secret good things; but many of those called, being careless, did not go, but, occupying themselves, some with fields, some with trades, some with newly-wedded wives, deprived themselves of the splendour of the bridal chamber. And when those had of their own will estranged themselves from the delightful gladness, others were called; and the wedding was filled with guests reclining. But the king, coming in to behold those reclining, saw there a man not clothed in a wedding garment, and says to him: 'Friend, how did you come in here not having a wedding garment?' And he was speechless. Then the king said to the servants: 'Bind his hands and feet, take him, and cast him into the outer darkness; there will be the weeping and the gnashing of teeth.'" Those, then, who excused themselves and did not at all obey the call are those who have not run to the faith of Christ, but have remained either in idolatry or in some heresy; while the man not having the wedding garment is he who believed, but stained the spiritual garment with filthy deeds, and who was justly cast out from the joy of the bridal chamber. And he set forth another parable in accord with this, picturing certain ten virgins, "of whom five were prudent, and five foolish;

and the foolish, taking their lamps, did not take oil with them; but the prudent took oil" — by the oil signifying the possession of good works. "And at midnight," he says, "a cry arose: Behold, the bridegroom comes; go out to meet him" — by the midnight setting forth the uncertainty of that day. "Then all those virgins arose; and the ready ones went out to meet the bridegroom, and went in with him to the wedding, and the door was shut; but the unready ones, whom he fittingly called foolish, seeing their lamps going out, went away to buy oil. And coming when the door was already shut, they cried, saying: Lord, Lord, open to us; but he," he says, "answering, said: Truly, I say to you, I do not know you." Through all these things, then, it is plain that there is requital not only of opposite deeds, but also of words and of the very thoughts. For the Saviour said: "I say to you that for every idle word which men speak, they will render an account concerning it on the day of judgement." And again: "But of you," he says, "even the hairs of the head are numbered" — by the hairs setting forth the finest of the reasonings and thoughts.

In accord with these things the blessed Paul also teaches: "For the word of God," he says, "is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, and piercing to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart; and there is no creature hidden before him, but all things are naked and laid bare to the eyes of him with whom we have to do." These things also the prophets, shining with the grace of the Spirit, proclaimed most clearly many ages before. For Isaiah says: "I know their works and their reasonings, and I will requite them; behold, I come to gather all the nations and the tongues, and they will come, and will see my glory. And the heaven will be new and the earth new, which I make before me; and all flesh will come to worship before me, says the Lord, and they will go forth, and will see the carcasses of the men who have transgressed against me; for their worm will not die, and their fire will not be quenched, and they will be a spectacle to all flesh." And again, concerning that day, he says: "And the heaven will be rolled up like a book, and all the stars will fall like leaves from a vine; for behold, the day of the Lord comes, incurable, of wrath and anger, to make the whole inhabited world desolate and to destroy the sinners out of it; for the stars of heaven and Orion and all the array of heaven

will not give their light, and it will be darkened at the sun's rising, and the moon will not give its light; and I will destroy the insolence of the lawless and humble the insolence of the proud." And again he says: "Woe to those who draw their sins to themselves as with a long cord, and their iniquities as with the strap of a heifer's yoke; woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who make darkness light and light darkness, who make bitter sweet and sweet bitter. Woe to your mighty men, the powerful, who mix strong drink, who justify the impious for the sake of gifts and take away the justice of the just, who turn aside the judgement of the poor and snatch away the cause of the needy, so that the widow becomes their plunder and the orphan their prey. And what will they do on the day of visitation? And to whom will they flee for help? And where will they leave their glory, that they may not fall into captivity?" As stubble is burned by a coal of fire and consumed by a kindled flame, their root will be as chaff, and their flower will go up as dust; for they would not have the law of the Lord of Hosts, but provoked the oracle of the Holy One of Israel. In accord with this another prophet also says:

"Near is the great day of the Lord, near and exceedingly swift; the voice of the day of the Lord is appointed bitter and harsh; that day is a mighty day of wrath, a day of affliction and distress, a day of misery and ruin, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and mist, a day of the trumpet and the cry; and I will afflict the wicked, and they will walk as the blind, because they have sinned against the Lord; and their silver and their gold will not be able to deliver them in the day of the Lord's wrath; for in the fire of his zeal the whole earth will be consumed, because he will make a full end of all those who dwell upon the earth." Besides these things David also, the king and prophet, cries out: "God will come openly, our God, and will not keep silence. Fire will burn before him, and round about him a mighty storm; he will call to the heaven above and to the earth, to judge his people." And again: "Arise," he says, "O God, judge the earth, for the thought of man will confess to you; and you will render to each according to his works." And many other such things the psalmist and all the prophets, initiated by the divine Spirit, proclaimed concerning the judgement and recompense to come; whose words the Saviour also, confirming them most surely,
taught us to believe in the resurrection of the dead and the recompense of the things one has lived and the unending life of the age to come.

Josaphat, filled with deep compunction at all this, was in tears. He said to the old man: You have made everything clear to me, and have set out this awesome and wonderful account with certainty. Since, then, these things lie before us, what must I do to escape the punishments prepared for sinners, and to be found worthy of the joy of the righteous? Barlaam answered: It is written that once, when Peter—who was also called the chief of the apostles—was teaching the people, they were pricked to the heart, just as you are today; and when they said, "What shall we do?" Peter said to them: Repent, and let each of you be baptized for the forgiveness of sins, and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the promise is to you and to your children and to all who are far off, as many as the Lord our God shall call. See, then, that he has poured out his rich mercy upon you also, and has called you—you who in your mind were far from him and were serving gods that are not your own, but rather destructive demons and idols deaf and senseless. Therefore, before all else, draw near to the one who has called you, from whom you will receive a knowledge of things seen and unseen that does not lie. But if, after being called, you are unwilling, or you delay, by the just judgment of God you will be cast out of your inheritance,

unwilled because you yourself were unwilling; for so the same apostle Peter spoke to one of the disciples. But I believe that you have indeed heeded the call, and that, heeding it still more plainly, you will take up the cross and follow God your Master who calls you, who summons you from death to life and from darkness to light. For ignorance of God is in truth darkness and the death of the soul, and to be a slave to idols, to the ruin of all nature, seems to me to lie beyond all senselessness and folly. To what shall I liken them, and what image of their stupidity shall I set before you? Let me set before you an illustration told to me by a most wise man. He used to say that the worshippers of idols are like a bird-catcher who caught one of the smallest of the little birds—they call it a nightingale. Taking up a knife to kill it and eat it, the nightingale was given a voice with words. And it said to the bird-catcher:

What good will my killing do you, man? For through me you will not be able to fill your belly. But if you set me free from these bonds, I will give you three commandments, which, if you keep them, will profit you greatly throughout your whole life. Astonished at its speech, the man promised that, if he heard something new from it, he would quickly set it free from captivity. The nightingale turned and said to the man: Never attempt to attain what is beyond reach; do not grieve over a thing that is past; and never believe a word that is past belief. Keep these three commandments, and it will go well with you. Admiring the clarity and good sense of these words, the man loosed it from its bonds and sent it off into the air. Then the nightingale, wishing to learn whether the man had grasped the force of what had been said to him and whether he had reaped any benefit, said to him as it flew in the air: Alas for your folly, man—what a treasure you have lost today! For within my body there is a pearl greater in size than an ostrich's egg. When the bird-catcher heard this, he was overcome with grief, regretting that the nightingale had escaped his hands; and trying again to catch it, he said: Come into my house, and after entertaining you well I will send you off with honor.

But the nightingale said to him: Now I know for certain that you are utterly without sense. For though you received what was said to you eagerly and heard it gladly, you have gained no benefit from it. I told you not to grieve over a thing that is past; and see, you are overcome with grief that I escaped your hands, grieving over a thing that is past. I commanded you not to attempt to attain what is beyond reach; and you try to catch me, though you cannot reach my flight. Besides this, I charged you not to believe a word that is past belief; and see, you believed that within my body there was a pearl exceeding the measure of my whole frame, and you had not the wit to understand that I in my entirety do not reach the size of an ostrich's egg—so how could I have held such a pearl within me? In just this way are those without sense who put their trust in idols. For they made these things with their own hands, and they worship what their own fingers made, saying: These are the ones who fashioned us. How, then, can they regard as their fashioners the things they themselves crafted and shaped? And, what is more, keeping them safe so that they may not be plundered by thieves, they call them guardians of their own safety; and yet how great a folly is this, and what failure to recognize that, being unable to keep and help themselves,

how could they be guardians and saviors of others? For why, it says, do they seek out the dead concerning the living? They squander money to set up monuments and statues to the demons, and they babble that these are the givers of good things, asking to receive from them what these idols themselves have never possessed and never will. Therefore it is written: Let those who make them become like them, and all who put their trust in them—those who, it says, having hired a goldsmith, made things by hand, and bowing down worshipped them. They lift them upon their shoulders and carry them; but if they set them down in a place, they remain there and cannot move. And whoever cries out to them, they will not hear him, nor save him from evils. Therefore be ashamed with an everlasting shame, you who trust in carved images, you who say to molten images: You are our gods. For they sacrificed, it says, to demons and not to God, to gods whom their fathers did not know; they came new and recent, because they are a perverse generation, and there is no faith in them. Out of this wicked and faithless generation the Lord calls you, saying to you: Come out from among them and be set apart, and touch no unclean thing, but be saved from this crooked generation. Arise and go, for this is no rest for you; for the multiplicity of rulership among your gods is disordered and faction-ridden and altogether without existence.

But with us it is not so; there are not many gods and lords, but one God the Father, from whom are all things and we for him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him, who is the image of the invisible God, firstborn of all creation and of all the ages, for in him all things were created, the things in the heavens and the things on the earth, the visible and the invisible, whether Thrones or Dominions or Principalities or Powers. All things came to be through him, and without him not one thing came to be that has come to be; and one Holy Spirit, in whom are all things—the Lord and giver of life, God and maker of gods, the good Spirit, the upright Spirit, the Spirit who is our advocate, the Spirit of adoption. Each of these, considered in itself, is God: as the Father and the Son, as the Son and the Holy Spirit; yet there is one God in three, one nature, one kingdom, one power, one glory, one essence, divided only in the persons. For there is one Father, to whom belongs unbegottenness; one only-begotten Son, to whom belongs begetting; and one Holy Spirit, to whom belongs procession.

For thus do we, illumined by light from the Father, the Son, light in the light of the Holy Spirit, glorify one Godhead in three persons; and he is the true and only God, known in the Trinity, for from him and through him and to him are all things. By his grace I too, learning your situation, was sent to teach you what I have learned and kept from the beginning until these gray hairs. If, then, you believe and are baptized, you will be saved; but if you refuse to believe, you will be condemned. For the things you see today and take pride in—the glory and luxury and wealth and all the deceit of this life—will very soon pass away, and will cast you out from here even against your will. Your body will be shut up in a tiny tomb, left utterly alone, stripped of all the company of friends and kin; the delights of the world will be gone, and great loathsomeness and foul decay will spread over it in place of your present beauty and sweet scent; and your soul they will cast down into the depths of the earth, into the condemnation of Hades, until the final resurrection,

when the soul, taking up again its own body, will be cast out from the presence of the Lord and handed over to the fire of Gehenna that burns without end. These things will befall you, and far worse than these, if you remain in unbelief. But if you eagerly heed the one who calls you to salvation, and, running to him with longing and joy, are sealed with his light, and follow him without turning back—renouncing all things, clinging to him alone—hear what security and gladness you will attain. If you sit, you will be without fear; if you sleep, you will sleep sweetly, and you will not fear any sudden terror, nor the assaults of the impious demons coming upon you; but you will go your way confident as a lion, and you will live in gladness and everlasting exultation. For upon your head will be exultation and praise, and gladness will overtake you; there pain and grief and groaning have fled away.

Then your light will break forth early, and your healing will swiftly spring up, and your righteousness will go before you, and the glory of God will enfold you. Then you will cry out, and God will hear you; while you are still speaking he will say: Behold, I am here. For I am the one who blots out your iniquities and remembers them no more; but do you remember them, and let us be judged together. Tell your own iniquities, that you may be justified. And though your sins be as scarlet, I will make them white as snow; and though they be as crimson, I will make them white as wool. For the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things.

Josaphat said to him: All your words are good and wonderful, and I have believed and do believe, hating all idolatry from my heart. Even before you came to me, my soul was disposed toward it sidelong and with doubt; but now I hate it with a perfect hatred, having learned from you the emptiness of these idols and the folly of those who serve them. I long to become a servant of the true God, if only he will not push me, unworthy as I am, away because of my transgressions, but will pardon me all of them—being, as you teach, a lover of mankind and full of compassion—and count me worthy to become his servant. So I am now ready both to receive baptism and to keep everything you tell me. But what must I do after baptism? And is this alone enough for salvation—

to believe and be baptized—or must some other things be added as well? Barlaam said to him: Hear what one must do after baptism. One must abstain from all sin and every passion, and build upon the foundation of the orthodox faith the practice of the virtues, since faith without works is dead, just as works are dead without faith. For the Apostle says: Walk in the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desire of the flesh. Now the works of the flesh are plain, and these they are: adulteries, fornications, impurities, licentiousness, idolatries, sorceries, enmities, strife, jealousies, fits of anger, factions, dissensions, heresies, envyings, murders, love of money, abuse, love of pleasure, drunkenness, revelings, arrogance, and the like; of which I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God. But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control, sanctification of soul and body, humility of heart and contrition, almsgiving, the bearing of no grudges, love of mankind, watchfulness, exact repentance for all former failings, the tear of compunction, mourning for one's own sins and for one's neighbor's, and the like—which, like so many steps and rungs of a ladder, holding to one another and supporting one another,

raise the soul to heaven. See, then, we have been commanded to hold fast to these after baptism, and to abstain from their opposites. But if, after receiving the knowledge of the truth, we take up again our former dead works and turn back like a dog to its own vomit, what the Lord said will befall us. For when, he says, the unclean spirit goes out of a man—that is, by the grace of baptism—it passes through waterless places seeking rest and finds none; and, unable to wander long without house or hearth, it says: I will return to my house, from which I came out. And coming, it finds it swept and adorned, but empty and unoccupied—not having received the work of grace, nor filled itself with the wealth of the virtues. Then it goes and takes with itself seven other spirits more wicked than itself; and entering, they dwell there; and the last state of that man becomes worse than the first. For baptism, burying in its water the bonds of all former sins, delivers them over to utter destruction,

and thereafter is for us a sure wall and rampart and a mighty weapon against the array of the enemy. Yet it does not take away free will, nor does it carry forgiveness of the sins committed after baptism, nor a second descent into the font. For we confess one baptism; and we must keep ourselves with all watchfulness, lest we fall into a second defilement, but lay hold of the Lord's commandments. For when he said to the Apostles, Go and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, he did not stop there, but added: Teaching them to keep all that I have commanded you. And he commanded that we be poor in spirit, whom he blesses and calls worthy of the kingdom of heaven. Then he prescribes that we mourn in this present life, so that we may be counted worthy of the comfort to come; that we be gentle, and always hunger and thirst for righteousness, and be merciful and generous in giving, compassionate and full of sympathy,

pure in heart, abstaining from every defilement of flesh and spirit, peacemakers toward our neighbors and toward our own soul—that is, having subjected the worse to the better, and by right judgment having made peace in the perpetual war between them; that we endure every persecution and every affliction and reproach brought upon us for righteousness' sake, for the sake of his name, so that we may be counted worthy of eternal joy in the bright distribution of his gifts. And he likewise bids that our light so shine before men in the world that they may see, he says, your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven. For the law of Moses, given of old to the Israelites, says: You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness; but Christ says that everyone who is angry with his brother without cause shall be liable to judgment; and whoever says "You fool" shall be liable to the Gehenna of fire; and: If you bring your gift to the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; and: Everyone who looks at a woman to desire her

has already committed adultery with her in his heart—calling the defilement of the soul and the consent to passion adultery. And again, while the law forbade perjury, Christ commanded not to swear at all, but only to say Yes or No. There it was an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth; but here: Whoever strikes you on the right cheek, he says, turn to him the other also; and to the one who wishes to go to law with you and take your tunic, leave him your cloak as well; and whoever compels you to go one mile, go with him two; give to the one who asks of you, and do not turn away the one who wishes to borrow from you; love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat and persecute you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven, for he makes his sun rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the just and the unjust. Do not judge, that you be not judged; forgive, and you will be forgiven. Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal; but store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in

nor steal; for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. Do not be anxious for your soul, what you will eat and what you will drink, nor for your body, what you will put on; for your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things. He, then, who gave the soul and the body, will surely also give food and clothing—he who feeds the birds of heaven and adorns the lilies of the field with such beauty. But seek first, he says, the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. Do not be anxious about tomorrow; for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Whatever you wish that people should do to you, do so to them as well. Enter through the narrow gate, for wide is the gate and broad the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who go in by it; narrow and hard is the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it. Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven. Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me, and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me; and whoever does not take up his cross and follow after me is not worthy of me. See, these things and the like the Savior commanded the apostles

to teach the faithful; and all these we are bound to keep, if indeed we long to attain perfection and to be counted worthy of the incorruptible crowns of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will bestow on that day upon all who have loved his appearing. Josaphat said to the old man: Since, then, the precision of these doctrines requires this unalloyed way of life, if after baptism it happens that I fail in one or two of these commandments, shall I, by failing, miss the whole goal, and will all my hope be in vain? Barlaam said: Do not regard these matters in that way. For God the Word, who became man for the salvation of our race, knowing well the great weakness and wretchedness of our nature, did not leave us even in this respect to sicken without remedy; but, like an all-wise physician, he mixed for our slippery and sin-loving disposition the medicine of repentance, proclaiming it for the forgiveness of sins. For after we have received the knowledge of the truth and have been sanctified by water and the Spirit,

and have been cleansed of all sin and every defilement without toil, if it happens that we fall into certain trespasses of sin, there is not, through baptism, a second regeneration in the water of the font wrought by the Spirit and recasting us anew to perfection. For this gift is given once for all. But through laborious repentance and warm tears, through toils and sweat, there comes a cleansing and forgiveness of faults, by the tender mercies of our God. For the fountain of tears too has been called a baptism, by the grace of the Master—though one that requires toil and time—and it has saved many out of many faults; since there is no sin that overcomes the love of God for mankind, provided we make haste to repent and to wash away with tears the shame of our faults, and provided death does not first cast us out from this life still defiled; for in Hades there is no confession, nor repentance. But so long as we are among the living, the foundation of the orthodox faith remaining unbroken, even if something of the roof or the inner structure is loosened, it is possible to renew again by repentance what the faults have rotted. For it is impossible to number the multitude of God's compassions or to measure the greatness of his mercy; but sins and faults, whatever they may be, are subject to measure and can be counted. Our faults, then, being subject to measure and number, cannot overcome the immeasurable mercy and the

uncountable compassions of God. Therefore we have not been bidden to despair over our sins, but to recognize the goodness of God, and to condemn the sins whose forgiveness is set before us through the love of Christ for mankind, who poured out his own blood for our sins. And from many places in Scripture we are taught the power of repentance, and above all from the commands and parables of our Lord Jesus Christ. For from that time, it says, Jesus began to teach and to say: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand. And in a parable he introduces a son who, having taken his father's substance and journeyed into a far country, there squandered everything in dissolute living; then, a famine arising in that land, he went and attached himself to one of the wicked citizens of that sin-ridden country, who sent him, it says, into his fields to feed swine—so calling the harshest and most loathsome sin. After many hardships, then, and reduced to the utmost wretchedness, so that he could not even fill his own belly with the foul food of the swine, coming at last to a sense of such shame, he lamented over himself and said:

How many of my father's hired servants have bread in abundance, while I am perishing with hunger! I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you, and I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me as one of your hired servants. And he arose and came to his father. But the father, seeing him from afar, was moved with compassion, and running to him embraced him and kissed him tenderly; and counting him worthy of his former honor, he made a joyful feast at his recovery, slaughtering the fattened calf. See, this parable he set forth for us concerning those who turn back from sins and fall down in repentance. And again he tells of a certain good shepherd who had a hundred sheep and, one of them being lost, left the ninety-nine and went out in search of the one that had strayed, until he found it; and taking it up on his shoulders, he mingled it with those that had not strayed, calling together his friends and neighbors to celebrate at its recovery. So, says the Savior, there will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, more than over ninety-nine righteous who have no need of repentance. Indeed, even the chief of the disciples, Peter, the rock of faith, at the very time of the Savior's passion, being for a little while abandoned by a certain providential abandonment—so that he might learn the cheapness and wretchedness of human weakness—fell into the charge of denial; then at once, remembering the Lord's words,

he went out and wept bitterly; and by those warm tears he recalled his defeat and won the victory back to the other side. For being practiced in war, even though he had fallen, he was not undone, nor did he despair of himself; but, springing up, he brought forth most bitter tears from an afflicted heart; and at once the enemy, beholding them, as though his eyes were scorched by a most violent flame, leapt away and fled far off, wailing terribly. And the chief was again the chief—appointed teacher of the world, and so likewise becoming a pattern of repentance. After the divine resurrection, Christ, addressing him three times, Peter, do you love me? set right the threefold denial, the apostle answering: Yes, Lord, you know that I love you. From all these, then, and from many other examples beyond number, we learn the power of tears and of repentance; only let its manner be worthy—let it spring from a disposition that abhors sin, hating and condemning it, and that makes use of tears, as the prophet David says:

I am weary with my groaning; every night I will wash my bed; with my tears I will drench my couch. And then the cleansing of sins will come through the blood of Christ, in the greatness of his mercy and the multitude of the compassions of God, who said: Though your sins be as scarlet, I will make them white as snow, and so on. These things, then, are so, and so we believe. But after receiving the knowledge of the truth, and being counted worthy of regeneration and adoption, and tasting the divine mysteries, we must with all our power guard ourselves against falling. For falling does not befit the athlete, since many who have fallen have not been able to rise: some, having opened a door to the passions and clung hard to them, no longer had the strength to run back to repentance; others, snatched away beforehand by death, and not having made haste to wash themselves of the defilement of sin through a change of mind, were condemned. And for this reason it is dangerous to fall into any passion whatever; but if it happens that one falls, he must spring up at once and stand again for the noble contest;
and as often as this happens, that too—the rising and standing—must follow at once, until the end. For turn back to me, and I will turn back to you, says the Lord God.

To this Josaphat said: How, then, will anyone keep himself pure of all sin after baptism? For even if there is, as you say, repentance for those who fall, yet it is in toil and labor, in weeping and mourning, which seem to me not easily accomplished by most people. I would rather find a way of keeping the commandments of God exactly and not swerving from them, nor, after the forgiveness of former evils, provoking again the most sweet Master and God. Barlaam said: You have spoken well of these things, my lord and king; this is my own wish too. But it is hard, and altogether impossible, for one who keeps company with fire not to be smoked by it. So it is hard to accomplish, and very steep going, for one bound to the affairs of this life, taken up with its cares and turmoils, living amid wealth and luxury, to walk unswervingly the way of the Lord's commandments and to preserve himself pure of them. For the Lord says: No one can serve two masters;

for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will hold to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and mammon. And his beloved disciple, John the evangelist and theologian, writes likewise in his epistle: Do not love the world, nor the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him, because all that is in the world—the desire of the flesh and the desire of the eyes and the pride of life—is not from the Father, but is from the world. And the world is passing away, and the desire of it; but the one who does the will of God abides forever. Our divine and God-bearing Fathers, then, considering these things, and hearing the Apostle's word that through many afflictions we must enter the kingdom of heaven, hastened after holy baptism to keep the garment of incorruption spotless and unstained; and so some of them set themselves to receive a second baptism as well—I mean the one through blood and martyrdom. For this too has been called a baptism, and a most honorable and venerable one; for it is not defiled by a second defilement of sin. This our Lord himself, accepting it for our sake, fittingly called a baptism. From that source, then, becoming his imitators and his zealous followers,

first those who had seen him with their own eyes, his disciples and apostles, and then the whole chorus of holy martyrs, gave themselves over for the name of Christ to the idol-serving kings and tyrants, and endured every kind of torment, encountering wild beasts and fire and the sword; and, confessing the good confession, finishing the course and keeping the faith, they obtained the prizes of righteousness, becoming the companions of the Angels and fellow-heirs with Christ. Their virtue shone so brightly that their sound went out into all the earth, and the splendor of their achievements flashed to the ends of the world. Of these, not only the words and deeds, but their very blood and bones are full of all holiness, driving out demons by main force and granting healings of incurable diseases to those who touch them in faith; and their garments, and whatever else came near their precious bodies, are forever held in reverence by all creation. Of them there is much to be told, to recount their exploits one by one. But when those cruel and beastlike tyrants perished, evil men evilly, and the persecution ceased, and faithful kings reigned throughout the world,

there came others to succeed them, imitating the zeal and the divine longing of those men—I mean the martyrs—and, wounded in their souls with the same love, they devised most excellently how to present soul and body undefiled to the Lord, cutting away all the workings of the passions and cleansing themselves of every defilement of flesh and spirit. And since they knew that this is achieved in no other way than by keeping the commandments of Christ, and perceived that keeping the commandments and practicing the virtues comes about with difficulty amid the tumults of the world, they took up a certain other way of life, strange and altered; and, according to the divine voice, leaving all things—parents, children, friends, kin, wealth and luxury—and hating all that is in the world, they departed to the deserts like fugitives, in want, afflicted, ill-treated, wandering in wildernesses and mountains and caves and the holes of the earth, removing themselves far from all the delights and enjoyments of earth, and having very scant supply even of bread itself and of covering;

and they did this with two purposes: that, not seeing the materials of the passions, they might tear up the desires of them by the roots out of the soul, and, wiping out the memories of them, might plant in themselves love and longing for the things of God and of heaven; and besides this, that, having consumed the flesh through hardship and become martyrs in their resolve, they might not fall short of the glory of those perfected through blood, but, becoming imitators as far as in them lay of the sufferings of Christ, might be sharers also in the kingdom that has no end. So, having considered all this most excellently, they took up the solitary and quiet life—some enduring in the open air, worn down by the blaze of scorching heat and by savage frosts and rains and the buffeting of winds; others, having fixed huts for themselves, or hidden in caves and grottoes, lived out their days. Pursuing virtue thus, they renounced to the end all comfort and rest of the flesh, holding to a diet of raw vegetables and herbs, or wild fruits, or dry and very hard bread—not only renouncing the quality of pleasant things, but, by their surpassing self-control, stretching their devotion to the matter of quantity as well. For they partook of even these cheap and most necessary foods only so far as merely to stay alive. Some of them, continuing without food through all the days of the week, took nourishment on the Lord's day;

others remembered to eat twice in that week; others ate every other day, or in the evening, only so much as to taste food. By prayers and vigils they came near to rivaling the life of the angels, having said farewell altogether to the possession of gold and silver, and forgetting that buying and selling existed at all among men. Envy and arrogance, which are most apt to follow good works, found no place in them. For neither did the lesser man, in the sweat of his ascetic labor, harbor within himself any thought of jealousy against the one who shone more brightly; nor again did boastful pride lift up the man who accomplished great things to conceit against the weaker, deceiving him into despising his neighbor, or glorying in his asceticism, or thinking highly of himself for his achievements. For the one who had the greater share in virtue, ascribing the whole not to his own labors but to the power of God, persuaded himself by a humble mind that he was accomplishing nothing at all, but was rather a debtor for more, as the Lord says: When you have done all that was commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants, for we have done what we ought to have done. And others again did not even persuade themselves that they had ever done what was commanded, but that what was lacking was more than what had already been accomplished. And the one who fell short in asceticism,

perhaps through bodily weakness, belittled himself, counting himself wretched and reckoning his deficiency to slackness of mind, not to weakness of nature. Thus, then, each was more modest than the other, and all than all; and where among those men was the passion of vainglory or of pleasing men? They who had fled the inhabited world and for this reason dwell in the desert, wishing to show their achievements not to men but to God, from whom also they hope for the rewards of their achievements—knowing well that ascetic labors performed for vainglory are without reward, since they are done for the praise of men and not for God; whence such men are doubly wronged, wasting the body and receiving no reward. But those who reach out for the glory above and press on toward it despised all earthly and human glory. As for their dwellings: some carry through the contest in utter withdrawal and solitude, removing themselves from the company of men for the whole time of their lives and drawing near to God; others, having fixed their dwellings far from one another, gather on the Lord's days into a single church, and share in the divine mysteries—I mean the bloodless sacrifice, the undefiled body and the precious blood of Christ, which the Lord gave to the faithful for the forgiveness of sins and for the illumination and sanctification of soul and body; and, feasting one another with the exercise of the divine words and with moral exhortations, and making public the hidden warfare of their adversaries, so that no one ignorant of the method of the struggle may be caught by them,

each returns again to his own home, laying up devotedly the honey of virtue in the hives of their hearts, and cultivating a most sweet fruit worthy of the heavenly table. Others take up the common life: who, gathered in great numbers in one place, set themselves under one captain and superior, the most excellent of all, slaughtering every will of their own with the sword of obedience; and, reckoning themselves of their own accord to be bought slaves, they no longer live to themselves, but to him under whom, for love of Christ, they have subjected themselves—or, to say it more properly, they live no longer to themselves, but Christ lives in them, whom they have followed, renouncing all things. For this is withdrawal: a willing hatred of the world, and a renunciation of nature out of longing for the things above nature. These men, then, live as angels upon the earth, singing psalms and hymns to the Lord with one accord, and proving themselves confessors in the contests of obedience; in whom also the word of the Master is fulfilled. For he says: Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them—not confining the gathering in his name to this measure, but by "two or three" indicating an unbounded number. For whether few or many be gathered for his holy name, serving him with fervent longing, there we believe him to be present in the midst of his servants. By these patterns and such ways of life the earthly and dust-born have rivaled the life of the

heavenly: in fastings and prayers and vigils, in warm tears and unwavering mourning, in living as strangers and the remembrance of death, in gentleness and freedom from anger, in silence of the lips, in poverty and possessing nothing, in chastity and self-control, in a humble mind and stillness, in perfect love toward God and toward one's neighbor—completing the present life and becoming angels in their ways. Whence God adorned them with wonders and signs and various powers, and made the sound of their wondrous way of life echo to the ends of the world. And if I bring before you the life of one of them, telling it in detail by word of mouth—he who is said to have been the founder of the monastic way of life, Antony by name—you will surely know from the one tree the sweetness of the fruits of its kind and like, and what a foundation of asceticism that man laid, and what a roof he fixed upon it, and what gifts he was counted worthy to receive from the Savior. And many others after him, contending the same contest, obtained the like crowns and rewards. Blessed are these, and thrice blessed, who loved God and for love of him despised all things. For they wept and mourned day and night, that they might attain the comfort that has no end; they humbled themselves willingly, that there they might be exalted; they wasted their flesh with hunger and thirst and vigil, that there the luxury and exultation of paradise might receive them;

they became a dwelling of the Holy Spirit by purity of heart, as it is written: I will dwell in them and walk among them; they crucified themselves to the world, that they might stand at the right hand of him who was crucified; they girded their loins in truth, and kept their lamps always ready, awaiting the coming of the immortal Bridegroom. For having acquired spiritual eyes, they continually foresaw that awesome hour, and held the contemplation of the good things to come and of the eternal punishment inseparable from their hearts; and they were eager to labor, that they might not fall short of everlasting glory. They became free of passion like the angels; and now they dance with those whose life they imitated. Blessed are these, and thrice blessed, because with the undeceived eyes of the mind they perceived the emptiness of present things, and the unsteadiness and unevenness of human prosperity, and, renouncing it, laid up for themselves the eternal good things, and laid hold of the life that never fails nor is cut short by death. These wondrous and holy men, then, we too, cheap and unworthy as we are, are eager to imitate,

though we do not attain the height of their heavenly-citizen way of life; but, so far as is possible to our weak and wretched strength, we mark out the character of their life and have clothed ourselves in their habit, even if we fall short of their works. For we know that this divine profession is a procurer of sinlessness and a fellow-worker of the incorruption given to us through holy baptism. And, following the words of those blessed men, we utterly condemn these corruptible and perishable affairs of life, in which nothing can be found that is secure, or even, or standing fast in the same state; but all things are emptiness and a grasping after wind, bearing many changes in a moment. For they are weaker than dreams and a shadow and a breeze blowing through the air; small and brief is their charm, and not even a charm, but a kind of wandering and deceit of the world's wickedness, which we have been taught not to love at all, but rather to hate from the heart. And it is in truth hateful and to be shunned; for whatever it gives to its friends, it snatches away again in anger, and sends them off to eternal affliction stripped of every good and clothed in shame, with heavy burdens laid upon them;

and those again whom it exalts, it soon brings down to the utmost wretchedness, making them footstools and a mockery of all their enemies. Such, then, are its favors; such are its gifts. For it is an enemy of its friends, and a plotter against all who do its will, and it dashes down terribly those who lean upon it, and unnerves those who trust in it. It makes agreements and false promises with the foolish, only to draw them in; but when they have been treated faithlessly, it shows itself faithless and false, fulfilling none of what it agreed. For having today smoothed their throats with sweet foods, tomorrow it sets them all as food for their enemies. Today it shows a man a king, and tomorrow hands him over to some wretched slavery; today flourishing with countless good things,

tomorrow a beggar and the slave of slaves. Today it sets the crown of its glory on his head; tomorrow it dashes his face to the ground. Today it adorns his neck with the splendid honors of high office; tomorrow it humbles him, bound in chains of iron. For a little while it makes him desirable to all; and after a little, strongly hated and abhorred. Today it gladdens him, and tomorrow wastes him away with laments and beatings of the breast. And what end it lays upon them, hear: it makes those who loved it pitiably the dwellers of Gehenna. Such is its mind always, such its purpose, plainly. It neither laments those who have passed away nor pities those who are left. For having dreadfully deceived those and shut them up in its nets, it tries to turn its skill again upon these, wishing none to escape its grievous snares. Those, then, who serve such a cruel and wicked master, who have in their madness removed themselves from the good and loving God, and stand gaping after present things and cling fast to them, taking no thought at all for the things to come,

and who press on without ceasing toward the enjoyments of the body, but let their souls waste away with hunger and be tormented with countless evils—these I think to be like a man fleeing from the face of a raging unicorn, who, unable to bear the sound of its roar and its fearful bellowing, and running hard to escape becoming its food, in his swift flight fell into a great pit; and as he fell into it, stretching out his hands and grasping a certain tree, he held it firmly, and, planting his feet on a kind of ledge, thought himself henceforth to be in peace and safety. But looking, he sees two mice, the one white, the other black, gnawing without ceasing at the root of the tree from which he hung, and all but reaching the point of cutting it through. And gazing at the bottom of the pit, he saw a dragon fearful to behold, breathing fire and glaring most fiercely, with its mouth gaping terribly and straining to swallow him. And looking again at the ledge on which he had set his feet, he saw the heads of four asps jutting out from the wall on which he was resting. And lifting up his eyes, he sees a little honey dripping from the branches of that tree. So, leaving off to consider the calamities surrounding him—

how outside the unicorn, raging dreadfully, sought to devour him, and below the bitter dragon gaped to swallow him, and the tree he had grasped was all but about to be cut down, and his feet rested on a slippery and untrustworthy ledge—forgetting unreasonably all these so many and so dreadful sights, with his whole mind he hung upon the sweetness of that little honey. This is the likeness of those who cling to the deceit of the present life, the meaning of which I will tell you at once. The unicorn would be the figure of death, which always pursues and presses to overtake the race of Adam; the pit is the world, full of all kinds of evils and death-bearing snares; the tree, ceaselessly gnawed by the two mice, which he had grasped, is the course of each one's life, spent and consumed through the hours of day and night, drawing little by little nearer to being cut off; the four asps signify the structure of the human body, set upon four treacherous and unstable elements, by whose disorder and disturbance the constitution of the body is dissolved. Besides this, that fiery and cruel dragon represents the fearful belly of Hades, raging to receive those who prefer the present delights to the good things to come. And the drop of honey shows the sweetness of the world's pleasures, by which it deceives its own friends and does not let them take thought for their salvation.
Josaphat, very well pleased with this

parable, said: How true this word is, and most fitting. Do not, then, hesitate to keep showing me such figures, that I may know exactly what our life is like, and of what things it becomes the procurer for its own friends. The old man said: Again, those who are enamored of the delights of life and made sweet by its pleasantness, who prefer the fleeting and feeble things to the things to come that do not waver, are like a certain man who had three friends. Two of them he honored with passionate affection, and clung strongly to their love, contending for them even unto death and choosing to face danger on their behalf; but toward the third he behaved with great contempt, never counting him worthy of honor or of the love that was his due, but feigning only some small and worthless friendship toward him. Now one day certain fearful and extraordinary soldiers came, hastening with great speed to bring this man to the king, that he might render account for a debt of ten thousand talents. In his distress he sought a helper, one able to take his part in the king's terrible reckoning. So running to the first and most genuine of all his friends, he said: You know, my friend, that I always laid down my life for you; now I need help on this day of the necessity that holds me.

How much, then, do you undertake to assist me now? And what hope is there for me from you, dearest friend? That friend answered and said: I am not your friend, man; I do not know who you are. For I have other friends, with whom I must make merry today and whom I must gain as friends for the future. But see, I give you two rags, to have with you on the road you are traveling—which will be of no use to you at all. And expect no other hope from me. Hearing this, and despairing of the help he had hoped for from him, the man goes to his second friend, and says: You remember, my comrade, how much honor and good regard you enjoyed from me; but today, having fallen into affliction and the greatest misfortune, I need a fellow-worker. How much, then, are you able to labor with me? Let me know at once. He says: I am not free today to contend alongside you; for I too have fallen into cares and troubles and am in affliction. Still, I will go a little way along the road with you, even if I am of no use to you; and then, turning back home quickly, I will be busy with my own cares. So returning from there too with empty hands and at a loss on every side, the man counted himself wretched for the vain hope he had set on his ungrateful friends, and for the useless hardships he had endured for love of them. He goes at last to his third friend,

whom he had never served, nor invited to share his gladness; and he says to him, with a shamed and downcast face: I have no mouth to open to you, knowing well that you do not remember my ever doing you a good turn or being affectionately disposed toward you. But since a most grievous misfortune has overtaken me, and I have found no hope of deliverance from any of my other friends, I have come to you, entreating you, if you have the strength, to grant me some small help. Do not, then, refuse, holding a grudge against my ingratitude. He says, with a cheerful and gracious face: Yes indeed, I confess you to be my most genuine friend; and remembering that small kindness of yours, I will repay you today with interest. Do not fear, then, nor be afraid; for I will go before you, I will entreat the king on your behalf, and I will by no means hand you over into the hands of your enemies. Take courage, then, dearest friend, and do not grieve. Then, pierced to the heart, the man said with tears: Alas, what shall I lament first, and what shall I weep for first? Shall I condemn my vain attachment to those forgetful and thankless and false friends? Or shall I count wretched the senseless ingratitude

that I showed toward this true and genuine friend? Josaphat, receiving this word too with wonder, sought its meaning. And Barlaam said: The first friend would be the abundance of wealth and the love of money, on account of which a man falls into countless dangers and endures many hardships; but when the last appointed day of death comes, he takes none of all those things, except the useless rags for his burial. The second friend is called wife and children and the rest of one's kin and household, to whose attachment we cling and from which we are hard to be torn, despising the love of our very soul and body for their sake; but no one has gained any benefit from them in the hour of death—rather they only accompany him as far as the tomb, following along, and then, turning back at once, are taken up with their own cares and troubles, covering the memory with forgetfulness no less than they covered with the grave the body of the one once dear to them. But the third friend, the neglected and burdensome one, the unapproachable, but rather shunned and as it were repugnant, is the company of the noblest works—such as faith, hope, love, almsgiving, love of mankind, and the rest of the throng of the virtues—which is able to go before us when we leave the body, and to entreat the Lord for us, and to ransom us from our enemies and the dreadful tax-collectors who set in motion a bitter reckoning against us in the air and seek bitterly to overpower us. This is the good and grateful friend,
who keeps our small good deed in remembrance and repays us all of it with interest.

Again, then, Josaphat said: May it go well with you from the Lord God, O wisest of men. For you have gladdened my soul with your fitting and excellent words. Therefore sketch for me yet another image of the emptiness of the world, and how one might pass through it in peace and safety. Taking up the discourse, Barlaam said: Hear also the likeness of this problem. I have learned of a certain great city whose citizens had from of old this custom: that they would take some stranger, a man unknown, who knew nothing at all of the laws and traditions of the city, and set him up as their king, who enjoyed all authority and held to his own will unhindered until the completion of a year's time. Then, suddenly, while he was in complete freedom from care, living in luxury and reveling without fear, and thinking that the kingship would abide with him forever, they rose up against him, and stripping off the royal robe, and parading him naked through the whole city, they sent him into exile to a great island far away and remote, where, with no supply of food or clothing, he was dreadfully worn down by hunger and nakedness—the luxury and gladness given to him beyond hope being changed again into grief, beyond all hope and expectation. Now, according to the custom that prevailed among those citizens, a certain man was put forward to the kingship who had a mind richly furnished

with much understanding, who at once was not carried away by the abundance that had suddenly fallen upon him, nor did he envy the carefree state of those who had reigned before him and had been wretchedly cast out, but kept his soul anxious and earnest as to how he might arrange his affairs well. By constant reflection he made careful inquiry, and learned through a most wise counselor the custom of the citizens and the place of perpetual exile; and he was taught without error how he ought to make himself secure. When, then, he knew this, and that he must very soon reach that island and leave again to others this acquired and alien kingship, he opened his treasuries—of which until then he had free and unhindered use—and taking a quantity of money, gold and silver and a most weighty mass of precious stones, he handed them to his most trusted servants and sent them ahead to that island to which he was to be led away. And when the appointed year was completed, the citizens rose up and sent him, naked like those before him, into exile. So the rest of the foolish and short-lived kings starved dreadfully;

but he, having laid up that wealth beforehand, lived in perpetual abundance and had luxury without cost, and, having shaken off all fear of the disorderly and wicked citizens, counted himself blessed for his most wise good counsel. Understand, then, by the city this vain and deceitful world; by the citizens, the principalities and powers of the demons, the world-rulers of the darkness of this age, who allure us with the smoothness of pleasure, and lead us to think of the corruptible and perishable things as though they were incorruptible—as if the enjoyment of them abided with us and existed together with us immortally. So when we have been deceived and have taken no thought for those abiding and eternal things, nor stored up anything for ourselves for the life beyond, the ruin of death stands suddenly upon us. Then indeed, then, the wicked and bitter citizens of darkness receive us, stripped of the things here, as those who spent all their time on them, and lead us away into a dark and gloomy land, into a land of eternal darkness, where there is no light, nor the sight of the life of mortals. And by the good counselor, who made known all the truth and taught the saving practices to the prudent and most wise king, understand my own cheap and lowly self, who have come to point out to you the good and unerring way, leading you to the eternal and unending things and counseling you to lay up everything there, but leading you away from this deceitful world,

which I too, unhappily, used to love, and to whose delights and enjoyments I clung. But considering with the unerring eyes of the mind how the whole life of men is worn away among these things—some arriving, others departing, and none having what is fixed and secure: neither the rich in their wealth, nor the powerful in their strength, nor the wise in their wisdom, nor again the prosperous in their prosperity, nor those who live in luxury in their reveling, nor those who think they live securely in their vain and most feeble security, nor in any other of the things here praised, but the matter resembles the passage of torrents falling into the measureless deep of the sea (for so fleeting and short-lived are all present things)—I understood that such things are all empty and that there is no benefit in them, but, just as all former things are hidden in forgetfulness—whether you speak of glory, or kingship, or the splendors of high offices, or the weight of dominion, or the boldness of tyrants, or any of such things—so too the present things will be dimmed in the times that follow and come after. And I, being one of these, will surely fall under the customary change, and just as those before me were not allowed to delight in present things for an age, so will it be with me also. For I saw what this tyrannical and tumultuous world does to men, removing them from here to there—

some from wealth to poverty, others from poverty to glory; leading these out of life, and again bringing in others in their place; rejecting some who are wise and prudent, and making the honored and conspicuous dishonored and cheap, while seating others, unwise and unprudent, on the throne of glory, and showing the honorable to all as dishonored and obscure. And one may see the race of men in no way at all standing fast before the face of its cruel tyranny; but, as when a dove, fleeing from an eagle or a hawk, changes place after place, now to this tree, now to that bush, then dashing herself at once against the clefts of the rocks and all kinds of thorns, and finding nowhere a safe refuge, is worn out with perpetual tossing and trembling, so are those who are agog after present things—laboring wretchedly under an unreasoning impulse, having nothing at all firm or secure, neither knowing to what end they come, nor where this vain life is leading them, to which they have subjected themselves most unhappily and wretchedly, choosing evil things instead of good, taking up wickedness instead of goodness—or who it is that inherits the cold fruit of their many and toilsome labors, whether one of their own household or a stranger; and often it is not even a friend or acquaintance at all, but an enemy and foe. All these things and what follows from them I judged in the tribunal of my soul, and I hated my whole life, spent in vain things, which I passed clinging to the labors of earth.

But when I cast off from my soul the attachment to these things and threw it away, the things that are truly good shone forth: to fear God and to do his will. For I knew this to be the sum of all good things; this is also called the beginning of wisdom and wisdom made perfect; for it is a life free of grief and of harm to those who hold to it, and secure to those who lean upon it as upon the Lord. So, having set my thought upon the most unerring way of the Lord's commandments, and knowing exactly that there is nothing crooked or tangled in it, nor is it full of ravines and crags and thorns and briers, but that the whole is smooth and even, delighting the eyes of those who travel it with the brightest sights, and making beautiful the feet, and shoeing them with the readiness of the gospel of peace, that they may walk securely and swiftly—this way I rightly preferred to all, and I began to build up the fallen and ruined house of my soul. While I was thus arranging my affairs and setting right the unsteadiness of my mind, I heard the words of a certain wise teacher crying out to me thus: Come out, he said, all you who long to be saved;

depart from the emptiness of the world; for its fashion is passing away in a very little while, and behold, it will not be. Come out without turning back—yet not for nothing and without reward, but bearing provisions of eternal life; for you are about to walk a long road that has much need of provisions from here. And you will reach the eternal place that has two regions, each having many dwellings within it: one of which God has prepared for those who love him and keep his commandments, filled with all kinds of good things, in which those counted worthy will live perpetually in incorruption, enjoying undying immortality, where pain and grief and groaning have fled away; the second, full of darkness and affliction and pain, has been prepared for the devil and his angels, into which will also be cast those who by their wicked works procured it for themselves—those who exchanged the present things for the incorruptible and eternal, and made their whole selves food for the eternal fire. When I heard this voice and recognized its truthfulness, I made it my work to reach that lodging which is free of all pain and grief, and is full of such great security and such good things—the knowledge of which is now in me only in part, since I am an infant in spiritual stature and see the things there as through a glass and in riddles;

but when the perfect comes, and I know face to face, then what is in part will be done away. I give thanks, then, to God through Jesus Christ our Lord; for the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed me from the law of sin and death, and has opened my eyes to see without error that the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace. And just as I, having recognized the emptiness of present things, hated them with a perfect hatred, so I counsel you too to know concerning these things, that you may be disposed toward them as toward things alien and quickly passing away; and, taking everything from here, may lay up for yourself in the incorruptible age a treasure that cannot be plundered, a wealth that cannot be spent, where you must go without delay, so that, when you depart, you may not be in want, but laden with wealth—just as I set before you above the most fitting image of these things.
Josaphat said to the old man: How, then, will I be able to send treasures of money and wealth ahead

to that place, so that when I depart I may find the enjoyment of them unplundered and unspoiled? And how shall I show my hatred of present things and hold fast to the eternal ones? Make it very clear to me. Barlaam said: The sending ahead of this wealth to the eternal place is done by the hands of the poor. For one of the prophets, the most wise Daniel, says to the king of Babylon: Therefore, O king, let my counsel be pleasing to you; redeem your sins by almsgiving and your injustices by compassion for the poor. And the Savior says: Make for yourselves friends out of the mammon of unrighteousness, so that when you fail, they may receive you into the eternal dwellings. And the Master makes much discourse, above and below, about almsgiving and sharing with the poor, as we learn in the Gospel. In this way, then, you will most securely send everything ahead to that place by the hands of those in need; for whatever you do for these, the Master, claiming it as done to himself, will repay you many times over;

for he always outdoes those who love him by the recompense of his gifts.
