In this way, then, having for now plundered the treasures of the darkness of this age, which you have wretchedly served for a long time now, you will be well provisioned out of them for the future; and, taking everything from what belongs to another, you will lay it up beforehand for yourself, purchasing through these fleeting and short-lived things the things that stand fast and abide. Then, God working with you, you will perceive the unsteadiness and unevenness of the world, and, having said farewell to all things, you will shift your moorings toward the future—passing by the things that pass by, and being added to the things hoped for and standing fast; leaving the darkness behind along with the shadow of death; hating the world and the world-ruler, and reckoning the corruptible flesh an enemy to yourself; and you will run to the unapproachable light, and, taking up the cross on your shoulders, you will follow him without turning back, that you may be glorified together with him and be shown to be an heir of the life that no longer changes nor deceives. Josaphat said: Is the disregarding of all things, then, and the taking up of so laborious a life as you have described above, an ancient tradition coming down from the teaching of the apostles? Or has it lately been devised by you in the knowledge of your own mind, as having chosen this to be better?

The old man said to him: I am not teaching you a law lately introduced—God forbid—but one given to us of old. For the Lord said to a certain rich man who asked him, What shall I do to inherit eternal life? and who boasted that he had kept all that was written in the law: One thing, he said, you lack; go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me, taking up the cross. But when he heard this he became deeply grieved, for he was very rich. And Jesus, seeing that he had become deeply grieved, said: How hard it is for those who have money to enter the kingdom of God! For it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God. All the saints, then, hearing this commandment, took care to separate themselves entirely from such a difficulty of wealth; and scattering everything, and through the distribution to the poor laying up beforehand for themselves eternal wealth, they took up the cross and followed Christ—some perfected by martyrdom, as I have already told you, others contending in the ascetic life, and falling short of those in nothing in the conduct of this true philosophy. Know, then, that this is a commandment of Christ our

King and God, leading us away from corruptible things and making us partakers of the eternal. Since, then, such a philosophy is ancient and so necessary, says Josaphat, how is it that many do not emulate this life today? The old man said: Many have emulated it and do emulate it, but most hold back and shrink from it; for few, as the Lord says, are the travelers of the narrow and hard way, but many of the loose and broad one. For those who have once been taken captive by the love of money and the evils of pleasure-loving, and cling to empty and vain glory, are hard to be torn from these, since they have willingly sold themselves as slaves to an alien master, and stand opposed to God who commands these things, and are held bound by him. For a soul that has once despaired of its own salvation, giving over its reins to irrational desires, is carried about everywhere. Therefore the Prophet, bewailing the folly poured out over such souls, and lamenting the thickness of the mist that lies upon them, said: Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love emptiness and seek a lie? With which one of our own wise teachers, a most theological man, agreeing, and adding something of his own,

cries out to all as from some lofty and most exalted watchtower: Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love emptiness and seek a lie?—supposing the life here, and luxury, and the little scrap of glory, and lowly power, and lying prosperity to be something great—things that belong no more to those who hold them than to those who hoped for them, nor more to these than to those who never even expected them; things that, like dust before a tempest, are tossed and flung about from some to others, or stream away like smoke, or sport like a dream, and like a shadow cannot be grasped; neither, when absent, beyond the hope of those who do not possess them, nor, when present, to be trusted by those who have them. So then, since the Savior commands these things, and the Prophets and Apostles proclaim them, and all the saints in deed and word press us toward the most unerring way of virtue, even if few are those who travel it and more are those who prefer the broad way that leads to destruction, the conduct of this godly philosophy will not be lessened on that account. But just as the sun, rising to give light to all, sends forth its rays ungrudgingly, urging all to be enlightened, so too the true philosophy lights up its lovers like the sun, and warms them, and makes them bright. And if some, closing their eyes, are unwilling to behold its radiance, the sun is not on this account to be blamed, nor overlooked by the rest, nor will the glory of its brightness be dishonored through their dullness;

but those, having deprived themselves of the light, will grope a wall like blind men, and will fall into many pits, and have their eyes pierced by many thorns, while the sun, standing in its own brightness, will give light to those who with unveiled face reflect its radiance. In the same way too the light of Christ shines richly upon all, imparting to us of its splendor; but each shares in it according to his longing and eagerness. For neither does the sun of righteousness deprive any who wish to gaze upon it steadily, nor does it force those who willingly choose the darkness; but each is left to his own free choice, so long as he is in the present life. When Josaphat asked, What is free will, and what is choice? the old man said: Free will is the willing of a rational soul, moved unhindered toward whatever it may wish, whether virtue or vice, the soul being so made by the Creator. Free will, again, is the self-governing movement of a thinking soul. Choice is the deliberative desire of things within our power, or a desiderative deliberation of things within our power; for we desire, by choosing, the thing preferred out of deliberation. Deliberation is an inquiring desire concerning the things within our power that can be done; for one deliberates whether he ought to undertake the matter or not. Then he judges the better course, and there comes judgment. Then he is disposed toward and loves what was judged from the deliberation, and this is called inclination; for if one judges,

but is not disposed toward what was judged—that is, does not love it—it is not called inclination. Then, after the disposition, there comes choice—that is, selection; for choice is, when two things are set before us, to take the one and select it before the other. And this is plain, that choice is deliberation together with decision, even from its very etymology; for the thing chosen is the one preferable before the other. But no one prefers anything without deliberating, nor chooses without preferring. For since we are not eager to bring into action everything that has seemed good to us, then what was preferred out of deliberation becomes choice and a thing chosen when it takes on desire. And so it is gathered that choice is the deliberative desire of things within our power; for we desire, by choosing, the thing preferred out of deliberation. For every deliberation is for the sake of action and on account of action; and so deliberation leads every choice, and choice leads every action. For this reason not only actions, but also the things in the mind, which represent the choices, procure both crowns and punishments. For the beginning of sin and of right-doing is choice, exercised in the things within our power; for of those things whose workings are in our power, the actions too that accord with the working are in our power; and the workings that accord with virtue are in our power; therefore the virtues too are in our power. For all the things of the soul, and those about which we deliberate, are properly in our power. So, men deliberating freely and

choosing freely, in proportion as a man chooses, in that proportion he also shares in the divine light and advances in the pursuits of philosophy; for there are differences of choice. And just as certain springs of water sent up from the hollows of the earth—some gush out near the surface of the earth, others a little deeper, others very deep; and of these waters some, gushing out close to the surface, are sweet to the taste, while others, coming out deep, are salt or sulphurous; and some are given forth abundantly, others drip out little by little—so too understand it with regard to the choices: that some are quick and most fervent, others sluggish and cold, and some have their whole inclination toward good things, while others incline with all their power to the opposite. According to their dispositions, then, the impulses toward actions also follow.
Josaphat said to the old man: Are there, then, others also now who proclaim these things as you do? Or are you alone today in teaching these things and describing the present life as so hateful?

He answered and said: In this most unhappy country of yours I know of no one. For your father's tyranny surrounded such men with countless deaths, and made it his work that the proclamation of the knowledge of God should not be heard among you at all. But in all the other tongues these things are sung and glorified—by some with the most upright doctrine, by others perversely, since the enemy of our souls has made them turn aside from the straight way and has parceled them out among alien doctrines, and has taught them to interpret certain sayings of the Scriptures otherwise and not according to the sense that lies within them. But the truth is one, that proclaimed through the glorious apostles and the God-bearing fathers, and shining out in the catholic Church from the ends to the ends of the world brighter than the sun—of which I have been sent to you as herald and teacher. Josaphat said to him: Has my father, then, learned nothing of these things? The old man said: Plainly and properly he has learned nothing; for, stopping up his senses, he willingly does not receive the good, having of his own choice inclined toward evil. But I would wish, said Josaphat, that he too were initiated into these things. The old man said: The things that are impossible with men are all possible with God. For what do you know but that you will save your father, and in a wonderful manner become the begetter of your own begetter?

For I have heard that there was a certain king who governed his kingdom very well, and treated the people under him gently and mildly, failing in this one thing only: that he was not rich in the illumination of the knowledge of God, but was held fast in the error of idols. He had a certain good counselor, adorned in every way both with piety toward God and with all the rest of virtuous wisdom; who, grieved and distressed at the king's error and wishing to reprove him concerning it, was held back from the impulse, fearing lest he become the cause of evils both to himself and to his companions, and cut off the benefit that came to many through him. Yet he sought a fitting occasion to draw the king toward the good. So one night the king said to him: Come now, let us go out and walk about the city, in case we may see something profitable. And as they walked about the city, they saw a gleam of light shining from a certain crevice; and casting their eyes on it, they see an underground, cave-like dwelling, in which there sat a man living in the utmost poverty and clothed in cheap rags. His wife stood by, mixing wine. And as the man took the cup in his hands, she sang a clear-toned tune and made him merry, dancing and charming her husband with praises. Those about the king, then, observing this for a good while, marveled that, pressed by such poverty as to have neither a house nor clothing, they passed their life so cheerfully;

and the king said to his chief counselor: How strange, my friend, that to you and me our life never pleased us even thus, shining as it does with such glory and luxury, as this cheap and wretched living delights these foolish people, and as this harsh and detestable life appears to them smooth and agreeable! Seizing the opportune moment, the chief counselor said: But to you, O king, how does their life appear? Of all that I have ever seen, said the king, the most distasteful and unhappy, abominable and to be shunned. Then the chief counselor said to him: Know well, then, O king, that our life is reckoned far more grievous by those who have seen and been initiated into that everlasting glory and the good things that surpass all understanding; and these houses gleaming with gold, and these splendid garments, and all the rest of the luxury of this life, are more distasteful than dung and squalor to the eyes of those who know the inexpressible beauties of the dwellings in heaven not made with hands, the God-woven robe and the incorruptible diadems which God, the Creator and Lord of all, has prepared for those who love him.

For in the same way that these were reckoned by us to be foolish, much more we, who wander about the world and please ourselves in this lying glory and senseless luxury, are worthy of laments and tears in the eyes of those who have tasted the sweetness of those good things. The king, hearing this and becoming as it were dumbstruck, said: Who, then, are those who have a life better than ours? All, said the chief counselor, who have preferred the eternal things to the temporal. Again the king sought to learn what the eternal things were, and the man said: A kingdom without succession, and a life not subject to death, and wealth that never fears poverty, and joy and gladness with no share of grief or vexation, and perpetual peace free of all enmity and contention. Those counted worthy to enjoy these are blessed, and that many times over; for they will live a life without grief and without toil forever, enjoying without labor all the pleasant and delightful things of the kingdom of God, and reigning together with Christ without end. And when the king said, Who is worthy to attain these things? he answered: All who have laid hold of the road that leads there; for the entrance is unhindered to those who only wish it. And the king said: And what is the path that leads there?

To him that man, bright of soul, said: To know the only true God, and Jesus Christ his only-begotten Son, and the Holy and life-giving Spirit. The king, then, having understanding worthy of the purple, said to him: And what has hindered you until now from making this known to me? For these things do not seem to me worthy of delay and postponement, if indeed they are true; and if they are doubtful, one must search laboriously until I find what is beyond dispute. It was not, said the man, out of negligence or slackness that I hesitated to make these things known to you, true as they are and altogether beyond dispute, but out of reverence for the surpassing greatness of your glory, lest I should seem too troublesome to you. If, then, you bid your servant remind you henceforth concerning these things, I will be obedient to your command. Yes, said the king, not only each day, but each hour renew the memory of these things continually; for one must attend to them not carelessly, but very warmly and earnestly. We have heard, then, says Barlaam, that this king lived piously thereafter, and, having passed the present life without storm, did not fail of the blessedness to come. If, then, someone reminds your father of such things at a fitting time,

perhaps he too will understand and recognize in what evils he is held fast, and, turning aside from them, will choose the good; since for the present he is blind, dim-sighted, having deprived himself of the true light and deserted to the darkness of impiety. Josaphat said to him: As for my father's affairs, may the Lord lead them as he wills; for to him, as you have said, all things are possible that are impossible with men. But I, through your matchless words, having condemned the emptiness of present things, have resolved to withdraw from them entirely, and to pass the rest of my life with you, that I may not, through these temporal and fleeting things, fall away from the enjoyment of the eternal and incorruptible. To him the old man answered: If you do this, you will be like a certain most prudent young man, of whom I have heard that he was of rich and renowned parents. His father betrothed to him the daughter of one distinguished by nobility and wealth, a most beautiful girl, and, having talked with the boy about the marriage and told him what he was planning, the boy, when he heard it, shook off the matter as something jarring and out of place, and went away a fugitive, leaving his father. As he traveled he was given lodging in the house of a certain poor old man, resting himself there from the day's scorching heat.

The poor man's daughter, who was his only child and a virgin, sitting before the doors, worked with her hands, but with her mouth blessed God without ceasing, giving thanks to him from the depths of her soul. The young man, hearing her hymns, said: What, woman, is your occupation? And for what reason, being so cheap and poor, do you give thanks as for some great gifts, hymning the giver? She answered him: Do you not know that, just as a small medicine often delivers a man from great diseases, so too giving thanks to God for small things becomes the procurer of great ones? I, then, being the daughter of a poor old man, give thanks for these small things and bless God, knowing that he who gave these is able to give greater ones as well. And these things are about the external things that are not our own,

from which neither does any gain come to those who possess much—not to say that there is often even loss—nor does harm come to those who have received less, since both travel the same road and press toward the same end; but in the most necessary and crucial things I have enjoyed many and very great gifts of my Master, gifts that have no number nor are subject to estimation. For I have been made in the image of God, and counted worthy of the knowledge of him, and adorned with reason above all living things, and called back from death to life through the tender mercies of our God, and have received authority to share in his mysteries, and the door of paradise has been opened, offering me unhindered entrance, if only I wish it. Of so many and such great gifts, then, in which rich and poor share alike, it is altogether impossible for me to give worthy thanks;

and if I do not offer even this small hymn to the giver, what defense shall I have? The young man, marveling exceedingly at her great understanding, called her father and said: Give me your daughter; for I have come to love her understanding and piety. The old man said: It is not lawful for you to take this poor man's daughter, you being of rich parents. Again the young man said: Yes, I will take her, if you do not forbid it; for the daughter of noble and wealthy parents was betrothed to me, and shaking her off, I took to flight; but, loving your daughter for her piety toward God and her sensible understanding, I have set my heart on being joined to her. The old man said to him: I cannot give her to you, to lead her away to your father's house and separate her from my arms; for she is my only child. But I, said the young man, will stay with you, and take up your way of life. Then, laying aside his splendid clothing, he asked for the old man's and put it on. The old man tested him much, and in various ways proved his mind; and when he knew that he was of steady purpose, and that it was not held captive by a love of folly that he asked for his daughter, but that out of love of piety he chose to live in poverty, preferring this to his own glory and noble birth, he took him by the hand and led him into his storeroom, and showed him much wealth laid up for him and an uncountable mass of money, such as the young man had never beheld;

and he said to him: My child, all this I give you, in return for your having chosen to become my daughter's husband and the heir of my substance. And taking possession of that inheritance, the young man surpassed all the renowned and rich of the earth.

Josaphat said to Barlaam: This account too fittingly represents my own case; whence I think these things have been spoken by you concerning me as well. But what is the test by which you seek to know the steadiness of my mind? The old man said: I, for my part, have already tested and known of what prudent and steady mind you are, and of what soul truly most upright. But the outcome of your conduct will confirm these things. For this reason I bend my knees to our God who is glorified in the Trinity, the Creator of all things visible and invisible, who truly is and ever is, who never had a beginning of his glorious existence nor has an end, the fearful and almighty, good and compassionate, that he may enlighten the eyes of your heart, and give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him,

so that you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what is the wealth of the glory of his inheritance among the saints, and what is the surpassing greatness of his power toward us who believe—that you may no longer be a stranger and a sojourner, but a fellow-citizen of the saints and of the household of God, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, the cornerstone being our Lord Jesus Christ himself, in whom the whole building, fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord. Josaphat, deeply pierced in heart, said: These things I too long to know, and I beg you: make known to me both the wealth of the glory of God and the surpassing greatness of his power. Barlaam said to him: I pray God to teach you these things and to put the knowledge of them into your soul; since to declare his glory and power among men is altogether impossible, even if all the tongues of men now living and of all who have ever lived were to become one. For God, says the evangelist and theologian, no one has ever seen; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known. And who of those born of earth could grasp the glory and majesty of the invisible and infinite One,

unless he himself reveal it to whom he will, so far as he wills—just as he revealed it to his prophets and apostles? But we, from their proclamation and from the very nature of things, learn as far as is granted to us. For the Scripture says: The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands; and: The invisible things of him, from the creation of the world, being understood by the things he has made, are clearly seen, both his eternal power and divinity. For just as a man, seeing a house splendidly and skillfully built, or a vessel cunningly fitted together, would at once think of the builder or the craftsman and marvel, so I too, having been shaped from things that were not and brought into being—even if I have not been able to behold the One who shaped and provided me—yet from my own well-fitted and most wonderful construction came to a knowledge of his wisdom, not as to what it is, but so far as I am able to conceive: that I was not brought forth of myself, nor did I come into being from myself, but he himself shaped me as he willed, appointing me to take precedence over all creatures, yet making me less than some, and, when I was broken, shaping me anew by a better renewal, and then leading me out from here by his divine command and transferring me to another life unending and eternal—in none of which I am able to resist the strength of his providence,

nor to add anything to myself nor to take away, whether in respect of stature or of the form of my shape, nor to have the power to renew what has grown old in me, nor to set right what has been corrupted. For no one among men has ever been able to accomplish any of these things—neither king, nor wise man, nor rich man, nor ruler, nor any other who pursues human enterprises; for no one, it says, of kings or of those in high places had any other beginning of birth, but there is one entrance for all into life, and an equal exit. From these things, then, that concern myself, I am led by the hand to a knowledge of the Creator's great work; and along with these, considering also the well-fitted construction and the preservation of all creation, that the things themselves are all of themselves subject to turning and change—the intelligible according to choice, both the advance in the good and the falling away from the good, and the perceptible according to generation and corruption, increase and decrease, and change in quality and movement in place—from these too they proclaim with unspeakable voices that they have been made by the uncreated and unturning and unchanging God,

and are held together, and preserved, and ever provided for. For how could opposite natures have come together with one another for the completion of one world, and remained undissolved, unless some almighty power had brought them together and ever preserved them undissolved? For how could anything have remained, unless he himself had willed it? Or how could what was not called by him have been preserved? says the Scripture. For if a ship without a helmsman does not hold together, but is easily sunk, and a small house would not stand without one to care for it, how could the world have held together for so many ages—a work of creation so great, so beautiful and wonderful—without some glorious and great and wonderful governance and all-wise providence? For behold, how long has the heaven endured, and it has not grown dim; the power of the earth has not failed, bearing fruit for so long a time; the springs have not ceased to gush forth since they came to be; the sea, receiving so many rivers, has not exceeded its measure; the courses of the sun and the moon have not been altered; the orderings of day and night have not been changed. From all these the unspeakable power and magnificence of God is made manifest to us,

witnessed by prophets and apostles; yet no one will be able worthily to conceive or to praise his glory. For all things, both the intelligible and whatever falls under perception, the divine Apostle, who had Christ speaking within him, considered and said: We know in part and we prophesy in part; but when the perfect comes, then what is in part will be done away. Therefore also, astounded at the infinite wealth of his wisdom and knowledge, he said outright: O the depth of the wealth and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out! And if that man, who reached as far as the third heaven and heard unspeakable words, uttered such words, who of those like me could at all look in the face the abysses of so many mysteries, and say anything to the purpose, or be able to conceive worthily of the things spoken, unless the giver of wisdom himself, the corrector of the unwise, should grant it? For in his hand are both we and our words, and all prudence and understanding are with him, and the knowledge of understanding; and he himself has given us the unerring knowledge of the things that are: to know the constitution of the world and the working of the elements, the beginning and end and middle of times, the alternations of the solstices and the changes of the seasons, and that he ordered all things by measure and weight.

For great strength is ever present with him, and who will withstand the might of his arm? For the whole world before him is as a turn of the scales, and as a drop of morning dew that has come down upon the earth. But he has mercy upon all, because he can do all things, and overlooks the sins of men for repentance; for he abhors nothing, nor turns away from those who run to him, the only good and soul-loving Master. Blessed be the name of his glory, the holy and most exalted and most highly praised, unto the ages. Amen.

Josaphat said to him: If you had pondered for a very long time, O wisest of men, how you might best make clear to us the solution of the questions put forward, you could not, it seems to me, have done this better than by telling me such things as you have now declared—teaching that God is the Creator and sustainer of all, and proving by irrefutable arguments that the glory of his majesty is incomprehensible to human reasonings, and that no other is able to attain to it,

but only those to whom he himself reveals it, so far as he commands. Therefore I have marveled exceedingly at your most eloquent wisdom. But tell me, most blessed one, how many years old you are, in what places you have your dwelling, and whom you have as your companions in philosophy. For my soul is strongly bound to yours, and I in no way wish to be parted from you for all the time of my life. The old man said: I am, as I reckon, forty-five years old; and, living in the deserts of the land of Senaar, I have as fellow-strugglers those who labor with me and contend together for the course of the journey above. How, said Josaphat, do you tell me these things? For you appear to me to be beyond some seventy years. What, then, do you mean by your forty-five years? For you do not seem to me to be speaking the truth in this. Barlaam said to him: If you are seeking to learn the years of my birth, you have well guessed them to be beyond some seventy; but to me they have in no way been reckoned in the measure of life, all those that were spent in the emptiness of the world. For when I lived enslaved in the flesh to sins,

I was dead in the inner man. The years of that deadness, then, I would never name as life. But from the time that the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world, and, having put off the old man, who is being corrupted according to the desires of deceit, I no longer live in the flesh, but Christ lives in me, and the life I now live I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me—these I would fittingly call both the years of life and the days of salvation; and reckoning them at about forty-five years, I have declared their number to you reasonably and not beside the mark. You too, then, hold to such a reckoning always, in no way supposing those to live who are dead to every good work, but live in sins and serve the world-ruler of the things dragged down below, spending their life in pleasures and wicked desires; but know well that these are put to death and dead to the working of life. For sin a certain wise man fittingly called the death of the immortal soul; and the Apostle too says:

When you were slaves of sin, you were free in regard to righteousness. What fruit, then, did you have at that time in the things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death. But now, having been freed from sin and enslaved to God, you have your fruit unto sanctification, and the end eternal life. For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life. Josaphat said to him: Since the life in the flesh is not reckoned by you in the measure of life, neither ought you to reckon as death the death which all undergo. The old man answered: Beyond dispute I hold thus concerning these things also, in no way trembling at this temporal death, nor calling it death at all—at least if it overtakes me while I walk the way of the commandments of God—but rather a passage from death to the better and more perfect life, hidden in Christ, which the saints, longing to attain, were much vexed with the present one. Therefore the Apostle says: We know that, if our earthly house of this tabernacle is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal, in the heavens; for in this we groan, longing to be clothed upon with our dwelling that is from heaven, if indeed, being clothed, we shall not be found naked;

for we who are in this tabernacle groan, being burdened, in that we do not wish to be unclothed, but clothed upon, that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life. And again: Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death? And once more: I desire to depart and to be with Christ. And the Prophet says: When shall I come and appear before the face of God? And that I too, the least of all, in no way seem to fear the perceptible death, you can know from the fact that, counting your father's threat as nothing, I came to you without fear and proclaimed to you the saving word, knowing exactly that, if these things came to his knowledge, he would, if he could, subject me to countless deaths. But I, preferring the word of God to all things and longing to attain it, neither dread the temporal death, nor call it at all worthy of such a name, obeying the Master's commandment that says: Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear the one who is able to destroy both soul and body in Gehenna. These, then, said Josaphat, are the achievements of your true philosophy, far surpassing the nature of the earthly-minded who are hard to be torn from the present life; and blessed are you who hold to such a most manly resolve.

But what is the food of you and those with you in such a desert, and from where are your garments, and of what sort? Make it known to me truthfully. Barlaam said: The food is from the wild fruits and herbs that are found, which the desert nourishes, watered by the dew of heaven and yielding to the command of the Creator—over which there is no one who fights with us and quarrels and seeks to snatch the greater share by the rule and reasoning of greed; but ungrudgingly there lies before all an unsown food and a table prepared of itself. And if at any time one of the faithful brothers who live near brings a blessing of bread, we receive it as sent by providence, for a blessing upon those who have faithfully offered it. The garments are of rags of hair and of sheepskins or palm-fiber, all old and much-patched, severely wearing down this weak flesh. For the same covering is ours in summer and in winter,

which it is in no way lawful, once we have put it on, to take off until, grown old, it is utterly worn out. For thus, worn down by the necessities of cold and burning heat, we provide for ourselves the clothing of the garments of incorruption to come. When Josaphat said: But from where is this garment that you are wearing? the old man said: I have taken it on loan from one of the faithful brothers, being about to make the journey to you; for it was not fitting for me to come in my usual garment. Just as someone who has a most beloved kinsman taken captive and carried off into a foreign nation, and wishing to lead him out from there, lays aside his own dress and, putting on the mask of the adversaries, reaches their country, and by many devices frees his kinsman from the bitter tyranny—in the same way I too, having been informed of your case, put on this guise and came to cast the seed of the divine proclamation into your heart, and to ransom you from the slavery of the dreadful world-ruler.

And now, behold, by the power of God, so far as in me lay, I have done my service, proclaiming to you the knowledge of him and making known the proclamation of the prophets and apostles, and teaching unerringly and truthfully the emptiness of present things and what evils the world is full of, grievously deceiving those who obey it and entangling them in many ways. It remains, then, for me to go back from where I came; and then, laying aside the borrowed guise, I shall be clothed in my own. So Josaphat entreated the old man to be seen by him in his usual garment. Then Barlaam, taking off the cloak he was wearing, was seen as a fearful sight by Josaphat. For all the substance of his flesh was wasted away, and his skin was blackened by the burning of the sun and stretched tight over his bones, as if one stretched a hide over thin reeds; and a hair-cloth rag, shrunken and very coarse, was girt about him from the loins to the knees; and a like cloak was thrown about his shoulders. Marveling exceedingly at the laboriousness of this hard way of life, and astounded at his surpassing endurance, Josaphat wept bitterly, and said to the old man: Since you have come to free me from the bitter slavery of the devil, set the seal upon your kindness: Bring my soul out of prison,

and, taking me with you, let us go from here, that, being completely ransomed from the deceit of the world, I may then receive the seal of saving baptism, and become a sharer with you in this wonderful philosophy and supernatural asceticism. Barlaam said to him: A rich man was raising the fawn of a gazelle. When it had grown, it longed for the deserts, drawn by its natural disposition. So going out one day, it finds a herd of gazelles grazing, and keeping with them it went about in the plains of the woodland, returning toward evening, but in the morning, through the carelessness of the servants, going out and herding with the wild ones. And when those moved farther off to graze, it followed along with them. But the rich man's servants, perceiving this, mounted on horses and pursued after them, and capturing their own gazelle and bringing it back home, made it go out no more thereafter; but of the rest of the herd they killed some and ill-treated others. In the same way I fear that it will happen to us also, if you follow me: lest I be deprived of your fellowship as well, and become the cause of many evils to my companions, and of eternal judgment to your father. But this the Lord wills for you: for now to be marked with the seal of holy baptism, and to remain in your place, holding fast to all piety and the practice of the commandments of Christ.

And when the giver of all good things grants the occasion, then you will come also to us, and we shall dwell together for the remainder of the present life. And I trust in the Lord that in the life to come too we shall be inseparable. Again Josaphat, weeping, said to him: If these things seem good to the Lord, let his will be done. Perfect me, then, with holy baptism, and, taking from me money and garments for the food and clothing of yourself and your companions, go to the place of your asceticism, guarded by the peace of God. And do not cease praying for me, that I may not fall away from my hope, but may quickly be able to reach you and, in deep stillness, enjoy the benefit that comes from you. Barlaam said: As for your receiving the seal of Christ, there is nothing to hinder it. Prepare yourself, then; and, the Lord working with you, you will be perfected. But as for the money you spoke of giving to my companions, how shall this be—that you, the poor man, give alms to the rich? For the rich always do good to the poor, but not the needy to the well-off. For the last of all my companions is incomparably richer than you. But I trust in the mercies of God that you too will very soon be exceedingly rich; and then you will not be ready to give. Josaphat said to him: Make the saying clear to me—how the last of all your companions surpasses me in wealth, those whom a little while ago you said lived in great poverty and were worn down with the utmost

destitution; and how it is that now you call me poor, while you say that when I become exceedingly rich I, who am now ready to give, will not be ready to give. Barlaam answered: I did not say that these are worn down by poverty, but that they exult in wealth that is never emptied. For always to add money to money, and not to bridle one's impulse, but insatiably to reach out for more, this is the utmost poverty. But those who have disregarded present things out of longing for the eternal, and counted these as dung that they might gain Christ alone, and have laid aside all anxiety about food and clothing and cast it upon the Lord, and rejoice in their possessing nothing as no lover of the world could rejoice though laden with wealth and money, and have gathered to themselves abundantly the wealth of virtue, and are nourished by the hopes of the unending good things—these I would fittingly call richer than you and than all the earthly kingdom. And, God working with you, you too will lay hold of such a spiritual abundance, which, keeping it in safety and always justly reaching for more, you would in no way wish to spend away at all. For this is the true abundance; but the mass of perceptible wealth would harm its friends rather than help them. Fittingly, then, I called it the utmost poverty—that wealth which the lovers of the heavenly good things have utterly renounced and fled from,

as one flees from a serpent. But if the enemy whom my fellow-ascetics and fellow-soldiers killed and trampled underfoot, I should take alive again from you and carry back to them, and become the cause of wars and passions, I would surely be to them an evil messenger; which God forbid that I should do. Think the same of me concerning garments too. For to those who have put off the corruption of the old man and laid aside, so far as in them lay, the garment of disobedience, and have put on Christ as a robe of salvation and a tunic of gladness, how could I again clothe them in the garments of skins and put about them the covering of shame? But knowing that my companions need none of such things, but are content with the asceticism of the desert and reckon this the truest luxury, distribute to the poor the money and garments you spoke of giving to them, and lay up for yourself a treasure unplundered for the future, setting God as your helper by their prayers; for so you would the better use wealth as a fellow-worker toward good things. Then, putting on the whole armor of the Spirit, and girding your loins in truth, and putting on the breastplate of righteousness, and setting on the helmet of salvation, and shoeing your feet with the readiness of the gospel of peace, and taking up in your hands the shield of faith, and the sword of the Spirit,

which is the word of God, and being most excellently armed and fortified on every side, go out thus confident to the war against impiety, so that, having routed it and dashed to the ground its leader the devil, you may be adorned with the crowns of victory from the life-giving right hand of the Master.

With such doctrines, then, and saving words Barlaam instructed the king's son, and prepared him for holy baptism, charging him to fast and pray, according to custom, for a number of days; and he did not cease coming often to him, expounding every doctrinal word of the orthodox faith and dictating to him the holy Gospel, and besides this interpreting the apostolic exhortations and the prophetic sayings. For the man, being taught of God, carried by heart the whole of the Old and New Scripture, and, moved by the divine Spirit, enlightened him toward the true knowledge of God. And on the very day when he was about to be baptized, teaching him, he said: Behold, you hasten to receive the seal of Christ and to be marked with the light of the face of the Lord. And you become a son of God, and a temple of the holy and life-giving Spirit. Believe, then, in Father and Son and Holy Spirit, the holy and life-originating Trinity, glorified in three persons and one Godhead,

divided in the persons and the personal properties, but united in the essence: knowing one God unbegotten, the Father, and one begotten Lord, the Son, light from light, true God from true God, begotten before all the ages. For of a good Father a good Son was begotten, and from the unbegotten light the eternal light shone forth, and from the life that truly is the life-giving fountain came forth, and from the self-power the power of the Son was made manifest, who is the radiance of the glory and the Word in his own person, being in the beginning with God and God without beginning and eternal; through whom all things came to be, the visible and the invisible. And knowing one Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father, perfect God, and life-giving, and the bestower of sanctification, of the same will, of the same power, coeternal, existing in his own person. So, then, worship the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit in three persons—that is, properties—and one Godhead. For common to the three is the Godhead, and one is their nature, one essence, one glory, one kingdom, one power, one authority; and common to the Son and the Holy Spirit is being from the Father,

but proper to the Father is unbegottenness, to the Son begetting, to the Spirit procession. So, then, believe these things; but do not inquire into the manner of the begetting or of the procession, for it is incomprehensible. In uprightness of heart and without prying accept that the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are in all things one, except for the unbegottenness and the begetting and the procession; and that the only-begotten Son and Word of God and God, for our salvation, came down to earth by the good pleasure of the Father and the working together of the Holy Spirit, conceived without seed in the womb of the holy Virgin and Mother of God, Mary, through the Holy Spirit, and born of her without corruption, and becoming a perfect man; and that he himself is perfect God and perfect man, made of two natures, Godhead and manhood, and in two natures—rational, willing, and active and self-determining, and perfect in all things according to the limit and principle proper to each, I mean Godhead and manhood—but in one composite person. And accept these things without prying, in no way seeking to learn the manner—how the Son of God emptied himself and became man from the virginal

blood, without seed and without corruption, or what is the conjunction of the two natures in one person. For we have been taught to hold by faith the things spoken to us in a godly manner from the divine Scripture; but the manner we do not know and cannot tell. Believe that the Son of God, who through the tender mercies of his compassion became man, took on all the natural and blameless sufferings of manhood—for he hungered, and thirsted, and slept, and grew weary, and was in agony by the nature of his manhood, and for our transgressions was led to death, was crucified and buried, tasting death, while the Godhead remained without suffering and unchanging; for we attach none at all of the sufferings to the impassible nature, but we know that he suffered and was buried in what he had assumed, and rose from the dead in the divine glory, and ascended into the heavens in incorruption, and will come again with glory to judge the living and the dead, by such principles of a more godlike body as he himself knows, and will render to each according to his just measures. For the dead will rise and those in the tombs will be raised; and those who have kept the commandments of Christ and departed with the right faith

will inherit eternal life, but those who have been corrupted in sins and have turned aside from the right faith will go away into eternal punishment. Believe that there is no substance or kingdom of evil, nor suppose it to be without beginning, or to have come into being of itself, or from God—away with the absurdity—but that this is the work of ourselves and of the devil, having come upon us through our own inattention, because we were made self-determining and choose this by self-determined will, whether good or evil. Besides this, confess one baptism of water and Spirit for the forgiveness of sins. Receive also the partaking of the undefiled mysteries of Christ, believing them in truth to be the body and blood of Christ our God, which he gave to the faithful for the forgiveness of sins. For on the night in which he was betrayed he established a new covenant with his holy disciples and apostles, and through them with all who believe in him, saying: Take, eat; this is my body, broken for you for the forgiveness of sins. And likewise also, taking the cup, he gave it to them, saying: Drink of it, all of you; this is my blood, that of the new covenant, poured out for you for the forgiveness of sins;

do this in remembrance of me. So then the Word of God himself, living and active and doing all things by his power, makes and transforms, through the divine working, the bread and the wine of the offering into his body and blood, by the coming of the Holy Spirit, for the sanctification and illumination of those who partake with longing. Worship, faithfully honoring and saluting, the venerable image of the Master's likeness, the Word of God who for our sake became man, thinking that you behold the Creator himself in the icon. For the honor of the image, says one of the saints, passes over to the prototype; and the prototype is the thing represented, from which the derived likeness is made. For looking at the painting in the image, we pass with the eyes of the mind to the true form of which the image is, piously worshipping the form of him who for our sake was made flesh—not deifying it, but embracing it as an image of the incarnate God, in longing and love for him who emptied himself for our sake even to the form of a servant; likewise embracing in the same sense the images of his undefiled Mother and of all the saints. And in the same way, faithfully worshipping the figure of the life-giving and venerable cross, salute it for the sake of him who was hung upon it in the flesh for the salvation of our

race, Christ our God and the Savior of the world, who gave us this as a symbol of the victory over the devil; for he shudders and trembles, unable to look upon its power. In such doctrines and with such faith you will be baptized, keeping this unchanged and unmixed with any heresy until your last breath. And every teaching and every doctrinal word that opposes this blameless faith, abhor, and reckon it to be an estrangement from God. For the Apostle says: Even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel other than what we preached to you, let him be accursed. For there is no other gospel and no other faith except that proclaimed through the apostles, and confirmed by the God-bearing Fathers in various councils, and established in the catholic Church. Having said these things, and having taught the king's son the symbol of the faith set forth in the council at Nicaea, Barlaam baptized him in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, in the font of water that was in his garden. And the grace of the Holy Spirit came upon him. And returning to his bedchamber, and performing the sacred celebration of the bloodless sacrifice, he imparted to him the undefiled

mysteries of Christ, and rejoiced in the Spirit, sending up glory to Christ our God. And Barlaam said to him: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy has begotten you again to a living hope, to an inheritance incorruptible and undefiled and unfading, kept in the heavens, in Christ Jesus our Lord through the Holy Spirit. For today, having been freed from sin, you have been enslaved to God, receiving the pledge of eternal life; and, leaving the darkness behind, you have put on light, ranked into the freedom of the glory of the children of God. For as many, it says, as received him, to them he gave authority to become children of God, to those who believe in his name; so that you are no longer a slave, but a son and heir of God through Jesus Christ in the Holy Spirit. Therefore, beloved, be eager to be found before him spotless and blameless, working the good upon the foundation of the faith; for faith without works is dead, just as works are dead without faith, as I remember telling you before.

Laying aside, then, henceforth all wickedness, and hating all the works of the old man, which are corrupted according to the desires of deceit, like a newborn infant long for the reasonable and guileless milk of the virtues to drink, that in it you may grow and come to the knowledge of the commandments of the Son of God, to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ—no longer being an infant in your mind, tossed and carried about by the storm and surging of the passions, but being an infant in regard to wickedness, while keeping your mind firm and settled toward the good, and walking worthily of the calling with which you have been called in the keeping of the Lord's commandments; having shaken off from yourself and estranged the emptiness of your former conduct, just as the nations walk in the emptiness of their mind, darkened in their understanding and estranged from the glory of God, subjected to their desires and irrational impulses. But you, just as you have drawn near to the

living and true God, so also walk as a son of light. For the fruit of the Spirit is in all goodness and righteousness and truth; and do not corrupt the new man you have put on today with the former oldness, but be renewed each day in righteousness and holiness and truth. For this is possible for everyone who wills it, just as you hear that he gave authority to become children of God to those who believe in his name; so that we can no longer say that the acquisition of the virtues is impossible for us. For the way is easy and ready. For even if it has been called somewhat narrow and hard because of the chastening of the body, yet it is nonetheless desirable and divine, because of the hope of the good things to come, to those who walk not unwisely, but understand exactly what is the will of God, and put on his whole armor for the battle against the methods of the adversary, and watch for this very thing in prayer and supplication, with all endurance and hope. You, then, just as you have heard from me and been taught, and have laid down a firm foundation, abound in it, growing and advancing, and waging the good warfare, having faith and a good conscience witnessed by good works,

and pursuing righteousness, piety, faith, love, endurance, gentleness, laying hold of the eternal life to which you have been called. And every pleasure and desire of the passions remove far from yourself, not only in the working of action, but also in the imaginings of thought, that you may show your soul undefiled to God. For not only our actions, but also our imaginings, being written down, become the cause of crowns or of punishments; and we know that Christ, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, dwells in pure hearts. And again, as smoke drives away bees, so we have learned that the grace of the divine Spirit drives away wicked thoughts. Therefore, attending carefully to this, wipe away from your soul every reasoning of passion, and plant in it the noblest thoughts, making yourself a temple of the Holy Spirit. For from our reasonings we come also to the actions of working; and every deed, advancing from a thought and an imagining, lays hold of a small beginning, then by little increases ends in great things. For this reason do not let an evil habit master you at all, but while it is still fresh, pluck out from your heart the wicked root, lest, taking root and fixing its roots in the depth, it require time and toil to be uprooted. For it is for this reason that the greater sins always come upon us and tyrannize over our souls: because the things that seem to be lesser,

such as wicked imaginings, unseemly words, evil conversations, do not meet with the proper correction. For just as in bodies those who have despised small wounds have often procured for themselves festering and death, so too in souls those who disregard small passions and sins bring in the greater; and in proportion as the greater come upon them, the soul, settling into the habit, despises them. For the impious man, it says, when he has come into the depth of evils, despises; and thereafter, just as a sow that wallows in mire takes pleasure in it, so too that soul, buried under evil habits, no longer takes any perception of the foul stench of its sins, but rather delights in them and is sweetened by them, clinging to wickedness as to some good; and even if late at last, rousing itself, it comes to perception, it is freed only with much toil and sweat from those things to which it willingly enslaved itself through the wicked habit. For this reason, with all your power, remove yourself from every evil thought and imagining and every passionate habit; rather accustom yourself to the virtues and come to be in the habit of practicing them. For if you labor a little in them and have the strength to come to be in the habit, you will thereafter advance without toil, by the working together of God. For the habit of virtue, having become a quality of the soul, as having a natural kinship with it and possessing God as fellow-worker,

becomes hard to change and very secure, just as you see that courage and prudence, self-control and righteousness are hard to change, being habits and qualities and workings of the soul that have penetrated to the depth. For if the passions of wickedness, which are not natural to us but have come upon us from without, are hard to change once they have become a habit, how much more will virtue—which has been naturally implanted in us by the Creator and has him as its helper—if, when we have struggled a little, it takes root in the soul as a habit, be hard to change?

Thus one who labours at this work described it to me, saying: "After I had taken hold of the contemplation of God in a most firm and settled habit, and my soul had been shaped by the practice of it, I once wished to make trial of it, and I held my mind back, not permitting it to apply itself to its accustomed exercise. And I found it grieved and distressed, straining toward that contemplation with an irresistible longing, and wholly unable to incline toward any contrary thought. But when I gave the reins a little slack, it at once ran swiftly back to its own work, as the Prophet says: As the deer longs for the springs of waters, so my soul longs for God, the strong, the living God." From all this it is proved that the possession of virtue lies within our power, and that we are masters of it, whether we choose to cling to it or to prefer sin. Those, then, who have been enslaved to vice are held by it and torn from it only with difficulty,

as I said earlier. But you, now set free from it through the tender mercy of our God, and having put on Christ by the grace of the divine Spirit, transfer your whole self to the Lord, and open no further door to the passions. Rather, having adorned your soul with the fragrance and splendour of the virtues, make it a temple of the Holy Trinity, occupying all the powers of your mind with the contemplation of it. For if a man who lives with an earthly king and converses with him is accounted blessed by all, what blessedness will he enjoy who is held worthy to converse with God and to be united with him in mind? Mirror him, then, always, and commune with him. And how will you commune with God? By drawing near to him through prayer and supplication. For the man who prays with the warmest longing and with a purified heart, having withdrawn his mind from all things material and earthbound, and standing before God as one face to face, offering his supplications to him with fear and trembling,

such a man communes with him and speaks with him face to face. For our good Master is present everywhere, listening to those who come to him sincerely and purely, as the Prophet says: The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are open to their supplication. And for this reason the Fathers define prayer as the union of man with God, and they call it the work of angels and the prelude of the joy to come. For since they reckon the nearness and contemplation of the Holy Trinity above all things as the kingdom of heaven, and since constancy in prayer leads the mind toward this, prayer is rightly called the prelude and, as it were, the foreshadowing of that blessedness. Yet not every prayer is of this kind, but only that which is truly worthy of this name: the prayer that has God for its teacher, who gives prayer to the one who prays; the prayer that is lifted above all things on earth and addresses the Lord God directly. Win this for yourself, and strive for this advance; for it is able to raise you from earth to heaven. But you will not advance in it unprepared or by chance. Rather, having first cleansed your soul of all the passions, and wiped it clean of every evil thought like a clean and newly polished mirror,

and having removed yourself far from all remembrance of wrongs and all rancour, which more than anything else hinders our prayers from rising to God, and having forgiven from the heart all who have sinned against you their offences, and having winged your prayer with almsgiving and compassion toward the poor, bring it to God with warm tears. Praying thus, you will be able to speak as the blessed David did; for he, though he was a king and was drawn this way and that by countless cares, yet purified his soul of all the passions and said to God: Iniquity I hated and abhorred, but your law I loved; seven times a day I praised you for the judgements of your righteousness; my soul kept your testimonies and loved them exceedingly; let my supplication draw near before you, O Lord; give me understanding according to your word. When you cry out thus, God will hear you; while you are still speaking, he will say: Behold, I am here. If, then, you acquire such prayer, you will be blessed; for it is impossible that a man

who prays with such eagerness and entreats God should not advance daily in the good and fly above all the snares of the enemy. For the man who has kindled his mind, as one of the saints has said, and lifted up his soul, and removed himself to heaven, and so called upon his own Master, and remembered his own sins, and spoken concerning their forgiveness, and with the warmest tears begged the Lover of mankind to be merciful to him — such a man, from his dwelling in these words and meditations, lays aside every care of this life and becomes higher than human passions, and is held worthy to be called the companion of God. And what could be more blessed or more exalted than this? May the Lord, then, count you worthy to attain such blessedness. For behold, I have shown you the way of the Lord's commandments, and I have held back nothing from declaring to you the whole counsel of God. And I, for my part, have now completed my ministry toward you. It remains for you to gird up the loins of your mind, and, after the pattern of him who called you, the Holy One, to be yourself holy in all your conduct: Be holy, for I am holy, says the Lord. The foremost of the apostles also writes: If you call upon as Father him who judges without partiality according to each man's work,

conduct yourselves in fear throughout the time of your sojourning, knowing that you were not redeemed from the empty way of life handed down by your fathers with perishable things, with silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot. Laying all this to heart, then, remember it without ceasing, keeping ever before your eyes the fear of God and his awe-inspiring judgement; the brightness of the righteous, which they are to receive in that age to come, and the gloom of sinners in the deepest darkness; the weakness and emptiness of present things and the endlessness of those to come; for All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of the grass: the grass has withered and its flower has fallen, but the word of the Lord abides forever. Meditate on these things continually; and may the peace of God be with you, enlightening you and giving you understanding and leading you into the way of salvation, driving every evil intention far from your mind, and sealing your soul with the sign of the cross, that nothing of the evil one's snares may come near you, but that you may be held worthy, in all perfection of the virtues, to attain the kingdom that is to come, which is without end and without succession, and to be encompassed with the light of the blessed and life-giving Trinity, which is glorified in Father and Son and Holy Spirit.
With such moral words, then, the most honoured old man admonished the king's son,

and went away to his own lodging. Now the young man's attendants and tutors marvelled to see how often Barlaam came into the palace. And one of the foremost among them, whom the king had set over his son's palace as most faithful and trustworthy — a man named Zardan — said to the king's son: "You know well, my lord, how great is the fear of your father that lies upon me, and how great my faithfulness toward him; for which reason he charged me, as his most trusted servant, to wait upon you. But now, seeing this stranger so often in conversation with you, I am afraid that he may belong to the religion of the Christians, toward which your father is most bitterly disposed; and I shall be found liable to a sentence of death. Either, then, make known to the king what concerns this man, or henceforth cease to converse with him. And if you will not, dismiss me from your presence,

so that I may not be held to blame, and ask your father to appoint another to be here." The king's son said to him: "Before all else, Zardan, do this: take your seat within the curtain, and listen to his conversation with me; and afterward I will tell you what must be done." So when Barlaam was about to come in to him, he brought Zardan inside the curtain, and said to the old man: "Sum up for me the points of your inspired teaching, that it may be planted more firmly in my heart." Then Barlaam took up the discourse and spoke much concerning God and reverence toward him: how God alone must be loved with the whole heart and with the whole soul and with the whole mind, and how his commandments must be kept with fear and with longing; and how he is the maker of all things visible and invisible. Upon which he also called to mind the fashioning of the first man, the commandment given to him and its transgression, and the condemnation laid by the Creator upon that transgression. Then in order he recounted the good things from which, by setting aside the commandment, we shut ourselves out;

and again he recalled the sorrows, all that befell us wretchedly after their loss. After this he brought forward the works of God's love for mankind: how the Creator, caring for our salvation, sent teachers and prophets to proclaim the incarnation of the Only-Begotten; then his coming down, his becoming man, his benefactions, his miracles, and his sufferings on behalf of us, the ungrateful — the cross, the spear, the voluntary death; and at last our restoration, our recall, our return to the first good; and after these, the kingdom of heaven that awaits the worthy, the torment laid up for the wicked, the fire that is never quenched, the darkness that never ends, the undying worm, and whatever other punishment the slaves of sin have stored up for themselves. Having gone through these things and brought his discourse to a close with moral teaching, having spoken much concerning purity of life, and condemned the emptiness of present things, and exposed the wretchedness of those who cling to them, he ended with prayer. And having prayed that the young man's confession of the orthodox faith might be unshaken and unbending, his life blameless and his manner of living most pure, he set an end to the prayer and went away again to his lodging. Then the king's son, calling Zardan to him and testing his disposition, said: "Did you hear what manner of things this idle babbler discusses with me, attempting to deceive me with his empty plausibilities and to rob me of this delightful joy and pleasure, and to make me serve a strange God?"

And Zardan said: "Why has it seemed good to you, O king, to put me, your servant, to the test? I know that the man's words have sunk deep into your heart; for were it not so, you would not converse with him so gladly and so unceasingly. We too are not ignorant of this teaching; but ever since your father raised an implacable persecution against the Christians, they were driven from these parts, and their preaching fell silent. But if now this doctrine has appeared pleasing to you, and you are strong enough to take up its hardness and toil, may your purposes be directed toward the good. As for me, what shall I do? I cannot so much as look such severity in the face, and the fear of the king divides my soul amid pains and griefs. What defence shall I make to him, if I have dealt carelessly with his orders and granted this man entry to you?" The king's son said to him: "I, knowing no other worthy return for your great goodwill toward me, and finding this — and more than worthy — for your benefit, have done you the work of a good beyond nature: to make it known to you for what end you were created, and that you might recognize the Creator, and, forsaking the darkness, run to the light;

and I hoped that, as soon as you heard, you would follow with an irresistible longing. But I have been disappointed of my hope, as I see, finding you lukewarm toward what was spoken. Yet if you disclose this to the king my father, you will do nothing else than fill his soul with cares and griefs and make it bitter. But if indeed you are well-disposed toward him, by no means report anything of these matters until the proper time." In saying this to Zardan, he seemed to be sowing upon water; for wisdom will not enter into a soul without understanding. On the next day Barlaam came and spoke of his departure; and the young man, not bearing to be parted from him, grieved in his soul, and his eyes filled with tears. The old man spoke much to him, and called him to witness that he would remain unmoved in the good, and steadied his heart with words of comfort, and asked to be sent away with gladness; and at the same time he foretold that before long they would be joined together in a union that knows no parting. Then the king's son, unable to lay further toil upon the old man or to keep him from the road he longed for,

and at the same time suspecting that Zardan might make known what concerned him to the king and subject the old man to punishments, said to him: "Since this has seemed good to you, spiritual father and best of teachers and broker to me of every good, that you should leave me to live amid the emptiness of the world and yourself go to the place of spiritual rest, I no longer dare to hold you back or hinder you. Go, then, guarded by the peace of God, and remember my wretchedness always in your precious prayers, for the Lord's sake, that I may be able to reach you and behold your honoured face forever. But grant me one request: since you would take nothing on behalf of your fellow ascetics, accept at least for yourself some small means for sustenance and a garment for clothing." He answered him: "If I did not take anything from you on behalf of my brothers — for they too have no need to take up the things of the world from which they have willingly withdrawn — how shall I procure for myself what I forbade to them? For if the possession of wealth were good, I would have shared it with them before myself; but since I know its possession to be ruinous, I will subject neither them nor myself to such snares." When the young man could not prevail in this either, he began a second entreaty, and made a second request:

that the old man should not wholly disregard his pleas, nor pour out all his disappointment upon him, but should leave him that worn-out garment and rough cloak — partly as a memorial of his teacher's ascetic life, partly as a safeguard against all the working of Satan — and take from him another in its place: "So that," he said, "seeing what was given by me, you may carry my lowliness in your memory." The old man said: "To give you the old and tattered garment and to take a new covering is not lawful, lest I be condemned to receive here the reward of my small toil; but, that I may not check your eagerness, let what is given to me by you be old and in no way different from my own." So the king's son sought out old hair-cloth rags, and gave them to the old man, and rejoiced to take his garments, accounting them beyond all comparison more precious than any purple or royal robe. Then the most godly Barlaam, wishing to depart without further delay, spoke of his going, and offered him a last teaching, saying: "Beloved brother and sweetest child, whom I have begotten through the Gospel, you know what King you have been enlisted under, and to whom you have made your confessions. You must keep these firm, then, and eagerly fulfil the terms of your service, all that you promised to the Master of all in the document of your confession,

while all the heavenly host stands present and bears witness, and at the same time records what was confessed — which, if you keep, you will be blessed. Therefore prefer none of the present things to God and his good gifts. For what among present things could be so fearful as the Gehenna of eternal fire, where what burns gives no light at all, and what punishes never ceases? And what again among the good things of the world could give such gladness as God himself, bestowed upon those who have loved him? — whose beauty is unutterable, whose power is unconquerable, and whose glory is everlasting; whose good things, laid up for his friends, surpass beyond all comparison everything that is seen, things which eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and which have not entered the heart of man. May you be shown forth as their heir, guarded by the most mighty hand of God."

The king's son, overcome with tears, grieved and was distressed, not enduring to be left without a tender father and the best of teachers. "And who," he said, "father, will fill your place for me? Under what shepherd and such a guide of the soul's salvation shall I come? What comfort shall I make for my longing for you? For behold, you brought me, the wicked servant and apostate, to God, and set me in the rank of a son and an heir; you sought out the lost one, taken captive upon the mountains, ready to be the prey of every beast, and mingled him with the unerring sheep of God; you showed me the short road of truth, leading me out of the darkness and the shadow of death, and, moving my feet from the slippery and death-bearing and most crooked and winding path, you have become to me the broker of great and wondrous goods, whose surpassing greatness no words would suffice to declare. May you yourself, on behalf of me the small one, share in the great gifts of God; and may the Lord fill up the deficiency of my thanksgiving, he who alone overcomes by the returns of his gifts those who love him." But Barlaam, cutting short his lamentation, rose and stood for prayer, and lifting up both his hands to heaven, he said: "O God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who enlightened things once darkened,

and brought this visible and invisible creation out of nothing into being, who have turned back your handiwork and have not let us walk after our folly, we give thanks to you, and to your wisdom and power, our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom you also made the ages, and raised us up when we had fallen, and forgave their sins to those who had transgressed, and brought back those who had wandered, and ransomed those who had been taken captive, and gave life to the dead by the precious and lordly blood of your Son. You, then, I call upon, and your only-begotten Son, and your all-holy Spirit: look upon this rational sheep of yours, which has come through me, the unworthy, as a sacrifice to you, and sanctify his soul by your power and grace; visit this vine that has been planted through your Holy Spirit, and grant it to bear the fruit of righteousness; strengthen him, confirming your covenant in him, and deliver him from the deceit of the devil. By the wisdom of your good Spirit teach him to do your will, and do not withdraw your help from him, counting him worthy, together with me your useless servant, to become an heir of your unending goods; for blessed are you and glorified unto the ages. Amen." When he had finished the prayer and turned, he embraced the child now of the heavenly Father,
and praying for him peace and eternal salvation, he went out of the palace, and departed rejoicing and giving thanks to God, who had prospered his way unto good.

After Barlaam had gone out, Josaphat gave himself to prayer and to the warmest tears, and said: "O God, attend to my help. Lord, make haste to help me, for to you the poor man is left; you were the helper of the orphan. Look upon me and have mercy on me, you who will that all be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth; save me and strengthen me, the unworthy, to walk the road of your holy commandments, for I am weak and wretched and unequal to doing the good; but you are able to save me, who hold together and uphold all things visible and invisible. Do not let me walk after the evil desires of the flesh, but teach me to do your will, and keep me unto your eternal and blessed life. O Father and Son and divine Spirit, the Godhead of one essence and undivided, you I call upon and you I glorify; for all creation hymns you, and the intelligent powers of the bodiless ones glorify you unto the ages. Amen." From that time, then, he kept himself with all watchfulness, securing for himself purity of soul and body, living in self-restraint and in prayers and supplications throughout the night.

For though by day he was often cut off by the company of those who were with him, and at times by the king's visits to him or his summons of the young man to himself, the night made up for him the day's deficiencies, as he stood in prayers and tears until daybreak and called upon God; whence that prophetic word was fulfilled in him: In the nights lift up your hands toward the holy place, and bless the Lord. But that Zardan, perceiving this manner of life and filled with grief, his soul stricken with terrible cares, did not know what to do; at last, worn down by his distress, he withdrew to his own house, pretending to be ill. When this came to the king's knowledge, he sent another of his most trusted men in his stead to wait upon his son; and he himself, caring for Zardan's health, sent him a most skilled physician and judged that he should be treated with much attention. The physician, since Zardan was a favourite of the king's, examined him carefully, and having diagnosed his condition perfectly, reported quickly to the king: "I," he said, "have not been able to find in the man the cause of any disease; whence I suppose that, his soul being stricken with some despondency, he has fallen sick." When the king heard these words, he supposed that his son had behaved grievously toward Zardan, and that for this reason he had grieved and withdrawn. Wishing to learn the matter accordingly, he sent word to Zardan,

saying: "Tomorrow I shall come to see you, and to learn about the illness that has befallen you." When Zardan heard this message, at early dawn he wrapped his garment about him and went to the king.
