And entering, he prostrated himself before him to the ground. The king said: "Why did you force yourself to come? For I myself wished to visit you, and to make known to all my friendship toward you." But he answered: "My weakness, O king, is not one of the illnesses common to men; rather, from a grieved and care-laden soul, the heart being in pain, the body has suffered with it. But it would have been folly for me, being in such a state, not to come like a servant before your majesty, but to expect your kingship to be troubled to come down to me, your servant." When the king inquired what was the cause of his despondency, Zardan took up the word and said: "Great is my danger, and I am worthy of great punishments, liable to many deaths, because, having dealt carelessly with your orders, I have all but become the cause of much grief to you." Then again the king asked: "And what negligence have you been guilty of? And what is the fear that grips you?" "In my watchfulness over my lord your son I have been negligent," he said. "For a wicked man and sorcerer came and spoke to him of the religion of the Christians." Then he related to the king in detail what the old man had said to his son, and with how much delight the young man had received the discourse, and how he had become wholly Christ's.

He disclosed besides the old man's name, saying that he was called Barlaam. For the king had also heard before of Barlaam and his most extreme ascetic life. When these things came to the king's ears, he was at once thrown into turmoil by the despondency that had fallen upon him, and was filled with anger, and was almost paralyzed by what he heard. And at once he summoned a man called Arachis, who held second place after the king, and was foremost with him in all his secret counsels; and the man was also skilled in astrology. When he had come, the king related to him what had happened with much despondency and distress. But Arachis, beholding his turmoil and the confusion of his soul, said: "Let your mind be untroubled and free from grief, O king; for it is not yet beyond our hope that the young man may change his course. Indeed, I know most surely that he will quickly renounce the teaching of that deceiver and consent to your will." So Arachis, having by these words turned the king toward better cheer, took counsel with him in deliberating about the matter. "And this, O king," he said, "let us do before all else: let us hasten to catch the cunning Barlaam. And if we lay hold of him,

we shall not, I am well assured, miss our aim, nor be disappointed of our hope. For that man himself, persuaded either by plausible words or by the many kinds of instruments of torture, would confess against his will that he had spoken false and erring things, and would persuade my lord your son to hold to his father's doctrine. But if we should not be able to catch him, I know another old hermit, called Nachor, like Barlaam in all respects, who cannot be told apart from him, a man of our own persuasion, and one who became my teacher in the sciences. To him I, going by night, will dictate and relate everything in detail. Then, having spread abroad that Barlaam has been seized, we shall produce this man; and he, naming himself Barlaam, will pretend to plead the cause of the Christians and will appear to defend them. Then, after much disputation, being defeated, he will be utterly overcome. And when the king's son sees this — that Barlaam has been defeated and our side prevails — he will surely consent to the victors; setting great store, besides, on reverencing your kingship and doing what is pleasing to you. For the one who has put on Barlaam's mask will also turn about, and affirm that he was deceived." The king was pleased at what was said, and thought he had taken excellent counsel, leaning upon empty hopes.

Whence, having just learned that Barlaam had withdrawn, he hastened to lay hold of him. So, having posted ambushes and captains over most of the roads out, he himself, mounting horses, pursued at full speed along one of the roads, the one he suspected above all the rest, intending by every means to overtake him first. But having toiled six whole days, he had laboured in vain. Then he himself remained at one of the royal palaces lying among the fields, and sent Arachis with no few horsemen as far as the desert of Senaar itself, in search of Barlaam. When Arachis reached the place, he threw all the dwellers round about into confusion; and when they affirmed that they had never seen the man, the commander went out into the deserts to hunt the pious. And having traversed a great stretch of desert, encircled mountains and crossed trackless and difficult ravines on foot, he reached, with the crowds that were with him, a certain mountain summit,

and standing upon it, he saw at the foot of the mountain a band of hermits walking. And at once, at the commander's order, all rush upon them without pausing for breath, each striving in the running to outstrip the other; and overtaking them, they poured around them like many dogs or like wicked, man-hating beasts; and they seized the men, most venerable in appearance and bearing, who carried upon their faces the marks of the hermit's life; and dragging them, they brought them before the commander, the men not at all disturbed, showing and uttering nothing ignoble or downcast. The one who went before them and was, as it were, their leader carried a hair satchel, full of the relics of certain holy Fathers who had departed before. When Arachis looked them over and did not see Barlaam — for he knew him — he was overwhelmed with grief. And he said to them: "Where is that deceiver, who led astray the king's son?" The one carrying the satchel answered: "He is not among us; God forbid; for he flees from us, pursued by the grace of Christ. But among you he has his dwellings." The commander said: "Do you know him, then?" "Yes," said the hermit; "I know the one called the deceiver, who is the devil, who dwells in your midst and is served and worshipped by you." The commander said: "It is about Barlaam that I am making my search, and I asked you to learn where he is."

The monk said: "And why, then, did you speak to no purpose, framing your question about the one who led the king's son astray? For if you were seeking Barlaam, you should certainly have said: Where is the one who turned the king's son from error and saved him? For that man is our brother and fellow ascetic; but for many days now we have not seen him." Arachis said: "Point out his dwelling." The ascetic answered: "If he wished to see you, he himself would have come out to meet you. But it is not lawful for us to make known his cell to you." At this the commander is filled with anger, and says to him, fixing upon him a glance at once wrathful and beastlike: "I will now put you to death by a strange death, if you do not at once produce Barlaam for me." "And what," said the ascetic, "do you see in us, that we should cling to this present life and be hard to tear from it, and fear the death you will bring upon us? Rather, we shall be the more grateful to you, that you have led us out of life while we hold fast to virtue. For we fear, and not a little, the uncertainty of our end, not knowing in what state it will overtake us,

lest some slip of the will, or some demonic assault, should overturn the firmness of our resolve, and persuade us to think or do otherwise than what we have confessed to God. Therefore, having wholly given up obtaining what you hope, do not hesitate to do what you will. For neither will we point out the dwelling of our God-loving brother, though indeed we know it, nor betray to you any other hidden monasteries, basely enduring to escape death by such means; rather, we shall die a noble death, having offered to God first the sweat of virtue, and now the blood of valour." When the wretch could not endure their speaking so boldly, but was most sharply stirred against the nobility of their spirit, he assailed them with many blows and tortures; and even to the tyrant their greatness of soul and nobility seemed worthy of wonder. But when after many torments he could not prevail, and no one would endure to point out Barlaam to him, he took them and ordered them led to the king, beaten and reviled, carrying also the satchel of relics.

After not a few days he brought them before the king and made their case known. Then he set them before his face as the king raged terribly. And the king, seeing them, boiled over with anger and seemed like a madman. He ordered them to be beaten without mercy;

and when he saw them grievously cut down by the blows, he scarcely recovered from his great fury and ordered the beaters to stop. And he said to them: "Why do you carry about these bones of the dead? If it is out of longing for those whose bones they are that you bear them, this very hour I will set you among them, so that, having obtained what you long for, you may be grateful to me." But the leader and guide of that godly band, accounting the king's threats as nothing, as though nothing painful had befallen him, said, with a free voice and a most radiant face that betokened the grace dwelling in his soul: "These pure and holy bones we carry about, O king, fulfilling our longing for the wondrous men whose they are, and bringing ourselves to remembrance of their ascetic life and God-loving conduct, and rousing ourselves to the like zeal, and mirroring the rest and delight in which they now abide; and counting them blessed, we spur one another to hasten to follow in their footsteps. Moreover, we secure for ourselves thereby the remembrance of death, which is most profitable and eagerly wings us toward the contests of the ascetic life,

and we draw sanctification from touching them." Again the king said: "If the remembrance of death is profitable, as you say, why do you not take up the remembrance of it from the bones in your own bodies — your own, and soon to perish — rather than from these alien and decayed ones?" And the monk said: "Though I gave five reasons for carrying the relics, you, replying to but one, seem to mock us; but know well that the bones of those who have died before set forth the remembrance of death more vividly than the bones of the living. Yet since you know that this is so, and the bones in your own flesh foreshadow death to you, why do you not yourself, mindful of the end that is soon to come, set your own affairs in order? Instead you have given up your soul to all lawlessness, and violently and pitilessly you destroy the servants of God and the lovers of piety, who have done you no wrong, who neither share in any of your present goods nor strive to take them from you." The king said: "I justly punish you, the dangerous deceivers of the people, because you lead all astray, urging them to abstain from the delights of life, and, instead of sweet life and the most desirable pleasure and enjoyment, you compel them to choose this hard and squalid and filthy way of living,

and you proclaim that the honour due to the gods should be rendered to Jesus. Lest, then, the peoples, following your deceit, leave the land desolate, and, forsaking their fathers' gods, serve a strange one, I have judged it just to subject you to punishments and to death." But the monk said: "If you desire that all should share in the good things of life, why do you not impart to all equally of luxury and wealth? Instead, the many are wretched in poverty, while you snatch away what is theirs and add it to your own. Then you do not care for the salvation of the many, but fatten your own flesh, preparing matter for the worms to devour. For this reason, having denied the God of all things, you have called gods those who are no gods, the inventors of every lawlessness, so that you, behaving lewdly and lawlessly in imitation of them, may earn the title of an imitator of your gods. For such things as your gods did, how shall the men who attend to them not do likewise? You have wandered, then, into a great error, O king. And you are afraid that we may persuade some of the people, who, consenting to our teaching, would withdraw from your hand and attach themselves to the hand that holds all things together; for you wish there to be many servants of your greed, that they may toil while the profits from them accrue to you. Just as a man who rears dogs or birds tamed for the hunt appears to flatter them before the chase,

but, when they have caught something of the prey, violently snatches what is caught from their mouths; so too you, wishing to have many who bring you tribute and revenue from land and sea, say that you care for their salvation, while you procure for them eternal ruin — and above all for yourself — that wealth more worthless than refuse and rottenness alone may weigh you down; and without knowing it you hold darkness in place of light. But come to your senses out of this nether sleep; open your closed eyes, and behold the glory of our God that shines round about all; and come at last to yourself; for Understand, you senseless among the people, and you fools, be wise at last, says the Prophet. Understand that there is no god but our God, and there is no salvation except in him." The king said: "Cease this foolish babbling of yours, and at once point out Barlaam to me, or you shall make trial of instruments of torture such as you have never experienced." But the high-minded and most noble ascetic, the lover of the heavenly philosophy, was in no way turned by the king's threats; rather, standing unshaken, he said: "We have not been commanded to do what you decree, O king, but what is enjoined by our Master and God, who teaches us self-control, so as to master all pleasures and desires,

and to practise courage, so as to endure every toil and every affliction for the sake of righteousness. Whatever terrible things, then, you bring upon us for the sake of piety, you will rather be doing us good. Do, then, what you will; for we will not endure to do anything beyond what is fitting, nor will we give ourselves over to sin. And do not reckon this a small sin, that we should betray our fellow contestant and fellow soldier into your hands. But you shall not have this laughter against us, though you surround us with countless deaths; for we are not so unmanly as to betray our philosophy through fear of your torments, and to do anything unworthy of the divine law. Against this, prepare whatever instrument of attack you know; for to us to live is Christ, and to die for him is the best gain." At this, kindled with anger, the ruler ordered that their God-praising tongues be cut out, their eyes gouged, and their hands and feet cut off together. And when the sentence was given, the shield-bearers and spearmen stood round them and maimed them in a man-hating and merciless manner;

and dragging out their tongues with little hooks from their mouths, they cut them off like beasts, and gouged out their eyes with iron claws, and with joint-wrenching instruments dislocated their hands and feet and cut them off. But those blessed men, modest and noble in spirit, came forward to the torments courageously, as though called to a feast, spurring one another on and going fearlessly to death for Christ. In such manifold torments, then, the holy ascetics commended their steadfast souls to the Lord, being seventeen in number. Confessedly, then, pious reason is sovereign over the passions, as one not of our own faith has said, recounting the contests of an aged priest and seven children with their like-minded mother, who contended valiantly for their fathers' law; and these wondrous fathers, citizens and heirs of the Jerusalem above, fell nothing short of their steadfastness and greatness of soul.

When these had been piously perfected, the king told Arachis, his chief counsellor, to look to the second plan, since the first had failed, and to summon that Nachor. So Arachis, reaching his cave in the dead of night — for Nachor lived in the deserts, busying himself with the arts of divination — and explaining to him all that had been resolved, returned to the king at early dawn. And again, seeking horsemen, he pretended to go out in search of Barlaam.

When he had gone out and was walking about the deserts, a certain man was seen by him coming out of a ravine. And when he ordered him to be pursued, they swiftly overtook him, and seizing him brought him before Arachis. When Arachis asked who he was, of what religion, and by what name he was called, the man called himself a Christian and named himself Barlaam, as he had been instructed. Filled with joy, as he made it appear, Arachis quickly took him and returned to the king; and announcing it, he set him before him. And the king said, in the hearing of all who stood by: "Are you Barlaam, the worker of the demon?" But he answered: "I am a worker of God, and not of the demons. Do not revile me, then. For you owe me many thanks, in that I taught your son to be devout, freeing him from all deceit and reconciling him to the true God,

and instructing him in every kind of virtue." Again the king, as though in anger, said: "I ought not to have granted you a word at all, nor given you room for defence, but to have put you to death without inquiry. Yet I bear with your insolence, for the sake of the clemency that befits me, until I examine your case on an appointed day. And if you obey me, you will be granted pardon; but if not, you will perish miserably." Saying this, he handed him over to Arachis, charging him to guard him most carefully. The next day he broke camp from there and returned to his own palace. And it was noised abroad that Barlaam had been seized, so that the king's son, hearing it, was grievously pained in his soul, and could in no way restrain his tears. With groans and laments he entreated God, and called upon him for the old man's help. The Good One, then, did not overlook him in his mourning; for he is gracious to those who wait upon him in the day of affliction, and knows those who fear him. He made all things known to the young man through a vision in the night, and put strength into him, and emboldened him for the contest of piety. And waking, he found his heart, which a little before had been grieved and pained, full of joy and courage and the sweetest light. But the king, having so acted and so reasoned, rejoiced, thinking that he had taken good counsel, and rendered the greatest thanks to Arachis.

But iniquity lied to itself, to use the words of divine David, and righteousness conquers lawlessness, casting it down utterly and destroying its memory with a great sound, as the story will show in what follows. Two days later, then, the king came to his son's palace. And when the son came out to meet him, the father did not greet him as was his custom; but, like one grieved and angered, he went into the royal bedchamber and sat down with a gloomy face. Then, calling his son, he said: "What is this report, my child, that rings in my ears and wastes my soul with despondency? For I think no man was ever filled with such joy at the birth of a child as the gladness I have had in you; nor, on the other hand, do I think any man was ever so grieved and so ill-treated by a child as you have now treated me, dishonouring my grey hairs,

taking away the light of my eyes and cutting off the strength of my sinews; for the fear that I feared concerning you has come upon me, and what I dreaded has met me. And you have become a delight to my enemies and a laughingstock to my adversaries. With an untaught mind and a childish judgement you have followed the words of deceivers, and preferred the counsel of the wicked-minded to my counsel, and forsaking the worship of our gods, you have served a strange God. Why, my child, have you done this? You whom I hoped to rear in all security, and to have as the staff and strength of my old age, and to leave behind as the best successor to my kingdom — were you not ashamed to show toward me the conduct of enemies and foes? Should you not rather obey me and follow my doctrines, than yield to the idle drivel of that crafty and rotten old man, who proposed to you a bitter life instead of a sweet one, and to travel the hard and rough road, instead of the most desirable luxury —

the road which the Son of Mary urges men to walk? And do you not fear the wrath of the greatest gods, lest they strike you with a thunderbolt, or kill you with a lightning-bolt, or sink you in a chasm of the earth — because, those who did us so many benefits, and crowned us with the diadem of kingship, and subjected populous nations, and prepared that you should be born beyond hope through my prayer and supplication and should share in this sweetest light — you have thrust aside and despised, and cleaved to the Crucified, deceived by the empty hopes of his servants, who fable certain new ages, and prate of a resurrection of dead bodies, and bring in countless other things to deceive the foolish? But now at least, dearest son, if you will obey me your father, bid a long farewell to these long-winded follies,

and approach and sacrifice to the kindly gods, and let us appease them with hecatombs and libations, that they may grant you pardon for your fault. For they are powerful and able both to do good and to punish; and we ourselves, who came through them to this rule, are a proof of what is said, rendering them thanks for their benefaction, and granting honours to those who worship them and punishments to those who do not obey them and sacrifice." When the king had gone through many such empty repetitions, mocking and slandering our faith and praising and extolling the worship of idols, the most godly young man, seeing that the matter no longer needed a corner and concealment, but a lampstand and a watchtower, so that it might be made plain to all, was filled with frankness and courage, and said: "What I have done, master, I will not deny. I have fled the darkness and run to the light; I have left error behind and made the truth my own;

and, having renounced the demons, I have joined myself to Christ, the Son and Word of God the Father, by whose word all things were brought forth out of nothing — who also, having fashioned man out of dust, breathed into him the breath of life, and set him to dwell in the paradise of delight; and when man transgressed his commandment and became liable to death, and was brought under the power of the terrible ruler of this world, he did not cease doing all things, wishing to bring him back to his former honour. Therefore the Maker himself of all creation and the Creator of our race became man for our sake, and coming to earth from a holy Virgin dwelt among men; and on behalf of us, his thankless servants, the Master accepted death, and death by the cross, that the tyranny of sin might be loosed, that the former condemnation might be removed, that the gates of heaven might be opened to us again. For there he raised up our nature and seated it on the throne of glory, and granted the unending kingdom to those who love him,

and good things better than word or hearing. For he is the mighty and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords, whose power is unconquerable and whose dominion beyond all likeness, the only Holy One who rests among the holy, who is glorified with the Father and the Holy Spirit, into whom I have been baptized. And I confess, glorify, and worship one God in three persons, of one essence and unconfused, uncreated and immortal, eternal, infinite, unbounded, bodiless, impassible, unchangeable, unalterable, indeterminable, the fountain of goodness and righteousness and everlasting light, the Maker of all creatures visible and invisible, who holds together and preserves all things, provides for all, masters all, and reigns over all. For nothing among existing things came to be apart from him, nor can anything subsist without his providence; for he himself is the life of all, the subsistence of all, the enlightenment of all, all sweetness and insatiable longing, and the highest of all things desirable. To forsake, then, a God so good, so wise, so powerful, and to serve unclean demons, the makers of all the passions, and to render worship to deaf and speechless images, which neither are anything nor ever shall be — to what depth of folly

and madness would this not be beyond? For when was any speech or word ever heard from them? When have they given even a small answer to those who pray to them? When have they walked, or received any perception? For neither did those that stand ever bethink themselves of a seat, nor were those that sit ever seen to rise. Having learned from a holy man the loathsomeness and foulness and senselessness of these things, and besides the rottenness and weakness of the demons that work in them and through them deceive you, and having spat upon their wickedness, and hated them with a perfect hatred, I have joined myself to the living and true God; and I will serve him until my last breath, that my spirit too may come into his hands. Since, then, such unspeakable good things have met me, I rejoiced to be freed from the slavery of the wicked demons and recalled from a terrible captivity, and to be illumined with the light of the Lord's face; yet I was grieved and my soul was divided, because you also, my master and father, did not share in such benefactions. But fearing the obstinacy of your mind, I held my grief within myself, not wishing to anger you, while I unceasingly entreated God to draw you to himself and to recall you from the long exile which you have procured for yourself,

having become, alas, a fugitive from piety and a servant of every wickedness and impiety. But since you yourself, father, have brought my case into the open, hear the whole of my purpose: I will not be false to my covenant with Christ — no, by him who redeemed me from slavery with his precious blood, even if I must die for him ten thousand times, I will die. Knowing my case thus, then, no longer trouble yourself by attempting to turn me from the good confession. For as it would be an idle and unaccomplished undertaking if you thought to seize heaven with your hand, or to dry up the seas of the deep, so know this to be also. Either, then, hearing my counsel, attach yourself to Christ, and you will receive good things beyond conception, and we shall be sharers with each other in faith, as we are in nature; or I will withdraw from your sonship —

know it well — and serve my God with a pure conscience." When the king heard all this, he was most sharply stirred, and overcome with uncontrollable anger, he spoke to him wrathfully, and bitterly gnashed his teeth, like one gone mad: "And who," he said, "is the cause of these evils to me, but I myself, who treated you so and did for you such things as no father ever did? Therefore the crookedness and contentiousness of your mind, gaining power from your freedom, has made you rage against my head. Justly, then, the astrologers at your birth said that you would turn out

a terrible and most wicked man, a braggart and disobedient to your parents. But now, if you nullify my counsel and withdraw from my sonship, I, disposed toward you as an enemy, will do to you those things that none has shown even to foes." Then he replied: "Why, O king, are you kindled to anger? Because I have been counted worthy of such good things, are you grieved? And who was ever seen to be vexed at his son's good fortune? Or how could such a man be reckoned a father, and not an enemy? Then neither will I henceforth call you father; rather, I will withdraw from you as one flees from a serpent, if I learn that you begrudge me my salvation and seek to drive me with a violent hand to ruin. For if you should wish to force and tyrannize me, as indeed you said, you will gain nothing else, know it well, than to be called, instead of a father, a tyrant and a murderer only; since it is easier for you to reach the tracks of an eagle and fly through the very air after it, than to turn my faith in Christ, and the good confession which I have confessed to him. But come to your senses, father, and, shaking off the rheum and mist from the eyes of your mind,

look up to behold the light of my God that shines round about all, and be illumined yourself at last with his sweetest light. For why have you given yourself wholly to the passions and desires of the flesh, and there is no lifting up of your head? Know that all flesh is grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of the grass: the grass has withered and its flower has fallen, but the word of my Lord, proclaimed to all, abides forever. Why, then, do you so madly cling to and embrace the glory that withers and vanishes like the flowers of spring, and the loathsome and foul-smelling luxury, and the most defiling passions of the belly and below the belly, which for a time gratify the senses of the foolish,

but afterward yield up returns more bitter than gall, when these shadows and dreams of this empty life pass away, and the lovers of them, the workers of lawlessness, are shut up in the continual anguish of the unquenchable and dark fire, where the sleepless worm devours them without end, and the fire burns them ceaselessly and unquenchably unto endless ages? Among whom, alas, you too, shut up and grievously tormented, will repent much of your terrible resolves, and long much for these present days and remember my words; but there will be no profit in your repentance. For in Hades there is no confession or repentance; rather, the present time has been appointed for labour, and the time to come for recompense. For if the present delights were not subject to vanishing and to flux, but were to abide forever with their possessors, not even so ought one to prefer these to the gifts of Christ and to good things beyond conception; for as much as the sun is brighter and clearer than the deep night, so much, and far more, are the good things promised to those who love God more glorious and magnificent than every earthly kingdom and glory, and one must by all means prefer the greater things to the meaner. But since all things here are fleeting and subject to corruption, and

pass away and vanish like a dream, a shadow, and a sleeping vision, and one may sooner trust the unstable breezes and the tracks of a ship crossing the sea than the prosperity of men, of how great simplicity — or rather, of how great folly and madness — is it to prefer the corruptible and perishable, the weak and worthless, to the incorruptible and eternal, the undefiled and unending, and by the brief enjoyment of these to be deprived of the unbroken enjoyment of those good things? Will you not understand this, father? Will you not pass by the things that pass by, and attach yourself to those that abide? Will you not prefer the dwelling-place to the sojourn, the light to the darkness, the spirit to the flesh, eternal life to the shadow of death, the things that are not dissolved to the things that flow away? Will you not escape from the grievous slavery of the terrible ruler of this world — the wicked devil, I mean — and attach yourself to the good and compassionate and all-merciful Master? Will you not, departing from the worship of the many false-named gods, serve the one true and living God? For even if you have sinned against him, blaspheming much and destroying his servants with terrible torments,

yet he will receive you, I am well assured, when you turn to him, the Good One, and will remember none of your offences; for he does not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn and live — he who came down from the unspeakable heights in search of us who had gone astray, and endured cross and scourges and death for us, and with his precious blood redeemed us who had been sold under sin. To him be glory and praise unto the ages. Amen." But the king was seized at once with amazement and with anger — the one at the young man's understanding and his irrefutable words, the other because he did not cease slandering the gods and altogether mocking and deriding his way of life. The brightness of the discourse he did not receive, because of the thickness of the darkness within; and being unable, by natural affection, to punish him or treat him ill, and wholly despairing of turning him by threats, and fearing that, if he stirred up more words against him while the young man spoke boldly and mocked and derided the gods, he might be kindled to greater anger and do something hostile against him, he rose in anger and withdrew, saying: "Would that you had never been born at all, nor come into the light, since you were to be such a one — a blasphemer of the gods and an apostate from your father's love and admonition. But you shall not mock the unconquered gods to the end, nor shall my adversaries rejoice for long, nor shall their sorceries prevail.

For unless you become obedient to me and well-disposed toward the gods, I will first give you over to many and various torments, and then put you to a most evil death, treating you not as a son, but as some enemy and apostate.

When the father had threatened these things and withdrawn in anger, the son went into his own chamber, and lifting up his eyes to his own Master of the contest, he cried out from the depth of his heart: "Lord, my God, sweet hope and unfailing promise, mighty refuge of those who lean upon you, look upon the contrition of my heart with a merciful and gracious eye, and do not forsake me, nor depart from me; but, according to your unfailing promise, be with me, the unworthy and worthless; for I know and confess you as the Maker and Provider of all creation. Strengthen me yourself, then, to remain in this good confession until my last breath; look upon me and have mercy on me, and stand by me, keeping me unharmed from all the working of Satan;

look upon me, King; for my soul is strongly inflamed with longing for you, and is kindled as with thirst in a waterless land of burning heat, longing for you, the fountain of immortality. Do not hand over to the beasts a soul that confesses you; do not forget to the end the soul of your poor one; but grant to me, the sinner, all my life long, to suffer all things for your name and your confession, and to offer up my whole self as a sacrifice to you; for when you strengthen them, even the weak shall prevail, since you alone are the unconquered ally and the merciful God, whom all creation blesses, the One glorified unto the ages. Amen." Praying thus, he perceived a divine comfort visiting his heart, and being filled with courage, he passed the whole night in prayer. But the king, having communicated to his friend Arachis what concerned his son, and having declared his blunt boldness and unalterable resolve, Arachis advised him to make his conversation with the young man as friendly and soothing as possible, hoping perhaps to draw him over by flatteries. So on the next day he came to his son, and sitting down he called him closer. Then, embracing him, he kissed him, approaching him gently and mildly, and said: "My most longed-for and beloved child, honour your father's grey hairs, and, hearing my request, come and offer sacrifice to the gods.

For thus you will have them gracious to you, and will receive from them length of days, and a share in all glory, an unassailable kingdom, and every kind of good; and you will be pleasing to me your father all your life long, and honoured and praised by all men. For it is a great matter, where praise is concerned, to obey one's father, and especially in what is good and in goodwill toward the gods. But what have you supposed, my child? Did I, declining the good road, willingly choose to go the contrary way, or did I, through ignorance and inexperience of the good, give myself over to ruinous things? But if you think that I willingly prefer evil to what is profitable and choose death over life, you seem to me, my child, to have wholly fallen away from right judgement. Do you not see how I often give myself over to hardship and toil in campaigns against enemies, or busy myself with other duties of the commonwealth, so that, when there is need, I spare myself neither hunger nor thirst, neither marching on foot nor sleeping on the ground? And toward wealth and money I have such disdain and contempt that I sometimes empty out lavishly all the treasuries of my palace, to build the greatest temples of the gods and to adorn them with every kind of ornament, or to distribute the treasures of money lavishly to the armies. Sharing, then, such contempt for pleasures and such endurance in hardships, if I knew the religion of the Galileans to be better than the one in my hands, of how much zeal would I not have judged the matter worthy,

to despise all things and to secure my own salvation? But if you charge me with ignorance and inexperience of the good, consider how many sleepless nights I have spent when some question was set before me, sometimes not even a very pressing one, granting myself no rest at all until I had found a clear and most fitting solution to what was sought. If, then, I hold not even the smallest of these temporary matters worthy of contempt until everything is accomplished profitably and to the advantage of all, and if the discernment of hidden things is, as I think, searched out by no one in all the world more precisely than by me, as is attested of me by all — how could I have reckoned divine things, and what it is lawful to worship and to declare of God, contemptible, and not have busied myself with all zeal, all power, with my whole soul and my whole mind, in the search for these, to find what is true and most fitting? And indeed I sought with toil, spending many nights like the days upon these things, and calling together many wise and learned men to this counsel, and conversing with many of those called Christians. And by tireless inquiry and ardent search the road of truth was found by me, attested by men honoured for their eloquence and understanding, that there is no other faith except the one we walk in today,

serving the greatest gods and holding fast to the sweet and pleasant life given to all men by them, a life full of the greatest delight and gladness, which the leaders and initiators of the Galileans foolishly rejected, so as to give up readily even this sweet light and all delightful things, which the gods have granted us for enjoyment, in hope of some other uncertain life, not knowing what they say or about what they make their assertions. But you, dearest son, obey your father, who has found, through careful and most true searching, what is truly good. For behold, it has been shown that neither willingly nor by way of ignorance did I miss the good, but I found and embraced it; and I long that you too should not wander foolishly, but follow me. Reverence, then, your father. Or do you not know how good a thing it is to obey one's father and to be pleasing to him in all things? — just as, on the contrary, it is ruinous and accursed to provoke a father and to count his commandments as nothing?

For all who did this perished miserably in their wickedness; among whom may you, my child, not be numbered. Rather, doing what is pleasing to your begetter, may you obtain all good things, and become heir of my blessing and my kingdom." But the high-minded and truly noble young man, hearing his father's verbose and senseless entreaty, and recognizing the devices of the crooked serpent, how he had set a snare for his feet from his right hand, contriving to bend down his godlike soul and to hinder it from the prize set before it, set before his eyes the Master's command, who said: I came not to bring peace, but strife and a sword; for I came to set a son against his father and a daughter against her mother, and so forth; and that He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and Whoever shall deny me before men, him will I also deny before my Father who is in heaven. Reasoning on these things, and fettering his soul with the divine fear,

and strengthening it with longing and love, he very seasonably took up that saying of Solomon: A time to love and a time to hate, a time of war and a time of peace. And first, praying in his mind, he said: Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me, for in you my soul has trusted, and in the shadow of your wings will I hope until iniquity passes by. I will cry to God the Most High, the God who has done me good — and the rest of the psalm. Then he said to the king: "To serve a father and to yield to his commands, and to minister to him with goodwill and friendship, our common Master teaches us, having sown such natural affection in us. But when the bond and friendship of parents brings the soul into danger and removes it far from the Creator, we are commanded to cut this off altogether, and in no way to yield to those who separate us from God, but to hate and turn from them, even if it be a father who commands what is hateful,

even if a mother, even if a king, even if the lord of life itself. For these reasons, to be deprived of God for the sake of a father's bond is impossible for me. Therefore neither trouble yourself nor me; but either be persuaded, and let us both serve the living and true God — for what you now worship are idols, the works of human hands, devoid of breath and dumb, procuring nothing at all but ruin and eternal punishment for those who worship them. But if you will not have this, do to me what seems good to you; for I am a servant of Christ, and neither by flatteries nor by punishments will I be turned from his love, as indeed I told you yesterday, setting in the midst the name of my Master and most surely establishing my word. But as for your saying that you do not willingly do evil, nor go astray from the good through ignorance, but that by much and toilsome inquiry you learned that it is truly good to serve idols and to be fastened to the pleasures of the passions — that you do evil willingly I cannot say. But that a great mist of ignorance is poured round about you, and that, walking as in palpable darkness, you do not see even a small gleam of light, whence, having lost the straight road, you have wandered among precipices and terrible ravines — this I too know surely, and I wish you, father, to know it.

Therefore, holding darkness in place of light, and clinging to death as though it were life, you think you have taken profitable counsel and devised what is advantageous; but it is not so, it is not so. For neither are the things you worship gods, but pillars of demons, holding within them all their abominable working; nor does the life you call sweet and pleasant, which you think is full of delight and gladness, have such a nature, but it is, according to the word of truth, loathsome and abominable. For a time it sweetens and soothes the throat, but afterward yields up returns more bitter than gall, as my teacher said, and sharper than a two-edged sword. And how shall I recount to you its evils? I will number them, and they shall be multiplied beyond the sand. For it is a hook of the devil, clothed about with loathsome pleasure as a bait, by which it drags down those who are deceived to the bottom of Hades. But the good things promised by my Master, which you called the hope of an uncertain life, are unfailing and unchangeable, know no end, and are not subject to corruption; there is no word able to set forth the greatness of that glory and delight, of the joy unspeakable, of the unceasing gladness.

For all of us, as you yourself see, die, and there is no man who shall live and not see death; but we shall all rise again, when the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, comes in unspeakable glory and fearful power, the only King of kings and Lord of lords, to whom every knee shall bow, of things in heaven and on earth and under the earth; and he will then bring such astonishment that even the heavenly powers themselves will be amazed; and there will stand before him with trembling a thousand thousands and ten thousand times ten thousand angels and archangels, and all will be full of fear and trembling. For one of the archangels will sound with the trumpet of God, and at once the heaven will be rolled up like a scroll, and the earth, breaking open, will send up the dead bodies of all the men who ever lived, from the time the first man Adam came to be until that day. And then all who have died from the beginning will in the twinkling of an eye stand living before the judgement seat of the immortal

Master, and each will give account of what he did. Then the righteous will shine like the sun — those who believed in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and finished the present life in good works. But how shall I recount to you the glory that will then succeed them? For though I compare their brightness and beauty to the light of the sun, though to the brightest lightning, I shall say nothing worthy of that brightness. For eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and it has not entered the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him in the kingdom of heaven, in the unapproachable light, in the unutterable and unending glory. And the righteous, indeed, will attain such good things and such blessedness; but those who denied the truly existing God, and were ignorant of the Maker and Creator, and served defiled demons, and rendered worship to dumb idols,

and longed for the pleasures of this empty life, and wallowed like swine in the mire of the passions, and made their own souls the base of operations for every wickedness — they will stand naked and exposed, ashamed and downcast, pitiable both in appearance and in fact, set forth as a reproach to all creation. And all their deeds, in word, in act, in thought, will come before their face. Then, after that most grievous shame and that unbearable reproach, they will be condemned to the unquenchable and lightless fire of Gehenna, to the outer darkness, the gnashing of teeth, and the venomous worm. This is their portion, this their lot, with which they will be together unto the unending ages, being punished, because, having thrust aside the good things of the promise, for a temporary pleasure of sin they chose eternal punishment. For these things, then — that one may attain that ineffable joy and enjoy the unutterable glory, and shine answering the angels, and stand with boldness before the good and most sweet Master, and escape those most bitter and unending torments and that painful shame —

of how much is it not worth to give up both money and bodies, or rather even our very souls? Who is so ignoble, who so without understanding, as not to undergo countless temporary deaths, that he may be delivered from eternal and unending death, and inherit the blessed and imperishable life, and be illumined with the light of the blessed and life-giving Trinity?"

When the king heard these words, and saw the firmness and immovability of the young man, who yielded neither to flatteries nor to the persuasion of words nor to the threats of punishments, he marvelled at the persuasiveness of his speech and his irrefutable answers, and was convicted by his own conscience, which showed him that the young man spoke true and just things; but he was dragged back by his wicked habit and by the passions confirmed in him as a settled state, by which he was held as in a muzzle and bridle, not being permitted to look upon the light of truth. Whence, leaving no stone unturned, as the saying goes, he held to his old aim, wishing to bring into effect the scheme he had premeditated with Arachis. And he said to his son: "You ought, my child, simply to yield to me in all my commands; but since, being hard and disobedient, you have so strongly resisted me, setting yourself to make your own opinion sovereign over all, come, let us both bid farewell to vain contention and proceed by persuasion. And since Barlaam, who deceived you, is

in my hands bound in iron, I will convene a great assembly, and call together to one place all of our own people and the Galileans, and proclaim by heralds, crying out expressly, that none of the Christians need fear, but that all may come in together without fear, and let us deliberate by common counsel. And either, having prevailed, you with your Barlaam will obtain what you have striven for; or, being persuaded, you will be eager with a willing mind to yield to my commands." But the truly prudent and sensible young man, forewarned through the vision shown him from God of the king's machination, said: "Let the will of the Lord be done, and be it as you have ordered; for the good God and Master himself grant that we be not led astray from the straight road; for in him my soul has trusted, and he will have mercy on me." Then indeed the king ordered all to be gathered, both idolaters and Christians, letters having been dispatched everywhere, and heralds crying through all the towns that none of the Christians need fear to suffer anything unexpected, but that all might come together fearlessly, by fellowship and kinship, to one place, for a truth-loving and unforced inquiry, which was to take place with their leader and guide Barlaam. Likewise he also called together the initiates and temple-keepers of the idols, and the wise men of the Chaldeans and Indians, those who were throughout the realm under him,

and certain augurs and sorcerers and diviners, that they might prevail over the Christians. And indeed a great multitude of his abominable religion came together to the king; but of the Christians only one was found who came to the help of the supposed Barlaam, by name Barachias. For some of the faithful had died, slaughtered by the madness of the rulers in the cities; others hid in mountains and caves through fear of the terrors hanging over them. And others dreaded the king's threat, and did not dare to bring themselves into the light; rather, they were devout by night, serving Christ in secret and in no way speaking openly. But that one alone, being noble in soul, came to contend on behalf of the truth. So the king, sitting before them on a lofty and elevated tribunal, ordered his son to sit beside him. But the son, unwilling, out of reverence and honour toward his father, to do this, sat on the ground near him. There stood, then, the masters of the wisdom that has been made foolish by God, whose senseless heart was led astray, as

the Apostle says: For professing to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of mortal men and of four-footed beasts and of creeping things. These came together to join battle of words against the king's son and those with him, and the proverb was fulfilled in them, that a gazelle joined battle against a lion. For the young man had made the Most High his refuge, and hoped in the shadow of his wings; but they had trusted in the rulers of this age that are coming to nothing, and in the ruler of the darkness of this world, to whom they had subjected themselves pitiably and wretchedly. So Nachor was led in, playing the part of Barlaam; and the king's party held to this aim, but the wise providence from above was ordering things otherwise. For when all these stood by, the king said to his orators and philosophers — or rather to those who lead the people astray and are without understanding in heart: "Behold, a contest is set before you, and the greatest of contests. For one of two things will happen to you: either, having upheld our cause,

and convicted Barlaam and those with him of error, you will obtain the greatest glory and honour from us and from the whole senate, and be crowned with crowns of victory; or, being defeated, you will with all shame be put to a most evil death, and all your goods will be given to the people, so that your memory may be utterly removed from the earth. For I will give your bodies as fodder to beasts, and your children I will reduce to perpetual slavery." When these things had been so spoken by the king, his son said: "A just judgement you have judged today, O king; may the Lord uphold this resolve of yours. And I say the same to my teacher." And turning, he said to Nachor, who was thought to be Barlaam: "You know, Barlaam, in what glory and luxury you found me; and by many words you persuaded me to forsake my fathers' laws and customs, and to serve an unknown God, drawing my mind, by promises of certain ineffable and eternal good things, to follow your doctrines and to provoke my father and master. Now, then, reckon that you stand as upon a balance. For if, having won the contest set before you, you show your doctrines to be true, which you taught me, and convict of error those who today oppose us, you will be glorified as none ever was, and be called a herald of truth, and I will abide in your teaching and serve Christ, as you have preached, until my last breath. But if, defeated whether by trickery or by truth, you become the cause of shame to me today, I will quickly avenge my outrage, tearing out with my own hands your heart and your tongue,

and giving these, with the rest of your body, as fodder to dogs, so that all may be taught through you not to lead astray the sons of kings." When Nachor heard these words, he was exceedingly gloomy and downcast, seeing himself fallen into the pit he had dug, and caught in the snare he had hidden, and perceiving his own sword entering his own heart. Reasoning, then, within himself, he resolved rather to side with the king's son and to uphold his cause, so as to escape the danger hanging over him, since the young man could justly punish him, if he were found to provoke him. But the whole matter belonged to the divine providence, which wisely confirmed our cause through its adversaries. For when the initiates of the idols and Nachor came to words with one another — Nachor like another Balaam, who once, in the time of Balak, having set out to curse Israel, blessed him with manifold blessings — so too Nachor strongly withstood the unwise and senseless wise men.

For while the king sat upon his throne, and his son sat beside him, as we said, and there stood the unwise orators who had sharpened their tongues like a sword for the destruction of the truth — who, in the words of Isaiah, conceive travail and bring forth lawlessness — and countless peoples had come together to behold the contest, that they might learn which side would carry off the victory, one of the orators, the most distinguished of all those with him, said to Nachor: "Are you the Barlaam who so shamelessly and rashly insults our gods, and has wrapped the king's dearest son in such error, and taught him to serve the Crucified?" And Nachor answered: "I am, I am Barlaam, who despise your gods, as you have said, but have not wrapped the king's son in error; rather, I have freed him from error and brought him near to the true God." And the orator said: "When the great and wondrous men who have discovered all the science of wisdom name those gods lofty and immortal, and all the kings and renowned men on earth bow down to them and worship them, how do you move your tongue against them, and dare at all to be so insolent in such matters? And what is the proof that these are not gods, but the Crucified?" But Nachor took up the discourse and did not deign to answer that orator at all;
and waving with his hand for the multitude to be silent, he opened his mouth, like the ass of Balaam, and spoke what he had not purposed to say; and he said to the king:

"I, O king, came into the world by the providence of God; and beholding the heaven and the earth and the sea, the sun and the moon and the rest, I marvelled at their ordering. And seeing the world and all that is in it, that it is moved by necessity, I understood that the one who moves and sustains it is God; for everything that moves is stronger than what is moved, and what sustains is stronger than what is sustained. Him, then, I say to be God, who established all things and sustains them, without beginning and everlasting, immortal and self-sufficient, above all the passions and defects — anger and forgetfulness and ignorance and the rest. Through him all things subsist. He has no need of sacrifice or libation, nor of any visible thing; but all things have need of him. These things having been so said concerning God, so far as it was given me to speak of him, let us come also to the human race, that we may see which of them share in the truth and which in error.

For it is plain to us, O king, that there are three races of men in this world: among whom are the worshippers of those you call gods, and the Jews, and the Christians. And these in turn, who worship many gods, are divided into three races: Chaldeans and Greeks and Egyptians; for these became the originators and teachers to the rest of the nations of the worship and adoration of the gods of many names. Let us see, then, which of these share in the truth and which in error. The Chaldeans, who did not know God, went astray after the elements and began to worship the creation rather than the One who created them; and making certain figures of these, they named them representations of the heaven and the earth and the sea, of the sun and the moon, and of the rest of the elements or luminaries, and, shutting them up in temples, they bow down and call them gods, and keep them securely lest they be stolen by robbers. And they did not understand that what keeps is greater than what is kept, and the maker is greater than what is made; for if their gods are powerless concerning their own preservation, how will they grant preservation to others? Into great error, then, the Chaldeans went astray, worshipping dead and useless images. And it comes to me to marvel, O king, how those called their philosophers did not at all understand that the elements themselves are corruptible. But if the elements are corruptible and subject to necessity, how are they gods?

And if the elements are not gods, how are the images, which were made in their honour, gods? Let us come, then, O king, to the elements themselves, that we may show concerning them that they are not gods, but corruptible and changeable, brought forth from nothing by the command of the truly existing God, who is incorruptible and unchangeable and invisible; but he himself sees all things, and, as he wills, alters and transforms them. What, then, shall I say concerning the elements? Those who suppose the heaven to be a god are in error. For we see it turning and moving by necessity, and composed of many parts; whence it is also called a kosmos (an ordered world). But a kosmos is the construction of some craftsman; and what is constructed has a beginning and an end. And the heaven moves by necessity with its luminaries; for the stars, borne in order and at intervals from sign to sign, some set, some rise, and at their seasons make their course, to bring about summers and winters, as has been appointed them by God; and they do not transgress their own bounds, by an inexorable necessity of nature, together with the heavenly order. Whence it is plain that the heaven is not a god, but a work of God. And those who suppose the earth to be a goddess are in error. For we see it abused by men and mastered and worked and made useless. For if it is baked, it becomes dead; for nothing grows from a potsherd. And further, if it is too much soaked,

both it and its fruits perish. And it is trodden under by men and the rest of the animals, defiled with the blood of the slain, dug through, becomes a tomb of dead bodies. These things being so, it is not possible that the earth is a goddess, but a work of God for the use of men. And those who suppose the water to be a god are in error. For it too was made for the use of men, and is mastered by them, defiled and corrupted, and altered by being boiled and changed in colour, and frozen by the cold, and brought to the washing of all unclean things. Therefore it is impossible that the water is a god, but it is a work of God. And those who suppose the fire to be a god are in error. For it too was made for the use of men, and is mastered by them, carried about from place to place for the boiling and roasting of all kinds of meats, and even of dead bodies. And it perishes in many ways, being quenched by men. Therefore it is not possible that the fire is a god, but it is a work of God. And those who suppose the breath of the winds to be a goddess are in error; for it is plain that it serves another, and was fashioned by God for the sake of men, for the conveying of ships and the gathering of grain, and for their other needs; it waxes and wanes by the command of God. Therefore the breath of the winds is not held to be a goddess, but a work of God. And those who suppose the sun to be a god are in error. For we see it moving by necessity and turning, and passing from sign to sign,

setting and rising, to warm the plants and shoots for the use of men, and further having divisions of its course with the rest of the stars, and being much less than the heaven, and failing of its light, and having no sovereignty of its own. Therefore the sun is not held to be a god, but a work of God. And those who suppose the moon to be a goddess are in error. For we see it moving by necessity and turning, and passing from sign to sign, setting and rising for the need of men, and being less than the sun, waxing and waning and having eclipses. Therefore the moon is not held to be a goddess, but a work of God. And those who suppose man to be a god are in error. For we see him moving by necessity, and nourished and growing old, even against his will. And at one time he rejoices, at another he grieves, having need of food and drink and clothing. And he is given to anger and jealousy and desire, and to regret, and has many defects. And he perishes in many ways, by the elements and by animals, and by the death that lies upon him. It is not possible, then, that man is a god, but a work of God. Into great error, then, the Chaldeans went astray, after their own desires. For they worship the corruptible elements and the dead images, and do not perceive that they are making these into gods.

Let us come, then, to the Greeks, that we may see whether they have any understanding concerning God. The Greeks, then, who say they are wise, became more foolish than the Chaldeans, introducing that many gods had come into being, some male, some female, the makers of all kinds of passions and of every sort of lawless deed. Whence the Greeks, O king, introduced ridiculous and foolish and impious words, calling those gods who are no gods, according to their wicked desires, so that, having these as advocates of their wickedness, they might commit adultery, plunder, murder, and do the most dreadful things. For if their gods did such things, how shall they too not do the like? From these practices of error, then, it came about that men have continual wars, and slaughters, and bitter captivities. But if we are willing to come in our discourse to each of their gods, you will see great absurdity. The first introduced among them before all is the god called Kronos, and to him they sacrifice their own children — he who had many children by Rhea, and going mad devoured his own children. And they say that Zeus cut off his members and threw them into the sea, whence Aphrodite is fabled to be born.

So Zeus bound his own father and threw him into Tartarus. Do you see the error and licentiousness they introduce against their god? Is it possible, then, for a god to be bound and mutilated? Oh, the folly! Who of those that have understanding would say these things? Second is introduced Zeus, whom they say reigned over their gods, and transformed himself into animals, that he might commit adultery with mortal women. For they introduce him transformed into a bull for Europa, and into gold for Danae, and into a swan for Leda, and into a satyr for Antiope, and into a thunderbolt for Semele; then that from these were born many children: Dionysus, and Zethus and Amphion, and Heracles, and Apollo and Artemis, and Perseus, Castor and Helen and Polydeuces, and Minos, and Rhadamanthus,

and Sarpedon, and the nine daughters whom they named the Muses. Then likewise they introduce the tale of Ganymede. So it came about, O king, that men imitate all these things, and become adulterers and given to unnatural lust, and workers of other dreadful deeds, in imitation of their god. How, then, is it possible for a god to be an adulterer or a pederast or a father-slayer? Together with this they also introduce a certain Hephaestus as a god, and him lame, holding a hammer and tongs, and working as a smith for the sake of food. So then he is needy; which it is not possible — that a god should be lame and have need of men. Then they introduce Hermes as a god, lustful and a thief and grasping and a sorcerer, and crook-handed and an interpreter of words. Which it is not possible — that a god should be such. And they introduce Asclepius as a god, being a physician and preparing drugs and the compounding of plasters, for the sake of food (for he was needy); but afterward he was struck by a thunderbolt by Zeus on account of Tyndareus son of Lacedaemon, and died. But if Asclepius, being a god and struck by a thunderbolt, could not help himself, how will he help others? Ares is introduced as a god, a warrior and jealous,

and a lover of flocks and of certain other things; but afterward, while committing adultery with Aphrodite, he was bound by the infant Eros and by Hephaestus. How, then, is he a god, who is lustful and a warrior and bound and an adulterer? And they introduce Dionysus as a god, holding nocturnal feasts and a teacher of drunkenness, and carrying off the wives of his neighbours, and raving and fleeing; but afterward he was slaughtered by the Titans. If, then, Dionysus, being slaughtered, could not help himself, but was also raving and drunken and a runaway, how could he be a god? And they introduce Heracles as having become drunk and gone mad, and slaughtered his own children, then consumed by fire and so died. How, then, could he be a god, a drunkard and a slayer of his own children, and burned up? Or how will he help others, being unable to help himself? And they introduce Apollo as a god, jealous, and further holding a bow and a quiver, and at times a lyre and a flute, and prophesying to men for hire. So then he is needy; which it is not possible — that a god should be needy and jealous and a lyre-player. And they introduce Artemis as his sister, a huntress, and that she has a bow with a quiver, and roams over the mountains alone with the dogs,

that she may hunt a deer or a boar. How, then, will such a woman be a goddess, a huntress and roaming with the dogs? And Aphrodite too they say is a goddess, an adulteress. For at one time she had Ares as a lover, at another Anchises, at another Adonis, whose death too she weeps, seeking her lover; and they say she even goes down to Hades, to buy back Adonis from Persephone. Have you seen, O king, a folly greater than this — to introduce as a goddess one who commits adultery and laments and weeps? And they introduce Adonis as a god, a huntsman, and that he died violently, struck by a boar, unable to help himself in his misery. How, then, will the adulterer and huntsman and one violently dead take thought for men? All these things, and many such, and many far more shameful and wicked, the Greeks introduced, O king, concerning their gods — things which it is not lawful to speak, nor to bring at all to remembrance; whence men, taking occasion from their gods, practised every lawlessness and licentiousness and impiety, defiling earth and air with their dreadful deeds.

But the Egyptians, being more stupid and senseless than these, went astray worse than all the nations. For they were not content with the objects of worship of the Chaldeans and the Greeks, but introduced still further that irrational animals, both of the land and of the water, and plants and shoots, are gods; and they were defiled in every madness and licentiousness worse than all the nations on earth. For from the beginning they worshipped Isis, who had as brother and husband Osiris, who was slaughtered by his brother Typhon. And for this reason Isis flees with Horus her son to Byblos in Syria, seeking Osiris, bitterly lamenting, until Horus grew up and killed Typhon. So then neither was Isis able to help her own brother and husband; nor was Osiris, slaughtered by Typhon, able to lay hold of himself; nor did Typhon the brother-slayer, perishing by Horus and Isis, find means to deliver himself from death. And being known by such misfortunes, they themselves were held to be gods by the senseless Egyptians.

Who, not being content even with these or with the rest of the objects of worship of the nations, introduced the irrational animals also as gods. For some of them worshipped the sheep, some the goat, others the calf and the pig, others the raven and the hawk and the vulture and the eagle, and others the crocodile, some the cat and the dog, and the wolf and the ape, and the serpent and the asp, and others the onion and the garlic and thorns, and the rest of created things. And the wretches do not perceive, concerning all these, that they are powerless. For seeing their gods eaten by other men, and burned and slaughtered and rotting, they did not understand concerning them that they are not gods. Into great error, then, went astray both the Egyptians and the Chaldeans and the Greeks, introducing such gods, and making images of them, and deifying the dumb and senseless idols. And I marvel how, seeing their gods sawn and hewn by the craftsmen, and made old by time and dissolved and melted down, they did not consider concerning them that they are not gods. For when they are powerless concerning their own preservation, how will they take thought for men? But their poets and philosophers, both of the Chaldeans and Greeks and Egyptians, wishing by their poems and writings to glorify the gods among them, the more uncovered their shame and set it forth naked before all. For if the body of man, being of many parts, casts off none of its own

members, but, having an indissoluble union with all its members, is in concord with itself, how shall there be in the nature of a god such strife and discord? For if the gods were of one nature, a god ought not to pursue a god, nor slaughter, nor do evil; but if the gods were pursued and slaughtered by gods, and seized and struck by thunderbolts, there is no longer one nature, but divided minds, all of them evil-doing, so that none of them is a god. It is plain, then, O king, that all the natural philosophy concerning the gods is error. And how did the wise and learned among the Greeks not understand that those who lay down laws are judged by their own laws? For if the laws are just, their gods are certainly unjust, having done lawless things — mutual slaughters and sorceries, and adulteries and thefts and lyings with males. But if they did these things well, then the laws are unjust, having been composed against the gods. But now the laws are good and just, praising the good and forbidding the evil; while the deeds of their gods are lawless. Their gods, then, are lawless, and all liable to death, and impious are those who introduce such gods. For if the stories about them are mythical, they are nothing but mere words; but if natural, then those who did and suffered these things are no longer gods; and if allegorical, they are myths and nothing else.

It has been shown, then, O king, that all these objects of polytheistic worship are works of error and ruin. It is not right, then, to name as gods things visible and that do not see; but the invisible One, who made all, must be worshipped as God. Let us come, then, O king, to the Jews also, that we may see what they too hold concerning God. For these, being descendants of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, sojourned in Egypt. And from there God led them out with a mighty hand and an uplifted arm through Moses their lawgiver, and made known to them his own power by many wonders and signs. But they too, showing themselves thankless and useless, often served the objects of worship of the nations, and killed the prophets and righteous men sent to them. Then, when the Son of God was pleased to come to earth, they outraged him, and betrayed him to Pilate the governor of the Romans, and condemned him to the cross, not reverencing his benefactions and the countless miracles which he worked among them. Therefore they perished by their own lawlessness. For even now they worship God the only Almighty, but not according to knowledge; for they deny Christ the Son of God, and are like the nations, even though they seem somehow to approach the truth, from which they have removed themselves far. So much concerning the Jews. But the Christians trace their genealogy from the Lord Jesus Christ. And he is confessed to be the Son of the Most High God, who, in the Holy

Spirit, came down from heaven for the salvation of men, and being born of a holy Virgin without seed and without corruption took flesh, and appeared to men, that he might recall them from the polytheistic error. And having completed his wondrous dispensation, he tasted death by the cross by his own will, according to a great dispensation; but after three days he rose again and ascended into heaven. The glory of his coming you may learn, O king, from the holy Scripture called by them the Gospel, if you will read it. He had twelve disciples, who, after his ascension into heaven, went out into the provinces of the world, and taught his greatness; just as one of them went round our regions, preaching the doctrine of the truth. Whence those who still serve the righteousness of their preaching are called Christians. And these are they who, beyond all the nations of the earth, have found the truth; for they know God, the Maker and Creator of all things, in the only-begotten Son and the Holy Spirit, and they worship no other god besides him. They have the commandments of the Lord Jesus Christ himself engraved on their hearts, and they keep these, awaiting the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come. They do not commit adultery, they do not fornicate, they do not bear false witness, they do not covet the goods of others, they honour father and mother, and love their neighbours, they judge justly, whatever they do not wish to happen to themselves they do not do to another, they comfort those who wrong them and make them their friends, they are eager to do good to their enemies, they are gentle and forbearing, they abstain from all unlawful intercourse and from all uncleanness,

they do not overlook the widow, they do not grieve the orphan; he who has supplies ungrudgingly to him who has not; if they see a stranger, they bring him under their roof, and rejoice over him as over a true brother; for they call one another brothers not according to the flesh, but according to the spirit. They are ready to give up their souls for Christ; for they keep his commandments securely, living holily and justly, as the Lord God commanded them, giving thanks to him at every hour in all food and drink and the rest of their good things. Truly, then, this is the road of truth, which leads those who travel it to the eternal kingdom, promised by Christ in the life to come. And that you may know, O king, that I do not say these things of myself, by looking into the Scriptures of the Christians you will find that I say nothing beyond the truth. Well, then, did your son understand, and justly was he taught to serve the living God and to be saved unto the age that is to come. For great and wondrous are the things said and done by the Christians; for they speak not the words of men, but those of God. But the rest of the nations are deceived and deceive themselves; for walking in darkness they dash against one another like drunken men. Thus far is my discourse to you, O king, dictated in my mind by the truth. Therefore let your senseless wise men cease their idle babbling against the Lord; for it is profitable for you to worship God the Maker and
to give ear to his incorruptible words, that, escaping judgement and punishment, you may be shown to be heirs of imperishable life."

When Nachor had gone through these things, the king was changed by anger; but his orators and temple-keepers stood speechless, unable to gainsay him except with a few rotten and worthless little arguments. But the king's son rejoiced in spirit, and with a radiant face glorified the Lord, who gives a way out of what has no way to those who trust in him, and who confirmed the truth even through the foe and enemy; and the leader of error was shown to be an advocate of right reason. The king, however, though terribly angered at Nachor, could nevertheless do him no harm, because of the decree proclaimed before all, by which he himself had urged him to speak fearlessly on behalf of the Christians; and though he gainsaid him much, he reminded him through riddling hints to give ground in his stand and to be defeated in the dispute with the orators. But Nachor prevailed all the more, dissolving all their propositions and syllogisms, and exposing the deceitfulness of their error. And when the dispute had been drawn out nearly until evening, the king ordered the council to be dissolved, intending to deliberate again about this matter on the next day. But the son said to the king: "As at the beginning you ordered a just judgement to take place, master, set justice also at the end, doing one of two things: either permit my teacher to remain with me this night,

that we may deliberate together about what we must say tomorrow to those who war against us, while you in turn, taking your men with you, may consider as is fitting whatever you wish; or, having yielded your men to me for this night, take mine to yourself. But if both are with you — mine in affliction and fear, yours in joy and ease — it does not seem to me a just judgement, but the force of power and a transgression of the agreements." The king, overcome by the elegance of the words, took his wise men and priests to himself, and yielded Nachor to his son, still cherishing hopes in Nachor and thinking he would keep what had been agreed. So the king's son went away to his own palace, like some Olympic victor who has overcome his adversaries, having Nachor with him. And calling him aside, he said: "Do not think your case is hidden from me; for I know precisely that you are not the most godly Barlaam, but Nachor the astrologer. And I marvel how it seemed good to you to play such a part, and to think you could throw such blindness over me in the middle of the day, that I should receive a wolf instead of a sheep. But the saying is well sung, that The heart of the fool will conceive vain things. This device and counsel of yours, then, was stale and altogether senseless; but the work you have done is full of all understanding. Therefore rejoice, Nachor, and be glad;

for I render you many thanks, that you have today become an advocate of the truth, and have not defiled your lips with abominable words and crafty pretence, but rather have cleansed yourself from many defilements, having convicted the error of the false-named gods and confirmed the truth of the Christian doctrines. But I was eager to bring you with me for two reasons: that the king might not, taking you aside alone, punish you because you did not speak what was to his liking; and that I might repay this favour which you have done today.
