And what is the repayment? To show you how to turn aside from the wicked and slippery road which you have travelled until now, and to walk the straight and saving path, which not in ignorance, but doing evil willingly, you fled, casting yourself down into pits and precipices of lawlessness. Understand, then, Nachor, being a man of understanding, and be eager to gain Christ alone and the life hidden with him, despising these fleeting and perishing things. For you will not live for all ages; but, being mortal, you will depart before long, like all who were before you. And woe to you, if, bearing the heavy burden of sin, you depart to that place where there is just judgement and recompense of works, and do not cast it off, since it is easy to lay it aside." So Nachor, pricked in his soul at these words, said: "Well have you spoken, O king, well. For I too know the true and unerring God, through whom all things came to be, and I understand the coming judgement, having heard of it from many words of Scripture; but the wicked habit and the assault of the old supplanter

blinded the eyes of my heart, and poured deep darkness round about my reason. But now, at your word, casting off the gloomy veil, I will run to the light of the Lord's face. Perhaps he will have mercy on me, and open a door of repentance to the wicked servant and apostate, even though it seems impossible to me that there should be forgiveness of my offences, which are heavier than the sand, . . . which in knowledge and in ignorance I have committed from childhood and until this age and grey hairs of mine." When the king's son heard this, he at once stood up and became more fervent in soul. And he began to lift up Nachor's reasoning, which was bending down toward despair, and to set it more firmly upon faith in Christ, saying: "Let there be no doubt for you about this, Nachor, none at all. For it is written that God is able even of these stones to raise up children to Abraham; which is nothing other than this, as my father Barlaam said: that out of the hopeless and those stained with all lawlessness men can be saved, and become servants of Christ, who through the utmost excess of his love for mankind opened the gates of heaven to all who turn to him, shutting the road of salvation against none at all, but compassionately receiving those who repent. For this reason also, to those who came to the vineyard at the first and third, the sixth and ninth and eleventh hour, the wage is apportioned equally, as the holy Gospel says; so that,

even though you have grown old in sins until now, if you come fervently, you will be counted worthy of the same rewards as those who have contended from their youth." When the most godly young man had spoken much else also concerning repentance to Nachor, who had grown old in evils, and had promised that Christ would be merciful and pledged forgiveness, and had assured him that the Good One is always ready to receive repentance, he softened his diseased soul as with certain medicines, and granted it pure health. For Nachor said at once to him: "May you, noble in soul rather than in body, well initiated into these wondrous mysteries, remain in the good confession until the end, and may no length of time or manner of life cut it out from your heart; but I will go away this very hour, seeking my own salvation, and through repentance reconciling the God whom I have provoked. For I will no longer look upon the king's face, if only you are willing." The king's son, becoming exceedingly glad and gladly receiving his word, embraced him and kissed him, and, earnestly praying to God, sent him out of the palace. Nachor, going out, pricked in his soul, leaped to the deepest part of the desert like a deer, and reached the cave of a certain monk who was clothed with the dignity of the priesthood, where the monk had hidden himself because of the fear that lay upon him. To him Nachor fell down most fervently, washed his feet with tears, imitating the harlot of old, and asked for holy baptism.

The priest, then, being full of divine grace, rejoiced greatly, and at once, as is the custom, having instructed him, after not a few days perfected him by baptism in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. And Nachor remained with him, ever repenting of his sins, and blessing God, who wills that none should perish, but awaits the conversion of all and compassionately receives those who repent. At dawn, when the king learned what concerned Nachor, and despaired of the hope he had cherished in him, and saw also his wise and senseless orators so utterly defeated, he was at a loss. And assailing them with terrible insults and dishonours, and some he scourged severely with ox-thongs and smeared their faces with soot, he cast them from his presence. But he himself began to condemn the weakness of the false-named gods, even though he did not yet wish to look fully upon the light of Christ. For the thick cloud of the mist surrounding him still held the sight of his heart. Yet he no longer honoured the temple-keepers, nor did he keep feasts and make libations to the idols; but he had his mind shaken from both sides, condemning on the one hand the weakness of his gods, and on the other dreading the strictness of the evangelical way of life, and being held hard to tear from his wicked habits.

For he was utterly enslaved to the pleasures of the body, and was wholly led toward the passions like a captive, and drunk, as Isaiah says, without wine, and dragged as by a muzzle of his wicked habit. While the king thus wrestled with two reasonings, his most noble son, who had truly acquired a most royal soul, lived quietly in his palace, displaying to all by his deeds the nobility of his nature, both orderly and steadfast. For theatres and horse-races and the practice of hunting, and all the empty pastimes and deceits of youth, the baits of foolish souls, he counted as nothing; but he was wholly devoted to the commandments of Christ, and longed for him, wounded in soul with divine love; he longed for the truly desirable One, who is wholly sweetness and longing, and insatiable yearning. And coming to the remembrance of his teacher Barlaam, and mirroring his life, he was charmed in soul with love, and took thought most carefully how he might see him; and carrying his words unforgettably in his heart, he was like a tree planted by the waters of the psalm, watered unceasingly and bringing forth fair fruit to the Lord. For he delivered many souls from the snares of the devil and brought them

to Christ, saved; for many who frequented him enjoyed his saving words, of whom not a few, fleeing error, ran to the saving Word; and others, bidding a long farewell to the things of life, entered the wrestling-school of the ascetic life. He himself busied himself with prayers and fasts, and frequently sent up this cry, saying: "O Lord, my Lord and King, in whom I have believed, to whom I have fled and from error been delivered, render a worthy reward to your servant Barlaam, in return for his showing me, who had gone astray, the road of truth and of life; and do not deprive me of seeing again that angel in the body, of whom the world is not worthy, and of finishing the rest of my life with him, that, walking in the footsteps of his way of life, I may be well-pleasing to you, my God and Master."

At that time there was a public festival of the false-named gods in that city; and the king was bound to be present at the feast and to adorn it with an abundance of sacrifices. But the temple-keepers were afraid, seeing him carelessly and lukewarmly disposed toward their worship, lest he should neglect to appear at the temple, and they themselves should be deprived of the royal gift given to them and of their other revenues.

So they rose up and reached a cave lying in the deepest part of the desert, where there dwelt a man given to magical arts, a most fervent champion of the idolatrous error, Theudas by name, whom the king honoured exceedingly, and held as a friend and teacher, saying that through his divination his kingdom prospered and flourished. So when the priests of the idols came to him, they called upon him for help, and made plain to him the contempt for the gods that had arisen in the king — what the king's son had done, and what Nachor had publicly declared against them — and said: "Unless you yourself come to help us, every hope is gone, all the objects of worship of the gods are lost; for you alone are left to us as the comfort of our misfortune, and on you we have set our hopes." So Theudas marched out with the satanic army present with him, and armed himself against the truth, calling up many of the wicked spirits, which he knew worked eagerly together for evil, and which that man always used as his servants; with these he came to the king. When his arrival was announced to the king, and he entered, holding a staff of palm and girded with a sheepskin cloak, the king rose from his throne,

and going to meet him greeted him, and bringing a throne made him sit beside him. Then Theudas said to the king: "O king, live forever, sheltered by the favour of the greatest gods. For I have heard that you fought a great contest against the Galileans and were crowned with the most brilliant diadems of victory. Therefore I have come, that we may together hold a feast of thanksgiving, and sacrifice comely young men and fair maidens to the immortal gods, and offer them a hundred bulls and very many animals, so that we may have them, for the time to come also, as unconquered allies, smoothing out the whole of our life." To this the king said: "We have not conquered, old man; we have not conquered, but rather have been utterly defeated. For those who were for us have suddenly become against us. Finding our battle-line frenzied and mad and weak, they cast it down completely. But now, if any power and strength is in you to help our religion that lies prostrate and to set it up again, tell me." And Theudas gave such answers to the king: "Do not fear the obstinacy and idle talk of the Galileans, O king; for what are the things said by them against men of reason and good sense? Which, if I think fit, will be cast down more easily than a leaf shaken by the wind. For they will not endure even to come before my face, much less to join words with me and proceed to propositions and rebuttals with me. But, that both this present contest and whatever else we may wish may go straight for us

and that matters may flow in their course, adorn this public feast, and put on the favour of the gods as some mighty weapon; and may it be well with you." Thus boasting, he who was mighty in evil, and had devised lawlessness all the day — for let David join his voice with ours — and given his neighbour, as Isaiah says, a turbid overthrow to drink, by the cooperation of the wicked spirits that accompanied him made the king altogether forget the reasonings that called him toward salvation, and again hold carefully to his accustomed ways. Whence, royal letters having been dispatched everywhere for all to come together at their abominable festival, one might see the multitudes streaming in, and sheep and oxen and various kinds of animals being led along. So when all had come together, the king rose with the deceiver Theudas and went to the temple, bringing a hundred and twenty bulls to sacrifice, and many animals. And they performed their accursed feast, so that the city was filled with the sound of the irrational animals, and the very air was defiled with the savour of the sacrifices. When these things had been so accomplished, and the spirits of wickedness had greatly boasted of the victory of Theudas, and the temple-keepers had rendered him thanks, the king returned again to the palace,

and said to Theudas: "Behold, as you ordered, we left out no diligence in the splendour of the festival and the abundance of the sacrifices. It is time, then, now to fulfil what you promised, and to rescue from the error of the Christians my son, who has apostatized from our objects of worship, and to reconcile him to the kindly gods. For I, having set in motion every art and every effort, found no cure for the evil; rather, I saw his resolve stronger than all. If I dealt with him gently and mildly, I found him not attending to my mind at all; if I treated him sternly and severely, I saw him raised rather to defiance. From now on I commit the matter of the misfortune that has come upon me to your wisdom. If, then, being delivered from it through you, I see my son again serving my gods together with me, and enjoying the desires of this pleasant life and kingdom, I will raise you a golden statue, and ordain that you be honoured by all like the gods for all the unending time to come." So Theudas, inclining a willing ear to the evil one, and initiated by him into a wicked and ruinous counsel, becoming a tongue and mouth for him, said to the king:

"If you wish to subdue your son and to make his resistance empty, I have found an art against which he will not even be able to hold out; rather, his hard and unyielding reasoning will be softened more easily than wax that has met a most violent fire." But the king, seeing the vain man so puffing himself up to no purpose, was at once changed to pleasure and gladness, hoping that that unbridled and bold tongue would prevail over a soul taught of God and full of philosophy. And he asked to learn what the art was. Then Theudas wove his crime like a sharpened razor, and dreadfully prepared his drugs. And behold the evil-crafted sophism and the suggestion of the evil one. "Remove from your son," he said, "O king, all who stand by him and serve him, and order that women fair of form and exceedingly beautiful, and adorned in the most alluring way, be with him continually and serve him, and live with him and lodge with him. And I, sending against him one of the spirits appointed to me for such things, will the more violently kindle the fire of pleasure. And the moment he consorts with even one single such woman, if everything does not go for you according to your wish, then let me henceforth be despised by you and useless, and worthy of the greatest punishments, not of honours.
For nothing is so apt to draw on and charm the reasonings of males as the sight of women. And hear a tale that bears witness to my word."

A certain king, having no male child, was greatly distressed in soul, weighed down with grief, and reckoned this no small misfortune. While he was in this condition, a son was born to him; and the king's heart was filled with joy at this. But those skilled in the art of medicine told him that, if within the first twelve years this child should look upon the sun or upon fire, he would be utterly deprived of his sight; for the very set of his eyes declared as much. On hearing this, the king is said to have hewn out of a certain rock a little cavern-like dwelling, and there to have shut the boy up together with those who nursed him, never, until the completion of the twelve years, to let so much as a gleam of light appear to him at all. After the twelve years were complete, he brought the boy out of the little dwelling, who had beheld nothing whatever of the world; and the king commanded his servants to set out everything kind by kind and show it to him: men in one place, women in another, and elsewhere gold and silver, and in yet another place pearls and precious stones, splendid and well-fashioned garments, very beautiful chariots with royal horses bridled in gold and decked with purple coverings, and mounted upon them armed riders, and herds of oxen and flocks of sheep. In a word, they showed the boy everything, set out in order. And when he asked what each of these things was called,

the king's shield-bearers and guards declared the name of each. But when he asked to learn the name of the women, the king's sword-bearer said, by way of jest, that they were called demons, who lead men astray. And the boy's heart was charmed with longing for these more than for all the rest. So when they had taken him round to everything and brought him back to the king, the king asked him which of the things he had seen had pleased him. "What," said the boy, "but those demons who lead men astray? For of all that I have seen today, my soul has been kindled with love for nothing so much as for them." And that king marvelled at the boy's words, and at what a tyrannous thing the love of women is. "You too, then, must think to subdue your son by no other means than this." The king received the counsel gladly. And there were brought to him chosen maidens, fair and very beautiful, whom he adorned with shining apparel and arrayed altogether for allurement; and he cast all his son's attendants and servants out of the palace, and set these women in their place. So they clung to him, embraced him, provoked him to that vile union, calling him to pleasure by every gesture and word. He had no one else to look upon, or to converse with, or to dine with; for they were everything to him.

This, then, the king did. But Theudas, again seizing upon that wicked cave of his, and poring over the books that have power to work such things, and summoning one of the wicked spirits, sent it out to do battle against the soldier of Christ's battle-line; not knowing, wretched man, what laughter he was about to undergo and how he would be filled with shame, together with all the demonic host beneath him. And the wicked spirit, taking with it other and more wicked spirits, came upon the chamber of the noble youth, and fell upon him, kindling most fiercely the furnace of the flesh. The evil one inflamed him within; while the maidens, fair of face but very foul of soul, supplied the wicked fuel from without.

But that pure soul, perceiving the assault of the evil one, and seeing the war of unseemly thoughts coming violently against it, was thrown into confusion; and it sought to find some release from so great an evil, to present itself pure to Christ, and not to defile with the mire of the passions that holy robe with which the grace of holy baptism had clothed him. At once, then, he set love against love, the divine against the unchaste, and called to mind that beauty and unspeakable glory of Christ, the immortal Bridegroom of the purest souls, and that bridal chamber and marriage feast, from which those who have stained their wedding garment are pitiably cast out, bound hand and foot, into the outer darkness. Pondering these things and bursting into tears, he beat his breast, driving out those wicked thoughts from there like evil drones. Then, rising up and lifting his hands to heaven, with hot tears and groans he called upon God for aid, and said: "Lord Almighty, who alone art mighty and compassionate, the hope of the hopeless, the help of the helpless, remember me, thy unworthy servant, in this hour, and look upon me with a merciful eye, and deliver my soul from the demonic sword, and my only one from the power of the dog; and let me not fall into the hands of my enemies, nor let those who hate me rejoice over me; and forsake me not, to be destroyed in iniquities,

and to do dishonour to my body, which I promised to present pure to thee. For it is thee I long for, and to thee I bow down, the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, now and ever and unto the ages." And when he had said the Amen, he was aware of a divine consolation coming upon him from heaven, and the wicked thoughts withdrew; and he continued in prayer until morning. And, having understood the devices of the deceiver, he began to press his body still harder with want of food and with thirst and with other hardship, keeping vigil through whole nights, reminding himself of his vows to God, sketching out in his thoughts the brightness of the righteous in that place beyond, and most vividly recalling the Gehenna threatened to the wicked; so that the enemy, finding the soul idle and unguarded, might not easily sow wicked thoughts in it, and muddy the purity of the mind.

When, therefore, the enemy was at a loss on every side, and had altogether despaired of taking the noble youth, that dreadful one resorted to another, more intricate deceit—he who is forever wicked and never leaves off contriving and doing harm. For he made countless efforts to bring to effect the things commanded him by Theudas. And so once more he prepares his drugs. For, entering into one of those young women—the one who was fairest of all, being the daughter of a king, and a captive, estranged from her own homeland and brought as a most precious gift to King Abenner, whom the father, because she was exceedingly beautiful, had sent to be the slip and the tripping-up of his son—into her the deceiver entered, and put words into her that showed the great cleverness and shrewdness of her reasoning. For the evil one readily makes use of every device that tends to wickedness. Then, falling upon the king's son from the right hand, he instilled in him a fondness for the girl, on the pretext of her good sense and modesty, and because, being so nobly born and of royal lineage,

she had been deprived at once of her homeland and of her glory. Besides this, he sowed in him thoughts of freeing her from her madness for idols and making her a Christian. But all these things were the contrivances of the crafty serpent. For the king's son, being thus disposed in soul, and seeing in himself no foul thought or passionate love stirring toward the girl, but only compassion and pity for her misfortune and the ruin of her soul, did not know that the matter was a demonic device; for that one is indeed darkness, and counterfeits the light. So when the king's son began to converse with the girl and to speak to her the words of the knowledge of God, saying, "Understand, O woman, the God who lives unto the ages, and be not destroyed by this error of the idols, but acknowledge the Master and Maker of this universe, and you shall be blessed, wedded to the immortal Bridegroom"—and as he admonished her at length in this way, at once the wicked spirit prompted the woman to spread out the snares of its deceit, and

to drag down into the pit of passion that soul beloved of God, just as once it did to the first father by means of Eve, miserably driving him, alas, out of paradise and from God, and contriving that he should become liable to death instead of to the blessed and immortal life. For when the girl heard those words filled with all wisdom, being without understanding she did not understand them; but she gave such answers as one who had become a tongue and a mouth for the evil one, and said: "If, my lord, you are concerned for my salvation, and are eager to bring me to your God and to save my humble soul, do you also grant one request of mine, and at once, renouncing all my ancestral gods, I shall join myself to your God, serving him until my last breath; and you shall receive a reward for my salvation and my conversion to God."

And when he said, "What is the request, O woman?" she, composing her bearing and her glance and her voice and her whole self for enticement, said, "Join yourself to me in the fellowship of marriage, and I shall gladly follow your commands." And he said, "In vain, O woman, have you put before me so hard a request. For I care strongly for your salvation, and I long to draw you up from the deep of perdition; but to defile my body by a shameful union is grievous to me and altogether impossible." And she, smoothing the whole road for him and making it level, said, "Why do you speak in this way, you who are filled with all wisdom? Why have you called the thing a defilement and a shameful union? For I too am not uninitiated in the Christian books; rather, I have come upon many writings in my homeland, and have heard many Christians who conversed with me. Is it not written in one of the books that are yours, 'Marriage is honourable, and the bed undefiled'? And, 'It is better to marry than to burn'? And, 'What God has joined together, let no man put asunder'? Do not your Scriptures teach that all the righteous of old, the patriarchs and the prophets, were joined in marriage?

Is it not written that even Peter, whom you say became the chief of the apostles, had a wife? By whom, then, are you persuaded to call this a defilement? You seem to me, my lord, to have strayed far from the truth of your own teachings." And he said, "Yes, O woman; all these things are just as you have said. For it is permitted to those who wish to share in marriage—but not to those who have once promised to keep their virginity for Christ. For I, from the time I was cleansed in the bath of divine baptism from the offences of my youth and ignorance, agreed to present myself pure to Christ; and how shall I dare to dissolve what I have promised to God?" Then the woman said again: "Let this too be your will, as you wish. But fulfil another small and trifling desire of mine, if indeed you truly wish to save my soul. Lie with me this one night only, and grant that I may take delight in your beauty, and do you yourself take your fill of my comeliness. And I give you my word that at dawn I shall become a Christian and flee from all the worship of my gods. And there shall be for you not only pardon for this dispensation, but also a recompense of gifts from your God for the sake of my salvation. For joy,'

says your Scripture, 'is in heaven over one sinner who repents.' If, then, there is joy in heaven over the conversion of a sinner, is not a great reward owed to the one who brings about that conversion? Yes, it is so; do not doubt it. Did not even the apostles, the founders of your religion, do many things by way of dispensation, sometimes transgressing a commandment for the sake of a greater commandment? Is not Paul said to have circumcised Timothy for the sake of a better dispensation? And yet circumcision was reckoned unlawful for Christians; but nevertheless he did not refuse to do this. And you will find many such things in your Scriptures. If, then, in truth, as you say, you are seeking to save my soul, fulfil this small desire of mine. And whereas I sought to be joined to you in the perfect fellowship of marriage, since this is not to your liking, I no longer compel you, but do all that pleases you; only do not you, in your turn, utterly abhor me, but, by granting me this one thing, you shall save me, delivering me from my superstitious error, and for the rest you shall do what you have resolved for the whole of your life." So she spoke—for indeed she had the one who prompted her, to whom she secretly lent her ears; and the robber, the very maker and teacher of wickedness, was skilled in the Scriptures—saying such things, then, and fawning, weaving nets and snares for him on the right hand and on the left, she began to shake the tower of his soul, to slacken the tension of his resolve, and to make his judgment softer.

But the sower of wickedness and enemy of the righteous, seeing his heart shaken, became full of joy, and at once called the spirits of wickedness that had come with him, crying, "Do you see how this girl is hastening to accomplish what we ourselves were not able to accomplish? Come, then, let us now fall upon him with all our strength; for we shall find no other moment so well suited to fulfil the will of him who sent us." Having said this to his own dogs, the crafty-minded one, they set upon the soldier of Christ, throwing all the powers of his soul into confusion, putting in him a terrible love for the girl, and kindling in him a most violent fire of desire. And seeing himself strongly inflamed and led captive toward sin, and his very thoughts—about the girl's salvation and her conversion to God—set as a bait upon a hook about the deed laid before him, troubling him with the enemy's suggestion that it was no sin to lie once with a woman for the saving of a soul, he groaned in the perplexity of his soul a deep and melting groan, and at once braced himself to prayer, and pouring streams of tears abundantly from his eyes, he cried out to him who is able to save those who trust in him: "In thee, O Lord, have I hoped; let me never be put to shame, nor let my enemies laugh me to scorn—me who hold fast to thy right hand—but stand by me in this

hour, and according to thy will direct my ways, that thy name, glorious and terrible, may be glorified upon me thy servant; for blessed art thou unto the ages. Amen." And having prayed with tears for many hours and bowed the knee many times, he let himself sink down upon the ground. And falling briefly asleep, he saw himself snatched up by certain dreadful beings, and led through places he had never seen, and brought into a vast plain luxuriant with beautiful and exceedingly fragrant flowers, where he saw plants of every kind and sort, heavy with strange and wonderful fruits, most pleasant to see and delightful to touch. And the leaves of the trees made a clear sound in a very gentle breeze, sending forth, as they stirred, a most charming and unwearying fragrance. There were set up thrones fashioned of the purest gold and of precious stones, casting forth such a brilliant radiance; and couches adorned with marvellous coverings, surpassing all description in their beauty. And waters flowed by, very clear and gladdening the very sight. And after they had led him across this wondrous and great plain, those dreadful beings brought him into a city shining with an ineffable splendour, having its walls of translucent gold and its battlements raised up of stones such as no one has ever seen. Oh, who could tell the beauty of that city and its radiance?

A light from above, darting thickly with its rays, filled all its streets; and certain winged hosts, each one of them itself a light, dwelt there, singing a song never heard by mortal ear. And he heard a voice saying, "This is the rest of the righteous; this is the gladness of those who have pleased the Lord." Leading him out from there, those most awesome men said they would take him back. But he, wholly taken up with that delight and gladness, said, "Do not deprive me—do not, I beseech you—of this unspeakable joy; but grant that I too may dwell in some corner of this great city." But they said, "It is impossible now for you to be here. But with much toil and sweat you shall come here, if indeed you compel yourself." Thus they spoke; and, crossing the great plain again, they carried him away to dark places, full of all loathsomeness, possessing a misery equal in measure to the brightness that had been seen. For there was a lightless and utterly murky darkness, and the whole place was filled with affliction and tumult. There a furnace blazed, flaming up; and there was a kind of punishing worm creeping there. And there were avenging powers standing over the furnace,

and certain ones being pitiably consumed by the fire. And a voice was heard saying, "This is the place of sinners; this is the punishment of those who have defiled themselves with shameful deeds." Upon this, those who had brought him in led him out from there. And, coming at once to himself, he was wholly trembling, and his eyes shed tears like a river. And all the comeliness of that unchaste girl, and of the rest, was reckoned by him more foul-smelling than mire and rottenness. And turning over in his soul the memory of the things he had seen, with longing for those good things and with fear of those grievous ones, he lay upon his bed scarcely able to rise. And the king was told of his son's illness. And he, coming, asked what had happened. And the son recounted to him the things he had seen, and said, "Why have you prepared a snare for my feet, and bowed down my soul? For if the Lord had not helped me, my soul had well-nigh dwelt in Hades. But how good is God to Israel, to the upright in heart; who also delivered my lowliness from the midst of the lions' whelps. For I lay down in confusion. But my God and Saviour visited me from on high, and showed me of what good things they have deprived themselves who provoke him, and to what punishments they have made themselves liable. And now, O father, since you have stopped up your ears so as not to hear my voice, which chants good things to you,

do not at least hinder me from walking the straight road. For this I long for, this I desire: to be released from all things, and to reach those places where Barlaam, the servant of Christ, has his dwelling, and to spend the rest of my present life together with him. But if you should wish to hold me back by force, you shall soon see me dead of grief and anguish; and then neither shall you any longer be called father, nor shall you have me any longer for a son"

Once again, then, despondency seized the king; once again he despaired of his whole life, and turning dreadful things over within himself he withdrew to his own palace. But the spirits of wickedness that had been sent by Theudas against the divine youth, returning to him, confessed their defeat in shame, lovers of falsehood though they were; for they bore clear tokens of the defeat upon their wicked countenances. And he said, "Are you so weak and wretched, then, that you cannot prevail over a single boy?" Then the wicked spirits, chastised by divine power, brought the truth unwillingly to light, saying, "We cannot endure even to look in the face of the power of Christ and the symbol of his passion, which they call the cross. For when that is traced, we, all of us—the rulers of the air and world-rulers of the darkness—flee headlong and are thrust away

before it is fully traced. Thus, when we fell upon this young man, we troubled him grievously; but he, calling upon Christ for aid and arming himself with the sign of the cross, drove us off in anger and set himself in safety. So, without delay, we found an instrument by which our ruler once spoke with the first-formed man and overcame him. And indeed we ourselves would have counted the young man's hope as nothing, but Christ, being called again to his aid, scorched us with the fire of wrath from above and made us fugitives. And we have resolved no longer to come near him." So plainly, then, did the wicked spirits make known to Theudas what had happened. But the king, at a loss on every side, summoned Theudas again, and said, "Most wise one, we have done all that you resolved, yet have found no benefit. Now, if any other contrivance is left to you,

let us make trial of that also; perhaps I may find some release from this evil." And when Theudas asked to come and converse with the son, the king took him along at dawn and went out to visit his son. And sitting down, the king began to speak, reproaching him and finding fault with his disobedience and his unyielding resolve. But when the son again confirmed the same things and cried out that he preferred nothing to the love of Christ, Theudas came forward into their midst and said, "Why have you condemned our immortal gods, Josaphat, that you have departed from their worship, and, provoking your father and king in this way, have become hateful to all the people? Is not your very life from them? Did they not themselves grant you to your father, hearing his prayer and freeing him from the bonds of childlessness?" And as the man grown old in wickedness put forward many vain words and useless arguments, stitching together syllogisms about the preaching of the Gospel, wishing on the one hand to mock it and on the other to strengthen the cause of the idols, the son of the kingdom above—a citizen of that city which the Lord set fast, and not man—held off a little and said to Theudas: "Listen, you abyss of error, you murkier than the darkness that can be felt, you seed of Babylon, you offspring of the tower-building of Chalane, by which the world was thrown into confusion, you vain-minded and wretched old man,

you for whom even the five cities burned up with fire and brimstone proved lighter in their sins. Why do you set out to mock the preaching of salvation, by which the things in darkness were enlightened, by which the wandering found the road, by which the lost and grievously captive were recalled? Tell me, which is better: to worship God Almighty, with his only-begotten Son and the Holy Spirit—God uncreated and immortal, the beginning and fountain of good things, whose power is beyond likening and whose glory is past comprehension, beside whom stand a thousand thousands and ten thousand times ten thousand of the ranks of angels and heavenly hosts, and full are heaven and earth of his glory; through whom all things were brought forth from nothing, through whom the whole is upheld and held together and governed by his providence—is it better to worship him, or destructive demons and lifeless idols, whose glory and praise is adultery and the corruption of boys and the rest of the works of lawlessness which are written about your gods in the books of your superstition? Are you not ashamed, wretches, food for the unsleeping fire, likeness of the Chaldean race,

are you not ashamed to bow down before dead images, the works of a man's hand? For having carved a stone or worked a piece of wood, you have called it god; and then, taking the fairest bull from the herds, or perhaps some other of the most comely animals, you sacrifice to a dead object of worship, you fools. The victim is more precious than your object of worship; for the image a man made, but the animal God created. And by how much is the irrational animal more understanding than you, the rational one? For it knows its feeder; but you have failed to know God, through whom you were brought forth from nothing, through whom you live and are kept in being; and you call him god whom a little while ago you watched being struck with iron and burned in the fire and melted down and beaten with hammers; whom you overlaid with silver and gold, and, raising up from the ground, set on high; and then, falling to the earth, you lie lower than the lowly stone, bowing down not to God but to the works of your hands, dead and lifeless.

Or rather, it would not even be right to call the idol dead. For how could that be dead which never lived? Rather, some new name had to be devised for it, worthy of so great a madness. For the one of stone is shattered, the one of earthenware is broken, the one of bronze rusts, the one of gold and the one of silver are melted down. And indeed your gods are sold, some cheaply, others for as great a price as possible. For it is not their divinity but their material that gives them their costliness. And who buys a god? Who sells a god? And how is a god that cannot move called a god? Or do you not see that the one standing never sits down, and the one sitting never rises up? Be ashamed, you fool; put your hand over your mouth, you who have lost your wits, praising such things. For having become estranged from the truth, you were led astray by false images, fashioning statues and putting the name of God upon the works of your hands. Sober up, wretch, and understand that you are older than the god made by you. This is great madness. You have persuaded yourself that, being a man, you can make a god. And how can this come to pass? So that you do not make a god, but a shape of a man or of some animal, having no tongue, no throat, no brain, nor any of the inner parts; so that it is neither a likeness of a man nor of an animal, but altogether useless and full of vanity. Why, then, do you flatter senseless things? Why do you sit beside things motionless and unprofitable? If the craft of the stone-cutter or the carpenter or the hammer-smith had not been at hand, you would not have had a god. If guards did not sit beside it, you would have lost your god. For the very thing to which a populous city of fools often prays

to be preserved, as to a god—beside that thing a few guards remain, so that it may not be stolen. And if it is of silver or of gold, it is carefully guarded; but if it is of stone or of clay, or of some other such cheaper material, it guards itself; for perhaps, according to you, the one of clay is stronger than the one of gold. Is it not fitting that you, the foolish, the blind and witless, should justly be laughed at—or rather, be mourned over? For your works are works of madness, not of piety. For the man who practised war set up an image in imitation of a military figure, and called it Ares; the man who shaped his soul to a woman-mad desire deified the passion, naming it Aphrodite. Another, for the sake of his love of wine, fashioned an idol which he called Dionysus. And likewise those who lusted after the other vices set up idols of their own passions; for they named their passions gods. And for this reason, beside their altars, there are voluptuous dances, the sounds of harlots' songs, and frenzied impulses. And who could tell in order their abominable practice? Who could bear to defile his own mouth in reciting their obscenities? But these things are plain to all, even if we keep silent. These are your objects of worship, Theudas, you who are more senseless than your images; to these you bid me bow down, these you bid me reverence. Truly this counsel is of your own malice and witless mind; but may you become like them, you and all who trust in them.

But I will worship my God, and to him I will sacrifice my whole self, to God the Creator and Provider of all things, through our Lord Jesus Christ our hope, through whom we have obtained our approach to the Father of lights in the Holy Spirit, through whom we were ransomed from bitter slavery in his blood. For if he had not humbled himself even to the form of a servant, we would not have been counted worthy of adoption. He humbled himself, then, for our sake, not regarding his divinity as a thing to be grasped at, but remaining what he was and taking up what he was not; he conversed with men, went up on the cross in his flesh, was laid in a tomb for three days, descended into Hades, and led out those whom the dread world-ruler held in bonds, sold under sin. What harm, then, came to him from these things, that you think to mock him? Do you not see this sun, into how many useless and foul places it sends down its ray? How many dead and stinking bodies it looks upon?

Does any stain cling to it? Does it not dry up and bind together what is foul and rotted, and enlighten what is in darkness, while it remains itself wholly unharmed and incapable of receiving any defilement? And what of fire? Taking the iron, black and cold in itself, does it not make the whole of it like flame and red-hot? Has it taken on any of the properties of the iron? When the iron is struck with hammers and beaten, does the fire suffer anything, or undergo any harm at all? If, then, these created and corruptible things naturally suffer nothing from contact with baser things, by what reasoning, you fool and stony-hearted one, do you dare to mock me when I say that the Son and Word of God, in no way departing from the Father's glory, but being himself God, for the salvation of men took up a human body, that he might make men sharers in the divine and intelligent nature; and, leading our essence out of the lowest depths of Hades, might honour it with heavenly glory; that, by the taking on of flesh having lured the ruler of the darkness of this age, he might overcome him, and free our race from his tyranny? Therefore, indeed, without suffering he takes part in the suffering of the cross, displaying his two natures: for as a man he is crucified, but as God he darkens the sun, shakes the earth, and raises many sleeping bodies from their graves;

again, as a man he dies, but as God he rises up, having despoiled Hades. Therefore the prophet cried out: 'Hades was embittered, meeting you below.' For it was embittered and mocked, supposing it had taken a mere man, but having fallen in with God, and suddenly become empty and itself a captive. He rises up, then, as God, and ascends into the heavens, from which he was never in any way separated. And our base nature—the most witless of all, the thankless and dishonoured—he has made higher than all, and seated it on a throne of glory, shining with immortal glory. What harm, then, came from this to God and the Word, that you do not blush to blaspheme? And what of it? Is it not better to confess these things, and to reverence such a God, good and loving toward mankind, who commands righteousness, enjoins self-control, lays down purity as law, teaches mercy, supplies faith, proclaims peace, who is named—and is—Truth itself, Love itself, Goodness itself? Is it not better to reverence him than your gods, the much-suffering and wicked ones, shameful both in their deeds and in their names? Woe to you, more stony than the stones and more irrational than the irrational beasts, sons of perdition, heirs of darkness; but blessed am I and all Christians, having a God good and loving toward mankind. For those who worship him, even if for a short time in this present life they suffer hardship, yet shall reap the immortal fruit of recompense in the kingdom of
unending and divine blessedness"

But Theudas said to him: "See, it is plain that our religion was established by many and great wise men, by interpreters, and by men wonderful in virtue and knowledge, and that all the kings of the earth and the powerful received it as good and having nothing perilous in it; whereas the religion of the Galileans was proclaimed by certain rustic men, poor and of no account, and these few, not exceeding the number of twelve. How, then, should the preaching of the few—obscure and rustic men—be preferred to the legislation of the many and great, who shone with such great wisdom? And what is the proof that these speak the truth and those lie?" The king's son answered again: "Perhaps, Theudas, you are, as the saying goes, an ass that hears the lyre and remains uncomprehending—or rather an asp that stops up its ears so as not to hear the voice of the charmers. Well, then, did the prophet say of you: 'If the Ethiopian can change his skin and the leopard its spots, then you also can do good, having learned to do evil.' Fool and blind man, how does the strength of the truth not bring you to your senses?

For this very thing—that your foul objects of worship are praised by many who are admired for wisdom, and upheld by many kings, while the preaching of the Gospel was proclaimed by few and obscure men—shows the strength of our worship of God and the weakness and ruin of your wicked teachings; for your doctrines, though they have wise advocates and powerful defenders, are nonetheless being quenched and growing weak, while the things of the worship of God, possessing no human help, shine brighter than the sun and have taken hold of the fullnesses of the world. For if it had been set forth by orators and philosophers, and had kings and rulers working with it, you, the wicked one, would have found grounds to say that the whole thing came about by human power; but as it is, seeing that the holy Gospel was composed by lowly fishermen, was persecuted by all the tyrants, and after this took hold of the whole inhabited world—

for its sound went out into all the earth, and its words to the ends of the world—what could you say, except that it is a divine and unconquerable power, confirming its own works for the salvation of men? And what proof do you seek, you fool, that your people lie and ours speak the truth, better than what has been said? For if all your doctrines were not nonsense and falsehood, they would not, having so much strength from men, be diminished and growing weak. 'For I saw the impious one,' it says, 'exalted on high and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold, he was not; and I sought him, and his place was not found.' These things the prophet said about you, the henchmen of the madness for idols. For in a very little while your place too will not be found, but, as smoke vanishes, you shall vanish, and as wax melts before the face of the fire. But concerning the knowledge of God in the Gospel the Lord said: 'Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away.' And again the psalmist says: 'You, Lord, in the beginning

laid the foundation of the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They shall perish, but you remain; and they shall all grow old like a garment, and like a mantle you shall roll them up, and they shall be changed; but you are the same, and your years shall not fail.' And the divine heralds of Christ's coming, the wise fishermen of the world, who drew all men up from the deep of error, whom you, the lowly one and truly a slave of sin, despise—they shone with signs and wonders and various works of power, like the sun in the world, giving sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, walking to the lame, freely granting life to the dead. For their shadows alone healed all the sufferings of men. The demons, whom you fear as gods, they not only drove out from the bodies of men, but chased from the very inhabited world, by the sign of the cross, through which they made all sorcery vanish and showed all witchcraft to be without effect. And those men, having thus healed human weakness by the power of Christ, and made the whole creation new, are rightly admired by all the sound-minded as heralds of the truth. But what

can you yourself say about your own people and orators—whose wisdom God made foolish—the advocates of the devil? What worthy of remembrance did they leave to the world? Tell me. And what could you say about them, except unreason and shamefulness, and a vain craft that with the fine speech of words conceals the mire of their foul-smelling religion? But even of the poets themselves, all who had power to lift their heads a little out of their great madness spoke the truer word: that those who are called gods were men, and that, because some of them ruled over lands and cities, and others did some trifling thing in their lifetime, men were led astray and called them gods. For at the beginning that Serug is recorded to have invented the making of statues.

For he is said to have honoured with statues and pillars those who in ancient times displayed some deed of courage or friendship or some other manly excellence worthy of remembrance. But those who came after, being ignorant of the intention of their forefathers—that they had set up statues and pillars for the sake of remembrance alone, for those who had done something praiseworthy—being little by little led astray by the working of the demon who is the author of evil, attached themselves, as to immortal gods, to men of like passions and corruptible, and devised sacrifices and libations for them; the demons, of course, having taken up dwelling in the images, and drawn the honour and the sacrifices to themselves. Those demons, then, persuade those who do not see fit to keep God in their knowledge to regard themselves as gods, for two reasons: that they themselves might be glorified by this title—for they delight, being full of arrogance, to be honoured as gods—and that they might drag those whom they have deceived into the unquenchable fire prepared for themselves. Hence they taught men all lawlessness and shamefulness, since they had once been subjected to their deceit. Having come, then, to this summit of evils, men, being darkened, each set up a pillar of his own passion and his own desire,

and called it god—abominable in their error, and become more abominable through the absurdity of the things they worshipped—until the Lord came, and through the bowels of his mercy ransomed us who believe in him from this wicked and ruinous error, and taught the true knowledge of God. For there is no salvation except in him, and there is no other god, neither in heaven nor on earth, except he alone, the Maker of all, who bears all things by the word of his power. 'For by the word of the Lord,' it says, 'the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their power'; and, 'all things came to be through him, and without him came to be not one thing that has been made.'" But Theudas, hearing these words, and that the discourse was full of God-taught wisdom, struck as it were by the crash of thunder, was held fast in speechlessness. And late and with difficulty coming to a sense of his own wretchedness—for the saving word touched the darkened eyes of his heart, and great repentance for his former deeds came over him—and condemning the error of the idols, he ran to the light of true religion. And from that time he so turned away from his wretched manner of life, and so set himself at war against the base passions and the magic arts, as great as had been the friendship he had once made with them. For then, standing in the midst of the council, with the king seated before him, he cried out with a loud voice:

"Truly, O king, the Spirit of God dwells in your son; truly we are defeated, and we have no further defence, nor are we able to look in the face of the things he says. Great indeed, then, is the God of the Christians, great is their faith, great are their mysteries." And turning to the king's son, he said: "Tell me, then, you who are enlightened in soul: does Christ receive me, if, departing from my wicked deeds, I turn to him?" "Yes," said the herald of the truth, "yes, he receives you too, and all who turn to him. And he receives them not in a bare way, but, as a son returning from a far country, he goes out to meet the one who turns back from the road of lawlessness; and embracing him he kisses him, and at once stripping off the disgrace of sin, he puts upon him the garment of salvation, and clothing him with a robe of most splendid glory, he holds a mystical festival of gladness for the powers above, celebrating the return of the lost sheep. For the Lord himself said that there is great joy in heaven over one sinner who repents. And again, 'I came not,' he says, 'to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.' And he says also through the prophet: 'As I live, says the Lord,

I do not wish the death of the sinner and the impious, but rather that he should turn from his way and live. Turn back, turn back from your evil way; and why do you die, house of Israel? For the lawlessness of the lawless one shall not harm him in the day in which he turns from his lawlessness and does righteousness; and if he walks in the ordinances of life, he shall surely live and shall not die; all his sins that he committed shall not be remembered; because he did a judgment of righteousness, in it he shall live.' And again, through another prophet he cries: 'Wash yourselves, become clean, take away the wickedness from your souls before my eyes; cease from your wickednesses; learn to do good. And come, let us reason together; and though your sins be as scarlet, I will make them white as snow; and though they be as crimson, I will make them white as wool.' Such promises, then, being set before those who turn back from God, do not delay, O man, nor put it off; but come to Christ our God who loves mankind, and be enlightened, and your face shall not be put to shame. For at the moment you go down into the font of divine baptism, all the disgrace of the old man and the whole burden of your many sins is buried in the water and passes into nothingness, and you come up from there new and clean of all defilement,

carrying no spot or wrinkle of sin; and for the rest it lies with you to preserve for yourself the cleansing that has come to you from there through the bowels of the mercy of our God." So Theudas, instructed by these words, went out at once, and reaching that wicked cave, took his books of magic—as the first-fruits of all wickedness, as treasuries of demonic rites—and burned them up with fire. And he himself reached the cave of that holy man, to whom Nachor too had withdrawn, and recounted to him all his story, pouring dust upon his head, heaving heavy groans and washing himself with tears, and relating to the old man in order his abominable deeds. And that man, being most skilled at saving a soul and snatching it from the throat of the crafty serpent, charmed him with saving words, pledged him forgiveness, promised that the Judge would be merciful. Then, having instructed him and bidden him fast for many days, he cleansed him by divine baptism. And the man was genuinely repentant all his days for the offences he had committed, propitiating God with tears and groans"

But the king, when matters had turned out thus, being at a loss on every side, was plainly tormented strongly and bearing a great storm in his soul. And calling together again all who belonged to the council of the senate, he considered what he should now do with his own son. And when the many had put forward many counsels, that Arachis mentioned above, who was more eminent in command and first in the council, said to the king: "What ought we to have done with your son, O king, and have not done, to persuade him to follow our teachings and worship our gods? But, as I see, we are attempting the impossible; for his contentiousness and implacability are his by nature, or perhaps by fortune. If, then, you should wish to give him over to tortures and punishments, you will be an enemy of nature and will no longer be called father, and you will lose him, since he is ready to die for Christ. It remains, then, to do this one thing only: to divide the kingdom with him, and to entrust to him the rule over the portion that falls to him. And if the nature of affairs and the cares of daily life draw him to embrace our purpose and way of life, the matter will go according to our aim; for habits firmly established in the soul are hard to erase, and are changed by persuasion rather than by force. But if he remains in the religion of the Christians, this very thing—that you have not lost your son—will be some consolation to you in your despondency." When Arachis had said this, all bore witness, approving the counsel. The king, then, agreed that these things should be so arranged. And so, summoning his son at dawn, he said to him:

"This is now my last word to you, my son; and if you are not at once obedient to it, and do not in this at least comfort my heart, then, be assured, I shall no longer spare you." And when the son asked what the meaning of the word was, he said, "Since, after much toil, I have found you unyielding in everything against being persuaded by my words, come, then; dividing the kingdom, I will make you ruler in your portion and king; and for the rest you shall be free to go whatever road you desire." And that divine soul, knowing that the king put forward even this for the tripping-up of his resolve, nevertheless saw fit to obey, so that, slipping from his hands, he might go the road he desired. He answered, then, and said to the king: "I longed to seek out that divine man who showed me the road of salvation, and, bidding farewell to all, to spend the rest of my life with him; but since, father, you do not allow me to do what is dear to my heart, I obey you in this. For in matters where there is no plain ruin and estrangement from God set before one, it is good to obey one's father." So the king, filled with the greatest joy, divided all the land subject to him into two, and appointed his son king, adorned him with the diadem, and, making him resplendent with all royal glory, sent him off to the kingdom marked out for him with a splendid bodyguard. And to the rulers and governors, the generals and satraps, he gave leave for anyone who wished to go away with his son and king. And he marked out for his

kingdom a certain great and populous city, and gave him everything befitting kings. Then indeed, when Josaphat had received the authority of the kingdom, as soon as he reached the city where the things of the kingdom had been prepared for him, he set the sign of the Master's passion, the venerable cross of Christ, upon every tower of the city; and besieging the temples and altars of the idols, he shook them down, dug up their ground, laid bare their foundations, leaving no remnant of the impiety. And in the midst of the city he raised up a great and very beautiful church to the Master, Christ. And he commanded the multitude, frequenting it continually, to bring their worship to God through the veneration of the cross, himself coming forward into their midst before all and giving himself to most fervent prayer. And all who came under his hand he admonished, exhorted, and did everything to draw away from their superstitious error and to bring near to Christ; he exposed the deceit of the madness for idols and proclaimed the preaching of the Gospel; he set forth the things concerning the condescension of the Word of God, proclaimed the wonders of his coming, made known the passion of the cross by which we have been saved, the power of the resurrection and the ascent into the heavens; and besides these he announced that dread day of his fearful second coming, and the good things laid up for the faithful and the punishments that await sinners. All these things he set forth with a kindly disposition and gentle words; for he did not so much wish, from the weight of his authority and royal magnificence,

to be venerable and feared, as from his humility and gentleness—by which he the more drew all to himself, being in his deeds wonderful, but in his mind mild and moderate. Hence his authority, taking moderation and mildness as a great helper, made all yield to his words. So indeed, in a little time, all the people subject to him, citizen and native alike, were initiated by his God-speaking words, so as to renounce the error of many gods and break away from the libations and abominations of the idols,

and to attach themselves to the unerring faith, and, transformed by his teachings, to be brought near to Christ. And all who, through fear of his father, had been shut up in mountains and caves—priests and monks and a few of the bishops—coming out of their hiding-places, went to him rejoicing. And he himself, going to meet those who for Christ's sake had fallen into such troubles and so suffered hardship, received them with honour, and brought them into his palace, washing their feet, cleansing their soiled hair, and tending them in every way. Then he enthroned the church newly built by him, and one of the bishops, who had suffered much hardship for the faith in Christ and had lost his own episcopal throne, he set up as high priest in it—a holy man, skilled in the canons of the Church, and his soul filled with divine zeal. And at once, improvising a font, he commanded that those who turned to Christ be baptized. And so the rulers are baptized first, and all who were in office, then those in the army, and the rest of the crowd. And those who were baptized received not only health of soul, but indeed all who were oppressed by bodily diseases and infirmities, laying all these aside, clean in soul

and whole in body, came up from the divine font, having reaped healing of souls and bodies together. Hence, then, the multitudes streamed to king Josaphat from every side, seeking to be initiated by him in true religion. And all the objects of idol-worship were torn down, and all the wealth and the moneys laid up in the idol-temples were taken away; and holy precincts were built up to God in their stead. And that wealth and the costly garments and the treasures, king Josaphat dedicated to them, thus making that dishonoured and superfluous material useful and profitable. But the foul demons that dwelt in those altars and temples were driven out by a most grievous persecution, and cried aloud the calamity that had come upon them in the hearing of many. And all that surrounding country was freed from their gloomy deceit, and shone round about with the light of the blameless faith of the Christians. So indeed the king was a good example to all, and inflamed and kindled many to a like resolve. For such is authority: the subject is always conformed to it, and loves to desire the same things, and to pursue those things in which it perceives the ruler to delight.

Hence, with God working together with them, true religion increased and made progress among them. And the king was wholly devoted to the commandments of Christ and to his love, a steward of the word of grace, and a pilot of many souls, bringing them to harbour in the haven of God. For he knew that this was, above all things, the work of a king: to teach men to fear God and to keep what is just. And this indeed he did, both fitting himself to reign over the passions, and holding firmly, like the best of pilots, the tillers of good order for those under him. For this is the mark of true kingship: to reign over and master the pleasures; which this man did. Yet he in no way prided himself on the nobility of his ancestors or on the royal glory that was about him, knowing that we all have a forefather of clay, and that rich and poor are of the same lump; but, casting his mind always into the abyss of humility, and remembering the blessedness of that other world, he reckoned himself a sojourner among the things here, and knew that those things were his own which he might obtain after his departure hence. And since all things stood well with him,

and, having freed all who were under his hand from the old error handed down from their fathers, he had made them servants of him who ransomed us from wicked slavery by his precious blood, he turns his mind to a second work: the virtue of well-doing. For self-control and righteousness had already been achieved by him beforehand, since he had bound on the crown of self-control and clothed himself in the purple of righteousness. He considered, then, that the instability of earthly wealth imitates the course of river waters. There, therefore, he hastened to lay it up, where neither moth nor rust destroys, and where thieves do not break through or steal. And so he began to distribute all his moneys to the poor, in no way sparing them. For he knew that one who has laid hold of great authority ought to imitate the giver of that authority as far as he is able, and that in this above all he will imitate God: in considering nothing more to be preferred than showing mercy. Above gold, then, and precious stones, he was gathering for himself the wealth of well-doing—the wealth that gladdens here in the hope of future enjoyment, and there sweetens by the experience of the blessedness that was hoped for. Hence prisons were searched out by him, those shut up in the mines, those choked by creditors; and, ungrudgingly supplying all things to all, he was a father to all the orphans and widows and poor,

a tender and good father, thinking that he benefited himself by the benefit done to them. For being rich-souled and truly most kingly, he gave generously to all in need; for he hoped to receive infinitely multiplied recompense for these things when the time should come for the repayment of works. And as such a fame of him spread everywhere in a little time, all streamed to him daily, as if moved by some fragrance of perfume, laying aside the poverty of bodies and souls alike, and he was on the lips of all. For it was not fear and tyranny that drew the people, but longing and the love for him from the heart, which was planted in the souls of all by God and by his most excellent way of life. Then indeed even those subject to his father attached themselves rather to him, and, laying aside all error, received the good news of the truth. And the house of Josaphat increased and grew strong, while the house of Abenner was diminished and grew weak, just as the book of
Kingdoms tells concerning David and Saul"

Seeing these things, king Abenner, coming late and with difficulty to an awareness, condemned the weakness and empty deceit of his falsely-named gods. And calling together again the chief men of the council, he brought to light what he was pondering. And when all confirmed the same things—for the dayspring from on high had visited them, the Saviour having heard the prayer of his servant Josaphat—it seemed good to the king to make these things known to his son. He writes, then, the next day a letter to Josaphat containing the following: "King Abenner to his most longed-for son Josaphat, greeting. Many thoughts, creeping into my soul, dreadfully tyrannize over me, dearest son. For seeing all that is ours fading away, as smoke fades, while the things of your religion shine above the sun, and coming to my senses, I have recognized that what you have always said to me is true, and that a deep darkness of sins and impiety covered us, so that from it we could not even look through to the truth and learn to know the Maker of all; but even when a light so far-shining was shown to us through you, we, closing our eyes, were unwilling to see,

having shown you many evils, and—pitiably, alas—having put to death not a few of the Christians, who, strengthened by the unconquerable power working with them, prevailed in the end over our cruelty. But now, having stripped that thick mist from our eyes, we see some small gleam of the truth, and repentance for the former evils comes upon me. Yet even this gleam another cloud of dreadful despair, rising up, tries to darken, putting forward the multitude of my evils, and that I am already abominable to Christ and unacceptable, as having become an apostate and his enemy. What, then, do you yourself say to this, sweetest child? Make it known to me as quickly as possible, and teach me, your father, what I must do, and lead me by the hand to the knowledge of what is profitable." This letter Josaphat received, and going over what it contained, he was filled in soul with pleasure and wonder together. And entering at once into his own chamber and falling on his face before the image of the Master, he wet the ground with tears, giving thanks at once to the Master and making confession, and moving his lips of exultation to song: "I will exalt you," he said, "my God and my king, and I will bless your name forever and ever; great are you, Lord, and greatly to be praised, and of your greatness there is no end. And who shall tell your mighty acts, and make heard all your praises—you who turned the rock into pools of water and the flint into fountains of water?

For behold, this flint, this heart of my father harder than rock, when you willed it, was softened like wax. For you are able even from these stones to raise up children to Abraham. I give you thanks, Master who love mankind, God of mercy, that you have been long-suffering, and are long-suffering, toward our transgressions, and have until now allowed us to remain unpunished. For we were long ago worthy to be cast away from your face and made an example in this life, like the lawless men who dwelt in the Pentapolis, burned up with fire and brimstone; but your incomparable long-suffering dealt kindly with us. I give you thanks, lowly and unworthy as I am, even though I am not sufficient to glorify your goodness. And I beseech your measureless compassions, Lord Jesus Christ, Son and Word of the invisible Father, who brought all things into being by a word and hold them together by your will, who delivered us, your unworthy servants, from the slavery of the enemy who is the author of evil, who were stretched upon the tree and bound the strong one, and awarded eternal freedom to those bound by him: do you now also stretch out your invisible and all-working hand, and free your servant and my father utterly from that grievous captivity of the devil; and show him most plainly that you are the ever-living God, who does not lie, and the only eternal and immortal king. Look upon, Master,

the contrition of my heart with a merciful and gracious eye; and according to your unfailing promise be with me, who know and confess you as the Maker and Provider of all creation. Let your living water spring up in me; and let a word be given me in the opening of my mouth, and a mind well founded on you, the cornerstone, that I, your unworthy servant, may be able to declare to my begetter, as is fitting, the mystery of your dispensation, and to draw him away by your power from the vain error of the wicked demons, and to bring him to you, the God and Master who does not wish the death of us sinners, but awaits our conversion and repentance; for you are glorified unto the ages. Amen." Having prayed thus and received full assurance that he would not fail of what he longed for, taking courage in the compassion of Christ, he set out from there with the royal bodyguard and reached the palace of his own father. And when the father was told of his son's arrival, he came out at once to meet him, embraced him, kissed him, and made the greatest joy and a public festival at the coming of his son. And what after this? They sat down alone with one another. And who could tell the things the son then discussed with the king, and with how great wisdom? What else but the things

prompted to him by the divine Spirit, through which the fishermen draw the whole world in their net for Christ, and the unlettered are shown wiser than the wise? Made wise by this grace, he too spoke to the king his father, enlightening him with the light of knowledge. For before, having toiled much to draw his father away from his superstitious error—what did he not say, what did he not do, to lead him back—he seemed to be singing in vain, and speaking into the ears of those who do not hear; but when the Lord looked upon the lowliness of his servant Josaphat, and, hearing his prayer, opened the closed gates of his father's heart—for it says, "He will do the will of those who fear him, and will hear their prayer"—the king readily understood the things spoken; so that, finding a fitting moment, the son by the grace of Christ won a victory over the wicked spirits that had taken mastery of his father's soul, and freed him completely from their error, and made known to him plainly the word of salvation, and brought him near to the living God in the heavens. For taking up the discourse from the beginning, he announced to him things great and wonderful which he had not known, which he had not heard with the ears of his heart, speaking much to him about God and showing him true religion,

how there is no other God in heaven above, nor on earth below, except the one God known in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit; and making known many mysteries of theology, among which he also declared the things concerning the invisible and visible creation: how the Creator, having brought all things forth from nothing, and fashioned man according to his own image and likeness, and honoured him with free will, made him share in the good things of paradise, commanding him to abstain from this one thing only, which was the tree of knowledge; but when he set aside the commandment, drove him out of paradise; whence, having slipped from his intimacy with him, the human race fell into these many errors, enslaved to sins and subjected to death through the tyranny of the devil; who, having once taken men into his power, made them utterly forget God and the Master, and persuaded them to serve him through the abominable worship of idols. Having compassion, then, God who fashioned us, by the good pleasure of the Father and the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, was pleased to be born like us of a holy Virgin, Mary the Mother of God; and, having taken part in suffering, though himself without suffering, and having risen from the dead on the third day, he ransomed us from the former penalty and counted us worthy of the former glory. For he led us up with him as he ascended into the heavens, from which he had come down;

whom we believe will come again, that he may raise up his own handiwork. And he will repay each according to his works. Upon this he initiated him into the kingdom of the heavens that awaits the worthy, and the unspeakable good things. He set forth the torment laid up for the wicked, the unquenchable fire, the outer darkness, the unending worm, and all the other punishment that the slaves of sin have stored up for themselves. Having gone through all these things at great length, and with words that abundantly bore witness to the grace of the Spirit dwelling in him, then, recounting also the unsearchable sea of God's love for mankind, and how ready he is to receive the repentance of those who turn to him, and that there is no sin that overcomes his compassion, if only we are willing to repent—and showing this from many examples and from the testimonies of Scripture—he at last brought his discourse to an end"
And king Abenner, pierced to the heart by this God-taught wisdom, confessed Christ the Saviour with a loud voice and a most fervent soul, departing from all his superstitious error.

He bowed down before the sign of the life-giving cross in the sight of all, and in the hearing of all proclaimed our Lord Jesus Christ to be the true God; and going through his former impiety, and convicting his own cruelty and bloodshed against the Christians, he became a great help to the cause of true religion; so that hence the saying of Paul was known in deed: that where there was the abundance of impiety, there also came the overflowing of grace. So when the most wise Josaphat had discoursed much about God and true religion toward him to the generals and satraps and all the people who had then come together, and, as it were with a fiery tongue, was warbling something beautiful and full of song, the grace of the Holy Spirit, coming upon them, moved all to the glorifying of God, so that all the crowds cried out as with one voice: "Great is the God of the Christians; there is no other god but our Lord Jesus Christ, glorified together with the Father and the Holy Spirit." And being filled full of divine zeal, king Abenner leaps boldly upon the idols that were in his palace, made of gold and silver, and drags them down to the ground. Then, dividing them into small pieces, he distributes them to the poor, thus making useful the useless things;

so indeed, with his son, going round the temples and altars of the idols, they razed them down to their very foundations; and in their stead they built holy precincts to God. And not only in the city, but throughout all the country, they did these things with zeal. And the wicked spirits that dwelt in the altars were driven out howling, and cried aloud, trembling at the unconquerable power of our God. And all the surrounding country, and most of the neighbouring nations, were led by the hand to the faith of true religion. Then indeed, when the most divine bishop mentioned above had come, king Abenner is instructed and made perfect by divine baptism in the name of the Father,

the Son, and the Holy Spirit. And Josaphat received him up out of the divine font, being shown—a most novel thing—the begetter of his own father, and becoming for the one who had begotten him in the flesh the agent of his spiritual rebirth. For he was a son of the heavenly Father and truly a most divine fruit of the divine root—that root which cries out: "I am the vine, you are the branches." Thus reborn through water and the Spirit, king Abenner rejoiced with unspeakable joy; and with him the whole city and the surrounding country were counted worthy of divine baptism, and those who before were darkened were shown to be sons of light. And every disease and every demonic assault was driven far from the believers; and all were whole and healthy in their souls and bodies. And many other wonders were worked for the confirmation of the faith. And churches were built up, and the bishops who had been hidden through fear were made manifest and received back their own churches,
