and others from among the priests and the monks were appointed to shepherd the flock of Christ. King Abenner, however, having thus departed from that former wretched manner of life and being repentant for what he had done, handed over all the royal power to his son; while he himself, living in quiet by himself, ever pouring dust upon his head, heaving heavy groans and washing himself with tears, conversed, alone with the one who is everywhere present, begging from him forgiveness for his own offences. And he let himself down into so great an abyss of contrition and humility that he refused even to name the name of God with his own lips, and only with difficulty, at his son's urging, dared to do so. And he was so changed with the good change, and walked the path that leads to virtue, that in true religion he surpassed the ignorance of his former lawless deeds. And having lived thus for four years in repentance and tears and all virtue, he fell into an illness, in which he also died. And when the end drew near, he began to fear and be in anguish, calling to mind the evils he had done. But Josaphat lightened the burden that had fallen upon him with words of comfort, saying, "Why are you very sorrowful, father, and why do you trouble yourself? Hope in God and confess to him, who is the hope of all the ends of the earth and of those far off on the sea; who

cried out through the prophet, saying: 'Wash yourselves, become clean; take away the wickedness from your souls before my eyes; learn to do good'; and, 'Though your sins be as scarlet, I will make them white as snow; and though they be as crimson, I will make them white as wool.' Do not fear, then, father, nor doubt; for the sins of those who turn to God do not overcome his boundless goodness. For they are under measure and number, however many they be; but his goodness is measureless and numberless. It cannot be, then, that what is subject to measure should prevail over the measureless." Charming his soul with such words of comfort, he made him full of good hope. Then the father, stretching out his hands, gave thanks and prayed for him beyond measure, and blessed the day in which his son had been born to him, saying: "Sweetest child—child not mine, but the heavenly Father's—what thanks shall I give you? With what blessings shall I bless you? What thanksgiving shall I send up to God concerning you? For I was lost, and was found through you; I was dead in sin, and have come to life again; an enemy and apostate of God, and have been reconciled. What, then, shall I repay you for all these things?

God is the one who will grant you worthy recompense." So saying, he kissed his dearest son repeatedly. Then, having prayed, and saying, "Into your hands, O God who love mankind, I commit my spirit," he gave up his soul to the Lord in repentance and peace. And Josaphat, having honoured his dead father with tears, and tended his remains with honour, laid him in the tomb of pious men, not clothing him, however, in royal raiment, but adorning him with the garments of repentance. And standing at the tomb, lifting his hands to heaven, and letting tears fall like a river from his eyes, he cried out to God, saying: "I give you thanks, O God, King of glory, alone mighty and immortal, that you did not overlook my prayer nor pass over my tears in silence, but were pleased to turn this your servant and my father back from the road of lawlessness and to draw him to yourself, the Saviour of all, removing him from the deceit of the idols and counting him worthy to know you, the true God who loves mankind. And now, my Lord and God, who have the unsearchable sea of goodness, appoint him in a verdant place, in a place of rest,

where the light of your face shines; and remember not his ancient lawless deeds, but according to your great mercy blot out the record of his offences, and tear up the bonds of his debts, and reconcile to him your saints whom he slew with fire and sword; command them not to be angry with him. For all things are possible to you, the Master of all, except this one thing only: not to show mercy to those who do not turn to you; this is impossible. For your mercy is poured out upon all, and you save those who call upon you, Lord Jesus Christ; for to you belongs glory unto the ages. Amen." Such prayers and supplications he offered to God for seven whole days, never departing from the tomb, taking no thought at all of food or drink, nor partaking of the rest of sleep; but he wet the ground with tears, and continued praying with unceasing groans. And on the eighth day, returning to the palace, he distributed all the wealth and the moneys to the poor, so that not one of those in need was left out"

And in a few days, having completed this service and emptied out all the treasuries, so that, when he was about to enter the narrow gate, the weight of money might in no way hinder him, on the fortieth day after his father's death, holding a memorial for him, he called together all those in office and those girt with military rank and not a few of the common people.

And taking his seat, as was the custom, he said in the hearing of all: "Behold, as you see, Abenner my father and king has died like one of the poor, and neither his wealth nor his royal glory, nor even I, the son who loved his father, nor any of the rest of his friends and kinsmen, had power to help him and rescue him from the inexorable sentence. But he goes away to the tribunals beyond, to render an account of his conduct in this present life, bringing with him no helper of all, but only his own deeds, of whatever sort they may be. And this same thing naturally befalls all who have received mortal nature, and it cannot be otherwise. Now, then, hear me, friends and brothers, people of the Lord and holy heritage, whom Christ our God ransomed with his precious blood and delivered from the old error and the slavery of the adversary. You yourselves know my conduct among you, how, from the time I came to know Christ and was counted worthy to become his servant, hating all things, I longed for him alone, and this was the desire of my heart: that, having withdrawn from the storm of life and its vain tumult, I might be with him alone, alone, and in the untroubled calm of soul serve my God and Master. But the opposition of my father held me back, and the commandment that bids us honour our parents. Hence, by the grace and cooperation of God, I have not toiled in vain, nor spent these days for nothing;

but I both brought him near to Christ and taught all of you to know him alone as the true God and Lord of all—not that I did this, but his grace that is with me, which both rescued me from superstitious error and the worship of idols, and freed you, my people, from grievous captivity. It is time, then, now at last to fulfil the works I promised to God; time to go away wherever he himself may lead me, and to render the vows that I vowed to him. Now, then, consider for yourselves whom you wish to lead you and to reign over you; for you are already fitted for the will of the Lord, and none of his commandments is hidden from you. Walk in these; turn not aside to the right hand or to the left; and may the God of peace be with you all." When that people and populace heard these things, there was at once an uproar and clamour and the loudest outcry and confusion, all weeping and lamenting their orphaned state. Lamenting in this way, they confirmed with oaths, besides their laments, that they would by no means let him go, but would hold fast to him, and not grant him his withdrawal at all. As the populace and all those in office cried out thus, the king answered and quieted the crowd with a gesture, and bade them be silent. And saying that he yielded to their opposition, he sent them home, sorrowful nonetheless and bearing the marks of wailing on their cheeks. But he himself, taking aside one of the rulers, who was preferred by him

and admired for his piety and the gravity of his life, Barachias by name—whom the narrative made known above also, when Nachor, playing the part of Barlaam, disputed with the philosophers, and Barachias alone was prepared to stand by him and join in the contest, his heart kindled with divine zeal—taking him aside, the king spoke gently with him, and most earnestly begged him to take up the kingship, and to shepherd his people in the fear of God, so that he himself might go the road he longed for. But when he saw him refusing and altogether declining, and saying, "O king, how unjust is your judgment; how unlike a commandment is your word; for if you were taught to love your neighbour as yourself, by what reasoning do you hasten to lay upon me the very burden you are eager to cast off? For if it is good to reign, hold the good thing yourself; but if this is a stumbling-block to the soul and a snare, why do you set it before me and wish to trip me up?"—when, then, he saw him saying and firmly maintaining such things, he ceased from the conversation.

And so in the dead of night he wrote out a letter to the people, full of much wisdom and prompting all true religion: what opinion they ought to have concerning God, what manner of life to offer him, what hymns, what thanksgivings; then he commanded that they receive no other than Barachias into the royal rule. And leaving the paper on which the letter was written in his own chamber, he went out of the palace unnoticed by all. But he was not able to escape notice to the end. For at dawn, when this became known, it at once produced disturbance and lamentation in the people; and all went out with great speed to seek him, intending by every means to forestall his flight; whence their zeal did not turn out in vain for them. For when they had occupied all the roads beforehand, and were circling all the mountains and going round the untrodden ravines, they found him in a certain torrent-bed, with his hands stretched out to heaven, performing the prayer of the sixth hour. And seeing him, they crowded round, beseeching him with tears and reproaching him for his departure. But he said, "Why do you toil in vain? For no longer hope to have me for your king."

And yielding a little to their great insistence, he returns again to the palace. And gathering them all together, he made his resolve plain. Then he confirmed his word with oaths, that he would be with them no day longer. "For I," he said, "have fulfilled my service toward you and left nothing wanting, nor have I held back from declaring to you and teaching what is profitable, testifying to all the faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, and showing the roads of repentance. And now, behold, I go the road I have long longed for; and you shall all no longer see my face. Therefore I testify to you this day, with the divine Apostle, that I am clean from the blood of you all. For I did not hold back from declaring to you all the counsel of God." Hearing these things, and knowing the firmness of his resolve, that nothing could hinder his purpose, they lamented their orphaned state, but could not by any means persuade him. Then the king, taking that Barachias, whom the narrative made known before, said, "This man, brothers, I appoint as your king." And when he strongly refused the matter, against his will and unwilling he set him in the royal rule, and put the diadem upon his head, and gave the royal ring into his hand. And standing toward the east he made a prayer for king Barachias: that his faith in God might be kept unshaken for him, and that he might find an unswerving

course according to the commandments of Christ. And along with this he prayed for the clergy and all the flock, asking from the Lord help and salvation for them, and whatever might be for them a request ordered toward their benefit. Having prayed thus, he turned and said to Barachias: "Behold, brother, I charge you as the Apostle once testified: 'Take heed to yourself and to all the flock, over which the Holy Spirit has set you as king, to shepherd the people of the Lord which he purchased through his own blood.' And as before me you came to know God and served him in a pure conscience, so now too show greater zeal to please him. For inasmuch as you have been counted worthy of great rule by God, by so much are you a debtor for a greater recompense. Repay, then, to your benefactor the debt of thanksgiving, keeping his holy commandments and turning aside from every road that leads to ruin. For as with those who sail, when a sailor goes wrong, he brings small harm to the passengers, but when the pilot does, he works the ruin of the whole ship; so too in kingdoms, if one of the subjects sins, he wrongs not so much the common body as himself,

but if the king himself does, he works harm to the whole state. As one, then, who will render great accounts if you overlook anything of your duty, guard yourself with much exactness in the good. Hate every pleasure that draws toward sin; for the Apostle says: 'Pursue peace with all, and the sanctification without which no one shall see the Lord.' Mark the circle that runs round the affairs of men, bearing them now this way, now that, and carrying them about; and in their swift-turning change keep your pious reasoning unchanged. For to change along with the changes of affairs is a sign of an unstable mind. But be steadfast, wholly fixed in the good. Be not lifted up through this temporary glory to vain swelling; but with cleansed reasoning understand the worthlessness of your own nature, the brevity and swift passing of life here, and the death joined to the flesh. And reckoning these things, you will not be cast into the pit of disdain, but will fear God, the true and heavenly King, and you will be truly blessed. For 'Blessed,' it says, 'are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways'; and, 'Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; in his commandments he shall delight greatly.' And what commandments above all ought you

to keep? 'Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy'; and, 'Be compassionate, as your heavenly Father is compassionate.' For this commandment above all is required of those who are in the greatest rule. And truly one who has laid hold of great authority ought to imitate the giver of authority as far as he is able; and in this above all he will imitate God: in considering nothing more to be preferred than showing mercy. But also nothing so draws the subject to goodwill as the grace of well-doing given to those in need; for the service done through fear is a disguised flattery, deceiving with a counterfeit name of honour those who attend to it; and what is subjected unwillingly rebels when it gets the chance; but what is held by the bonds of goodwill has firm obedience toward the one who holds it. Therefore be easy of access to those who beg, and open your ears to the poor, that you may find the ear of God open to you; for such as we become to our fellow-servants, such shall we find the Master toward us, and as we hear we shall be heard, as we see we shall be seen by the divine and all-seeing eye. Let us, then, offer mercy beforehand for mercy, that we may receive like for like. But hear also another commandment, the yoke-fellow of the former: 'Forgive, and you shall be forgiven'; and,

'If you do not forgive men their trespasses, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your trespasses.' Therefore bear no grudge against those who offend; but, asking forgiveness for your sins, forgive also yourself those who offend against you, because forgiveness is repaid with forgiveness, and by reconciliation with our fellow-servants comes release from the Master's wrath. And again, our lack of compassion toward those who offend makes our own offences unforgivable; just as you hear what the debtor of the ten thousand talents suffered, when by his lack of pity toward his fellow-servant he renewed against himself the exaction of so great a debt. Therefore we must attend carefully, lest we too suffer the like; but let us forgive every debt, and cast out all wrath from the heart, that to us too our many debts may be forgiven. And in all things and above all things, guard the good deposit, the pious word of the faith, which you have learned and been taught; and let no tare of heresy spring up among you; but keep the divine seed pure and undefiled, that you may show fruit many-fold to the Master, when he comes demanding an account from each of how they have lived, and repaying according to what we have done, when the righteous shall shine as the sun, and darkness shall cover the sinners

and everlasting shame. And now, brothers, I commend you to God, and to the Word of his grace, who is able to build you up and to give you an inheritance among all those who are sanctified." And having said these things, bending his knees, as it is written, he again prayed with tears. And turning, he kissed Barachias whom he had appointed king, and all those in office. Then indeed there came about a thing truly worthy of tears. For all, standing round him, as though living only by being with him and about to have their very souls taken away with the parting, what did they not say to move pity? What excess of laments did they leave untried? They kissed him, they embraced him; the grief made them beside themselves. "Woe to us," they cried, "for this grievous misfortune;

" and they called upon him as master, father, saviour, benefactor: "Through you," they said, "we came to know God; we were ransomed from error; we found rest from all evils. What shall be left to us after your departure? What evils shall not overtake us?" Saying such things, they beat their breasts and bewailed the calamity that had seized them. But he, having quieted the many wailings with words of comfort, and having promised to be with them in spirit—since in body this could now no longer be—saying such things, went out of the palace in the sight of all. And at once all followed him. They refused to return; they fled the city, as though no longer able to see it with their own eyes. And when they had gotten outside the city, at last, scarcely, as he urged them with the sharpness of his word and laid on a somewhat keener rebuke, they were torn from him, and unwillingly turned back, their eyes constantly turning round toward him, and their feet halting the march. And some of the more fervent, lamenting, followed him from afar,
until the coming of night separated them from one another"

So that noble man went out of the palace rejoicing, as when one returning from a long exile to his own land goes on his way with gladness. And he was clothed, on the outside, in his customary garments, but underneath in that hair-cloth rag which Barlaam had given him. And that night, coming to the little house of a certain poor man, he cast off the garments wrapped about him and gave them to the poor man as his last act of well-doing; and so, setting God as his helper through the prayers of that man and of many other poor men, and wrapping about himself God's grace and help as a garment of salvation and a tunic of gladness, he went out to the life of the desert, carrying no bread, no water, nor any other thing fit for nourishment, wearing no garment but only that harsh rag which we mentioned a little before. For wounded in soul by some surpassing longing and divine love of the immortal king Christ, he was wholly carried out of himself by what he longed for, wholly transformed toward God, held fast by his love; for 'Love,' it says, 'is strong as fire'; such a drunkenness did he receive from divine love,

and so was he kindled with thirst, according to him who said: 'As the deer longs for the fountains of waters, so my soul longs for you, O God; my soul thirsted for God, the strong, the living God'; and as the soul wounded with such love cries out in the Song of Songs: 'You have ravished our heart with your love, you have ravished our heart'; and, 'Show me your face, and let me hear your voice; for your voice is a sweet voice, and your face is beautiful.' Having received in their hearts the longing for this unspeakable beauty of Christ, the choir of the apostles and the multitudes of the martyrs disregarded all things seen, and all temporary life, and chose the ten thousand kinds of torments and deaths, in love with the divine beauty and reckoning the affection of the divine Word toward us. This fire, this man, beautiful and noble in body, but far nobler and most kingly in soul, having received in himself, despises all earthly things together, treads down all the pleasures of the body, looks down upon wealth and glory and honour from men, lays aside diadem and purple, reckoning these cheaper than spiders' webs, and gives himself readily to all the toils and griefs of the ascetic life, crying, 'My soul has cleaved, O my Christ, my soul has cleaved after you;

and your right hand has upheld me.' And thus, having gone without turning back into the depth of the desert, and having laid aside, like some burden and most heavy collar, the confusion of temporary things, he rejoiced in spirit, and gazing intently at the longed-for Christ, he cried out to him, conversing as with one present and hearing his voice: "Let not my eye see the good things of this world any more, Lord; let not my mind be lifted up henceforth by the present vanity; but fill my eyes, Lord, with spiritual tears, and direct my steps, and show me your servant Barlaam. Show me the one who became for me the agent of salvation, that through him I may learn the exactness of this life of the desert and of asceticism, and not, through inexperience of the enemy's wars, be tripped up. Grant me, Lord, to find the road by which I may attain to you, for my soul is wounded with longing for you, and I thirst for you, the fountain of salvation." These things he turned over always within himself, and conversed with God, united to him through prayer and the loftiest contemplation. And so intently he accomplished his journey, hastening to reach the place where Barlaam dwelt. And he was nourished by the herbs that grow in the desert; for he carried nothing else, as I said before, except only his own body and the rag he was wrapped in. But while he provided himself with moderate and scant nourishment from the herbs, he was utterly in want of water,

that desert being waterless and dry. So now, about midday, when the sun was burning fiercely, as he kept to his journey, he himself was burned more fiercely with thirst from the heat in that waterless place, and suffered the utmost suffering; but longing overcame nature, and the thirst with which he thirsted for God cooled the flame of his thirst for water. But the devil, who hates the good and is envious, not bearing to see in him such a resolve and so fervent a love toward God, raised up against him many temptations in the desert, suggesting to him the memory of his royal glory and the most splendid bodyguard that had attended him, of his friends and kinsmen and companions, and how the souls of all had hung upon his soul, and the other comforts of life; then he set before him the harshness of virtue and its many sweats, the weakness of the body and its unfamiliarity with such suffering, the length of time, the present urgency of thirst, and that from nowhere was he to expect comfort or an end of so great a toil; and in all he raised up much dust of thoughts in his mind, just as is written somewhere also concerning the great Antony.

But when the enemy saw himself weak against that man's resolve—for, thinking of Christ and burning with longing for him, well strengthened by hope and supported by faith, he reckoned the enemy's exaggerations as nothing—the adversary was put to shame, falling, as the saying goes, at the first assault. He comes, then, by another road—for many are his paths of wickedness—and tried to overthrow him with various apparitions and to cast him into cowardice: at one time appearing to him black, as he is; at another, holding a drawn sword, leaping upon him and threatening to strike him, unless he turned back quickly; at another time taking on the shapes of all kinds of wild beasts, roaring against him and making a most terrible bellowing and din; then changing into a serpent and an asp and a basilisk. But that noble and most valiant athlete was unmoved in soul, having set the Most High as his refuge. Sober in mind and mocking the evil one, he said: "You have not escaped my notice, deceiver, whoever you are, who raise these things against me—you who from the beginning contrive evils for the race of men, and are forever wicked and never leave off doing harm. But how fitting and proper to you is this shape, this very thing of likening yourself to wild beasts and creeping things,

displaying the beastliness and crookedness of your mind, and the venomous and harmful character of your purpose. Why, then, do you attempt the impossible, wretch? For since I knew that these contrivances and terrors are of your wickedness, I have no more care at all for you. The Lord is my helper, and I shall look upon my enemies; and upon the asp and the basilisk, which you make yourself like, I shall tread, and I shall trample you, the lion and the serpent, strengthened by the power of Christ. Let all my enemies be ashamed and put to confusion; let them be turned back and put to shame exceedingly and quickly." Saying these things, and wrapping about himself the sign of the cross as an invincible weapon, he brought to nothing all the apparitions of the devil. For at once the wild beasts and the creeping things, as smoke vanishes, vanished, and as wax melts before the face of the fire; and he himself, strong in the power of Christ, went on rejoicing and giving thanks to the Lord. But that desert also breeds many and various wild beasts and all kinds of serpents and dragon-shaped creatures, which, meeting him, were shown not now in apparition but in truth; so that from then on the road was full of fear and toil;

but he himself flew over both in his mind, love, as the Scripture says, casting out fear, and longing lightening the toil. So then, having wrestled with many and various calamities and hardships, after not a few days he reached that desert of the land of Senaar in which Barlaam dwelt; where, finding water also, he quenched the flame of his thirst"

And Josaphat remained a whole two years wandering across the sea of this desert and not finding Barlaam, God here too proving the firmness of his reasoning and the nobility of his soul. And he was thus in the open air, scorched by the burning heat and frozen by the cold, and ceaselessly seeking, as some precious treasure, the most venerable old man. And he endured many temptations and wars of the wicked spirits, and bore many toils from the scarcity of the herbs which he used for food, since the desert, being dry, brought even these forth scantily.

But that adamantine and unconquered soul, burning with longing for the Master, bore these griefs more easily than others bear pleasures. Therefore he did not fail of the help from above, but, according to the multitude of his pains and toils, the consolations that came from the longed-for Christ, both in sleep and in waking, gladdened his soul. And as the two years were being completed, Josaphat went about ceaselessly seeking the one he longed for, and made supplication to God, pouring tears like a river from his eyes, and crying: "Show me, Master, show me the one who became to me the cause of the knowledge of you and the agent of so many good things; and do not, because of the multitude of my lawless deeds, deprive me of so great a good. But count me worthy both to see him and to set my own contest of asceticism equal to his." And by the grace of God he finds a cave, having tracked the path of those who walked there. And he meets a certain monk pursuing the life of the desert.

And embracing him most warmly and greeting him, he asked to find the dwelling of Barlaam, and recounted his own story, making it plain to the man. Being taught by him, then, the place of the dwelling of the one he sought, he reaches it most quickly, as when a most experienced hunter comes upon the tracks of his prey. And coming upon certain signs taught him by the other old man, he went on rejoicing and strengthened by hope, like an infant hoping after a long time to see his father. For when longing according to God breaks out in a soul, it is shown to be far hotter and more violent than the natural kind. He stands, then, at the door of the cave, and knocking, said, "Bless me, father, bless me." And when Barlaam, hearing the voice, came out of the cave, he recognized in spirit the one who, by his outward appearance, could not easily be recognized, because of that wonderful change and alteration in which he had been changed and transformed from that former appearance and the beauty of his flowering youth—blackened by the burning of the sun, with long hair, his cheeks wasted away, his eyes sunk deep within, and his eyelids inflamed by the streams of tears and the great hardship of want. And Josaphat too recognized his spiritual father, who kept especially the same features of his countenance. Standing at once toward the east, then, the old man sent up a prayer of thanksgiving to God.

And after the prayer, having said the Amen, embracing and clasping one another, they greeted each other with most warm embraces, taking their fill insatiably of a long-felt longing. And when they had embraced and greeted each other enough, sitting down they conversed. Beginning the discourse, Barlaam said, "Welcome, beloved child, child of God and heir of the heavenly kingdom through our Lord Jesus Christ, whom you loved, whom you rightly longed for above the temporary and corruptible things; and, like a prudent and wise merchant, having sold all, you bought the priceless pearl, and having come upon the unviolated treasure hidden in the field of the commandments of the Lord,

you have given all, sparing nothing of the things that all but already pass away, that you might buy that field for yourself. May the Lord give you, in place of the temporary, the eternal; in place of the corruptible, the incorruptible and the unaging. Tell me, then, dearest one, how you came here, how matters went with you after my departure, and whether your father came to know God, or whether even now, carried along by his former folly, he is held captive by the deceit of the demons." When Barlaam had asked these things, Josaphat took up the discourse and recounted in detail all that had happened to him after that man's departure, and all the prosperity the Lord had granted up to the time of their meeting again. And the old man, hearing with pleasure and wonder, weeping warmly, said: "Glory to you, our God, who are ever present and helping those who love you. Glory to you, Christ, King of all and most good God, that you were pleased that the seed I cast down in the soul of your servant Josaphat should thus bring forth fruit a hundredfold, worthy of you, the husbandman and Master of our souls. Glory to you, good Comforter, the all-holy Spirit, that you have counted this man worthy to share in the grace which you gave to your holy apostles, and through him have freed populous multitudes from their superstitious error and enlightened them with the true knowledge of God." Thus God was given thanks by them both. And as they conversed of such things and rejoiced in the grace of God, evening came on.

And so, rising to prayer, they performed the customary offices. Then, calling food to mind, Barlaam set forth a costly table, full of spiritual seasoning, but having very little of bodily comfort. For there were raw vegetables, of which the old man was himself the worker and husbandman, and a few dates found in that same desert, and wild herbs. Having given thanks, then, and partaken of what was set before them, and drunk water from the spring that was at hand, they again gave thanks to God, who opens his hand and fills every living thing. And rising again, and having completed the night prayers, they took up again after the prayer the spiritual conversation, going through saving words full of heavenly wisdom all through the night, until the dawn made them call the customary prayers to mind again. And Josaphat remained with Barlaam for a good many years in this way, pursuing this wonderful and more-than-human way of life, accompanying him as a father and teacher with all submission and humility, and being trained for every form of virtue, and excellently taught the wrestling of the wicked and invisible spirits. From then on he put to death all the passions;

and the mind of the flesh he so subjected to the spirit, as a slave to a master, forgetting altogether delight and rest, and commanding sleep as a bad servant. And, to speak simply, so great was his contest of asceticism that even Barlaam, who had passed many years in it, marvelled, and was outdone by his steadfast firmness. For he partook of that harsh and comfortless food only so much as to keep alive, and not, by dying violently, to lose the wages of the working of good. And he so subjected his nature to wakefulness, as one fleshless and bodiless. And the work of prayer and of mental labour was for him unceasing, and the whole time of his life was spent in spiritual and heavenly contemplations, so that he lost not an hour, not a moment at all, from the time he dwelt in that desert. For this is the work of the monastic order: never to be found idle of spiritual labour; which indeed the noble and well-equipped runner of the heavenly course excellently achieved. And he kept his fervour unquenched from beginning to end, ever setting ascents in his heart, and passing from strength to higher strength, ceaselessly adding longing to longing and zeal to zeal, until he reached the hoped-for and longed-for blessedness"
Thus, then, Barlaam and

Josaphat, being together with one another and striving in the good contest, outside all care and all the turmoil of life, possessing a mind untroubled and unmixed with any confusion, after their many labours for true religion—on one of the days, calling to him the spiritual son whom he had begotten through the Gospel, Barlaam took up a discourse and spiritual conversation, saying, "Long ago, dearest Josaphat, you ought to have dwelt in this desert; and this Christ promised me, as I prayed for you, that I should see before the end of my life. I have seen, then, as I desired: I have seen you torn away from the world and the things in the world, joined to Christ with an undoubting mind, and come to the measure of perfection of his fullness. Now, then, since the time of my departure is at the doors, and the desire that has been my companion from youth, to be with Christ forever, is now being fulfilled, you must cover my body with earth and give back dust to dust, but remain henceforth in this place, holding to the spiritual way of life and keeping memory of my lowliness. For I fear lest at some time the gloomy multitude of demons should set itself in the way of my soul because of the multitude of my faults. Do you, then, child, not make light of the toil of asceticism, nor be afraid of the length of time and the plots of the demons; but, strengthened by the grace of Christ, boldly laugh at their weakness; and toward the harshness of the toils and the stretch of time

be so disposed as to expect your departure hence each day, and as though the same day were for you both the beginning of asceticism and its end. Thus, ever forgetting the things behind, and reaching out toward the things before, watching, pursue the prize of the upward calling of God in Christ Jesus, as the divine Apostle exhorts, saying, 'Let us not lose heart; but even if our outer man is being destroyed, yet the inner is renewed day by day; for the momentary lightness of our affliction works for us, beyond all measure, an eternal weight of glory, while we look not at the things seen but at the things unseen; for the things seen are temporary, but the things unseen are eternal.' Reckoning these things, beloved, play the man and be strong, and like a good soldier strive to please the one who enlisted you. And if the evil one brings you thoughts of fainthearted neglect and hastens to slacken the tension of your resolve, do not fear his plots, calling to mind the Master's command, who says, 'In the world you shall have affliction; but take courage: I have overcome the world.' Therefore rejoice in the Lord always, that he chose you and set you apart from the world, and placed you as in his presence. And he himself, who called you with a holy calling, is ever near. Be anxious for nothing; but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests

be made known to God. For he himself has said, 'I will never leave you, nor will I ever forsake you.' So then, in the harshness of your manner of life and the neglect of asceticism, acquiring such thoughts, be glad, remembering the Lord our God; for it says, 'I remembered God, and was glad.' But when again the adversary devises another mode of war against you, putting forward high-minded thoughts and showing you the glory of the kingdom of the world which you left, and the rest of the things in the world, set forth the saving word, as a shield, which says: 'When you have done all the things commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants, for what we owed to do we have done.' But indeed who of us can pay the debt we owe to the Master, for the things in which, being rich, he became poor for our sake, that we by his poverty might become rich, and the impassible one suffered, that he might free us from the passions? For what grace is it for a servant to suffer like the Master? But we fall far short of his sufferings.

Consider these things, casting down reasonings and every high thing that lifts itself up against the knowledge of God, and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ; and the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your heart and your thoughts in Christ Jesus." When these things had been said by the blessed Barlaam, the flow of Josaphat's tears had no measure, but, gushing as from a copious fountain, drenched the whole of him and the ground on which he sat. Lamenting the parting, he begged most fervently to become a fellow-traveller with him on his final journey, and to remain in life no longer after his departure, saying, "Why do you seek your own only, father, and not also your neighbour's? How do you fulfil in this the perfect love, according to him who said, 'You shall love your neighbour as yourself,' if you yourself depart to rest and life, but leave me to affliction and hardship, and, before I have been well trained in the contests of asceticism and learned the manifold approaches of the enemy, put me forward to single combat with their battle-line? What else can come of it, but that I be cast down by their evil contrivances, and die—alas—the truly spiritual and eternal death, which naturally befalls inexperienced and cowardly monks? But beseech the Lord,

I implore you, to take me too as a fellow-traveller out of life. Yes, by the very hope you have of receiving the reward of your toil, beseech him that I may sojourn in life no single day after your departure, and wander in the sea of this desert." When Josaphat said these things with tears, the old man, gently and evenly checking him, said, "We ought not, child, to resist the unattainable judgments of God. For I, having prayed much about this, and forced the unforced Master that we should not be separated from one another, was taught by his goodness that it is not profitable for you now to lay aside the burden of the flesh; but you must remain in asceticism, until you weave a more splendid crown for yourself. For you have not yet striven enough for the recompense prepared for you; but you must toil a little, that you may enter rejoicing into the joy of your Lord. For I am now near a hundred years, having already passed seventy-five years in this desert; but as for you, even if the time will not be stretched out so far, yet it must come near, as the Lord commands, that you may be shown a fellow-contestant, and in no way fall short of those who bore the burden of the day and the heat. Receive, then, my beloved, gladly the things resolved by God. For who among men is able to scatter the things that he himself has counselled? And endure, kept by his grace.

Be ever sober toward the contrary thoughts, and keep the purity of the mind, like some precious treasure, unviolated, raising yourself day by day to higher labour and contemplation, that there may be fulfilled in you what the Saviour promised to his friends, saying, 'If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him, and make our dwelling with him.'" Having said these things, and far more, worthy of his sanctified soul and theological tongue, the old man comforted the grieving soul of Josaphat. Then he sends him off to certain brothers who had their dwelling at a great distance, to bring the things fitting for the holy sacrifice. And so Josaphat, girding himself, fulfilled the service most quickly; for he feared lest in his absence Barlaam should pay the debt of nature, and, committing his spirit to the Lord, bring upon him the grievous loss of obtaining none of his words, none of his parting greetings, none of his prayers, none of his blessings. And when he had passed most manfully over that long road and brought the things for the holy sacrifice, the most divine Barlaam offered to God the bloodless sacrifice. And having himself communicated,

and having given to Josaphat also a share of the undefiled mysteries of Christ, he exulted in the Spirit. And having partaken of the customary food, he nourished the soul of Josaphat again with words profitable to the soul, saying, "No longer, dearest son, shall one hearth and table bring us together into one in this life; for I now go the last road of my fathers. You must, then, show your affection toward me by keeping the commandments of God, and by endurance in this place to the end, living as you have learned and been taught, and remembering always my humble and slothful soul. Rejoice, then, with joy, and be glad with the gladness in Christ, that for the earthly and corruptible things you have exchanged the eternal and incorruptible,

and that the reward of your works draws near, and the rewarder is already at hand, who will come to see the vineyard that you have cultivated, and will richly grant you the reward of your husbandry. For faithful is the word and worthy of all acceptance, as the divine Paul cries: 'For if we died with him, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him'—the eternal and unending kingdom, illumined by the unapproachable light, and counted worthy of the radiance of the truly blessed and life-giving Trinity." Such things Barlaam conversed of with Josaphat until evening and through the whole night, while Josaphat lamented with unrestrained tears and could not bear the parting. And just as day was breaking, having brought his conversation with him to an end, he lifted his hands and eyes to heaven, and sending up thanksgiving to God, said: "Lord, my God, who are everywhere present and fill all things, I give you thanks, that you looked upon my lowliness and counted me worthy to complete the course of my sojourn here in the orthodox confession of you and in the road of your commandments. And now, Master who love the good and are all-compassionate, receive me into your eternal dwellings, and remember not whatever I have sinned against you, in knowledge and in ignorance. And guard also this your faithful servant, over whom you counted me, your unprofitable servant, worthy to preside;

deliver him from all vanity and the spite of the adversary, and make him higher than the manifold snares which the evil one has spread for the stumbling of all who wish to be saved. Make vanish, all-powerful one, all the power of the deceiver from before the face of your servant, and give him authority to tread upon the ruin-breeding head of the enemy of our souls. Send down from on high the grace of your Holy Spirit, and strengthen him against the invisible battle-lines, that he may be counted worthy to receive from you the crown of victory, and that in him your name may be glorified—the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit—for to you belong glory and praise unto the ages. Amen." Having prayed thus, and having embraced Josaphat as a father, and given him a greeting with a holy kiss, and sealed himself with the sign of the cross, and drawn up his feet, and become very joyful, as though certain friends had arrived, he departed to the blessed journey, passing on to the reward of old age in that other world, being an old man and full of the days of the spirit"

And Josaphat, flinging himself upon his father with more reverence and lamentation than one could tell, and having washed the remains with tears, and wrapped them in the hair-cloth rag which Barlaam himself had given him in the palace, recited the appointed psalms, chanting through the whole day and the whole night, and at the same time wetting with tears the precious body of the blessed one. And on the following day, having made a grave near the cave,

and having most reverently borne up the holy remains, the good and most honoured son laid his spiritual father in the tomb. And kindled more fervently in soul, and bracing himself to more earnest prayer, he said: "Lord, my God, hearken to my voice with which I have cried out; have mercy on me and hearken to me, for I seek you from my heart. My soul has sought you out; turn not your face away from me, and turn not aside in anger from your servant. Be my helper; reject me not, and forsake me not, O God my Saviour, for my father and my mother forsook me; but you, Lord, take me up. Give me your law, Lord, in your way, and guide me in a straight path, because of my enemies. Deliver me not to the souls of those who afflict me, for upon you I was cast from the womb; from my mother's belly you are my God; depart not from me, for there is none to help me but you. For behold, in the sea of your compassions I have set the hope of my soul; steer my life, you who steer all creation by the ineffable providence of your wisdom, and make known to me the way in which I shall walk. And save me, as a good God who love mankind, by the prayers and intercessions of your servant Barlaam,

for you are my God, and I glorify you, the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, unto the ages of ages. Amen." Having prayed thus, he sat down near the tomb weeping. And as he sat, he fell asleep. And he sees those awesome men whom he had seen before coming to him, and leading him away to that great and wonderful plain, and bringing him into that glorified and exceedingly bright city. And as he was entering the gate, others met him, resplendent with much light, having in their hands crowns shining with ineffable beauty, such as mortal eyes have never beheld. And when Josaphat asked, "Whose are the exceedingly bright crowns of glory that I see?" "The one is yours," they said, "prepared for you for the many souls that you saved, and now adorned still more for the asceticism you pursue, if indeed you pass through it manfully to the end; but the other is yours as well—yet you must give this to your father, who through you turned aside from the evil road and genuinely repented to the Lord." But Josaphat seemed displeased, and said, "How is it possible that my father, for his repentance alone, should obtain gifts equal to mine, who have toiled so much?" He said these things, and at once seemed to see Barlaam, reproaching him as it were and saying: "These are my words, Josaphat, which I once spoke to you, that when you grow over-rich, you would not be ready to share; and you yourself were perplexed at the saying. But now how is it that you are displeased at the equal honour of your father,

and were not rather glad in soul that your much prayer for him was heard?" And Josaphat, as he was always wont to say to him, replied, "Forgive me, father, forgive me. But make known to me where you yourself dwell." "In this great and beautiful city," he said; "I have been allotted to dwell in the very middle street of the city, blazing with boundless light." And Josaphat seemed to ask Barlaam again to lead him away to his own dwelling and kindly show him round. But that man said the time had not yet come for him to come to those dwellings, while still subject to the burden of the body. "If, then, you endure manfully, as I charged you, you shall come a little later, and be counted worthy of the same dwellings, and obtain the same joy and glory, and be with me forever." Waking up at this, Josaphat had his soul still filled with that light and unspeakable glory, and with much wonder sent up a hymn of thanksgiving to the Master. And he remained to the end, truly accomplishing the angelic manner of life upon earth, and using a harsher asceticism after the passing of the old man—having left the earthly kingdom in the twenty-fifth year of his age and entered the ascetic contest, and having practised in this utter desert for thirty-five years, like one without flesh,

an asceticism beyond man—having first torn many human souls from the soul-destroying serpent and brought them to God saved, and being counted worthy in this of an apostolic grace, and having become a martyr in his resolve, and having confessed Christ with boldness before kings and tyrants, and shown himself a most loud-voiced herald of his greatness; and again, having wrestled down many spirits of wickedness in the desert, and prevailed over all by the power of Christ, and richly shared in the gift and grace from above—from then on he had the eye of his soul cleansed of all earthly mist, and foresaw the things to come as present, and Christ was to him in place of all: Christ he longed for, Christ he saw as present, the beauty of Christ he beheld continually as in a mirror, according to the Prophet who says: "I foresaw the Lord before me always, for he is at my right hand that I should not be shaken"; and again: "My soul cleaved after you; and your right hand upheld me." For his soul truly cleaved after Christ, joined to him with an unbreakable union. He did not turn away from this wonderful labour, did not alter the rule of his own asceticism, from beginning to end, keeping his zeal equal from a younger age to such great age, but rather advancing day by day to a higher virtue and being counted worthy of a purer contemplation. So indeed, having lived such a life, and rendered to the one who called him a labour so worthy of his calling,

having crucified the world to himself and himself to the world, he departs in peace to the God of peace, and goes forth to the Master ever longed for, and is presented before the face of the Lord immediately and purely, and is adorned with the crown of glory from that other world already prepared for him, and is counted worthy to see Christ, to be with Christ, to exult continually in the beauty of Christ; into whose hands committing his own soul, he passed over into the land of the living, where is the sound of those who keep festival, where is the dwelling of those who rejoice. But as for his precious body, a certain holy man who made his dwelling near him—who once also showed him the road to Barlaam—being instructed by some divine revelation, comes at the very hour of his perfection, and, having honoured him with sacred hymns, and poured out tears as a token of his longing for him, and performed all the rest of the things customary for Christians, laid him in the tomb of his father Barlaam. For it was fitting that the bodies should be together, of those whose souls were to abide forever with one another. And, persuaded by the command of a certain most awesome being who strongly enjoined it in a dream,

the hermit who buried him reaches the palace of the Indians, and coming to king Barachias, makes known to him all the matters concerning Barlaam and this blessed Josaphat. And he, without delay, goes himself with a force of a crowd, and stands at the cave, and beholds the tomb, and, having wept most warmly over it, raises the covering. And he sees both Barlaam and Josaphat with their limbs lying in order, and their bodies in no way altered from their former complexion, but whole and exactly sound, together with their garments. These holy dwellings of the holy souls, then, sending forth much fragrance and showing nothing at all unpleasant, the king, placing them in precious caskets, carries away to his own homeland. And when what had happened fell upon the ears of the people, a multitude beyond number streamed together from all the cities and the surrounding country for the veneration and viewing of those blessed bodies. Hence indeed, having sung the sacred hymns over them, and lit lamps in eager honour—fittingly, one might say, and very suitably there were lights about the sons and heirs of the light—they laid them, splendidly and magnificently together, in the church which Josaphat had raised up from its very foundations. And many wonders and healings, both in the carrying away and in the laying down,

and in the times that followed, the Lord worked through his holy servants. And king Barachias and all the crowd saw the works of power that came about through them; and many of the surrounding nations, sick with unbelief and ignorance of God, believed through the signs that came about at the tomb. And all who saw and heard of the angel-imitating life of Josaphat and his fervent longing for God from his tenderest years marvelled, glorifying God in all things—God who ever works together with those who love him and rewards them with the greatest gifts. Thus far the end of the present account, which I have set down from honourable men who handed it down to me without falsehood. And may it be granted to us, who read and hear this account profitable to the soul, to be counted worthy of the portion of those who have pleased the Lord, by the prayers and intercessions of the blessed Barlaam and Josaphat, of whom the account speaks, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong honour, power, majesty, and magnificence, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and ever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen"
